title: Dimension Free Theorems in Geometry
summary: Maurey’s empirical method gives dimension-free convex approximation. Gaussian projections preserve distances and approximate supporting half-spaces for finite point sets.
body: Mars-Dingdang · Original notes dated April 13, 2026 Many geometric bounds depend on the ambient dimension. For example, Carathéodory’s theorem guarantees that any point in the convex hull of a set in \(\mathbb R^n\) can be represented using at most \(n+1\) of its points. When the set lies in the Euclidean unit ball, allowing an error of \(\varepsilon\) reduces the required number to \(\lceil\varepsilon^{-2}\rceil\), independently of the dimension. This approximation is useful in the analysis of algorithms for high-dimensional data. In these notes we use Maurey’s empirical method to obtain that approximation, count the resulting cover of a polytope, and turn the cover into a volume bound. Then we use the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma to preserve distances and approximate supporting half-spaces under a linear map. Carathéodory’s theoremConvex combinations and convex hullsA convex combination of \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb R^n\) is a sum \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\). The convex hull of \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the set of all its finite convex combinations: \[\operatorname{conv}(T)= \left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i: x_i\in T,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,\ k\ge1\right\}.\] Theorem (Carathéodory). Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(T)\) is a convex combination of at most \(n+1\) points from \(T\). Proof. Write \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\), dropping zero coefficients. If \(m>n+1\), the \(m-1\) vectors \(x_2-x_1,\ldots,x_m-x_1\) are linearly dependent. Choose coefficients \(c_2,\ldots,c_m\), not all zero, with \(\sum_{i=2}^m c_i(x_i-x_1)=0\). Setting \(\mu_1=-\sum_{i=2}^m c_i\) and \(\mu_i=c_i\) for \(i\ge2\) gives \[\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i x_i=0.\] Since the \(\mu_i\) sum to zero and are not all zero, some are positive. Take \[\alpha=\min_{\mu_i>0}\frac{\lambda_i}{\mu_i}.\] The new coefficients \(\lambda_i-\alpha\mu_i\) are nonnegative and sum to one. They represent the same \(x\), and at least one is zero. Repeat until at most \(n+1\) coefficients remain. \(\square\) The bound is tight. The origin and the \(n\) standard basis vectors form an \(n\)-simplex. Each point in its interior has all \(n+1\) barycentric coordinates positive. Approximate Carathéodory by independent samplingTheorem. Suppose \(T\subseteq B_2^n\), the unit Euclidean ball. For every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(T)\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), there are \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in T\), with repetition allowed, such that \[\left\|x-\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^k x_j\right\|_2\le \frac1{\sqrt{k}}.\] Proof. Write \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i z_i\) and define a random vector \(Z\) by sampling \(z_i\) with probability \(\lambda_i\). Then \(\mathbb E Z=x\). Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k\) be independent copies of \(Z\). Cross terms have expectation zero, so \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E\left\|\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^k Z_j-x\right\|_2^2 &=\frac1{k^2}\sum_{j=1}^k\mathbb E\|Z_j-x\|_2^2\\ &=\frac{\mathbb E\|Z\|_2^2-\|x\|_2^2}{k} \le \frac1k. \end{aligned}\] At least one sample attains squared error at most \(1/k\). This is Maurey’s empirical method. \(\square\) Figure 1. The empirical mean approximates a point in a three-dimensional convex hull. Tightness. For \(1\le k\le n\), take \(T=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}\) and \(x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\). If \(u=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_j x_j\) is a convex combination from \(T\), merge coefficients on repeated points. Write \(u=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i e_i\), with \(\sum_i a_i=1\) and at most \(k\) nonzero entries. Then \[\|x-u\|_2^2 =\sum_{i=1}^n\left(a_i-\frac1n\right)^2 =\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2-\frac1n \ge \frac1k-\frac1n.\] The last step is Cauchy–Schwarz. Equality is attained by placing mass \(1/k\) on \(k\) distinct basis vectors. Thus even arbitrary convex weights cannot improve the \(k^{-1/2}\) order when \(n\) is large compared with \(k\). Covering a polytope and bounding its volumeLet \(P\subseteq B_2^n\) be a polytope with \(N\) vertices, and let \(k\ge1\) be an integer. Every point in \(P\) is within \(1/\sqrt{k}\) of the average of \(k\) vertices. Taking all ordered choices gives at most \(N^k\) centers. The order of the vertices has no effect on the average. Counting the possible multiplicities \(c_1,\ldots,c_N\ge0\) with \(\sum_i c_i=k\) gives a smaller upper bound by stars and bars: \[M\le \binom{N+k-1}{k}.\] Several multiplicity vectors can give the same center, which only reduces the cover size. Figure 2. A cover of a three-dimensional polytope by balls centered on averages of vertices. For a cover by \(M\) balls of radius \(1/\sqrt{k}\), volume subadditivity gives \[\left(\frac{\operatorname{Vol}(P)}{\operatorname{Vol}(B_2^n)}\right)^{1/n} \le \frac{M^{1/n}}{\sqrt{k}}.\] A first volume bound. With \(M=N^k\), \[\frac{\operatorname{Vol}(P)}{\operatorname{Vol}(B_2^n)} \le \left(3\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{n}}\right)^n.\] For \(N=1\) the volume is zero. When \(n<9\log N\), the right side exceeds one, which suffices since \(P\subseteq B_2^n\). Otherwise take \(k=\lceil n/(2\log N)\rceil\). Then \[k^{-1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{2\log N}{n}},\qquad N^{k/n}\le e^{1/2}N^{1/n}\le e^{11/18}.\] Now \(\sqrt2\,e^{11/18}<3\). \(\square\) A combinatorial estimate. For integers \(1\le k\le m\), \[\left(\frac{m}{k}\right)^k \le\binom{m}{k} \le\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{m}{j} \le\left(\frac{em}{k}\right)^k.\] For the first inequality, each factor \((m-i)/(k-i)\) in the product for \(\binom{m}{k}\) is at least \(m/k\). For the last, take \(t=k/m\in(0,1]\). Since \(t^j\ge t^k\) for \(j\le k\), \[\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{m}{j} \le t^{-k}(1+t)^m \le t^{-k}e^{mt}=\left(\frac{em}{k}\right)^k.\] Theorem (Carl–Pajor volume bound). If \(P\) is full-dimensional and has \(N\) vertices, then \[\frac{\operatorname{Vol}(P)}{\operatorname{Vol}(B_2^n)} \le \left(23\sqrt{\frac{\log(eN/n)}{n}}\right)^n.\] If \(P\) is lower-dimensional, its \(n\)-dimensional volume is zero. Proof. Full dimension implies \(N\ge n+1\). Write \(L=\log(eN/n)>1\). If \(n<2L\), the bound follows from \(P\subseteq B_2^n\). Otherwise take \(k=\lceil n/(2L)\rceil\). Then \(n/(2L)\le k\le n/L\le n\), so \[M\le\binom{N+k-1}{k}\le\left(\frac{2eN}{k}\right)^k.\] Using \(2eN/k\le 4eNL/n\) and \(k/n\le1/L\), we obtain \[\log(M^{1/n}) \le \frac{\log 4+L+\log L}{L} \le \log 4+1+1/e<2.76.\] Here \(\log L/L\le1/e\) for \(L\ge1\). Thus \(M^{1/n}<16\), while \(1/\sqrt{k}\le\sqrt{2L/n}\). Their product is bounded by \(23\sqrt{L/n}\). \(\square\) The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemmaTheorem. For \(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(n\ge2\), any set of \(n\) points in \(\mathbb R^d\) admits a linear map \(f\colon\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\) such that \[(1-\varepsilon)\|x-y\|_2^2 \le\|f(x)-f(y)\|_2^2 \le(1+\varepsilon)\|x-y\|_2^2\] for every pair of points, provided \(k\ge8\log n/\varepsilon^2\). Proof. Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}\) have independent \(\mathcal N(0,1/k)\) entries. For any fixed nonzero \(v\), \[X=\frac{k\|Av\|_2^2}{\|v\|_2^2}\sim\chi_k^2.\] Its moment generating function is \((1-2t)^{-k/2}\) for \(t<1/2\). Applying Markov’s inequality to \(e^{tX}\) with \(t=(r-1)/(2r)\) gives the upper tail when \(r>1\) and the lower tail when \(0<r<1\): \[\begin{aligned} \Pr(X\ge kr)&\le e^{-\frac k2(r-1-\log r)} &&(r>1),\\ \Pr(X\le kr)&\le e^{-\frac k2(r-1-\log r)} &&(0<r<1). \end{aligned}\] To obtain the stated constant, set \(s=\operatorname{arctanh}(\varepsilon)/\varepsilon\) and choose \(f(x)=Ax/\sqrt{s}\). The two thresholds for \(X/k\) are \(r_\pm=s(1\pm\varepsilon)\). We have \(r_+>1\) and \(0<r_-<1\) by bounding the integrand in \(\operatorname{arctanh}\varepsilon=\int_0^\varepsilon(1-t^2)^{-1}\,dt\). Since \(r_+-r_-=2s\varepsilon=\log(r_+/r_-)\), the two rate terms \(r_\pm-1-\log r_\pm\) are equal. Each is their average: \[s-1-\log s-\tfrac12\log(1-\varepsilon^2)\ge\tfrac12\varepsilon^2.\] Thus each fixed pair fails with probability at most \(2e^{-k\varepsilon^2/4}\). A union bound over the \(\binom n2\) pairs gives a failure probability at most \((n-1)/n<1\) when \(k\ge8\log n/\varepsilon^2\). \(\square\) Figure 3. The two Gaussian projections shown here go from 3D through 283D to 2D. The final panel illustrates the geometry. The theorem’s dimension bound determines when a uniform distortion guarantee applies. For fixed distortion, the order \(\log n\) is necessary for some sets of \(n\) points, even if the embedding may be nonlinear. Exercise 4 gives a packing argument. Approximate supporting half-spaces after projectionSuppose \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a convex body containing the unit ball, and \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\partial K\). The points lie on supporting hyperplanes in the original space. Under a suitable linear map to dimension \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2m))\), we can place the images inside a convex body whose boundary stays within \(O((1+D^2)\varepsilon)\) of each image, where \(D=\operatorname{diam}K\). We can also keep the projected supporting directions with a comparable one-sided error. Projection onto a closed convex set. If \(C\) is nonempty, closed and convex, every \(y\) has a unique closest point \(x\in C\). A minimizing sequence for \(\|y-z\|_2\) is bounded and has a subsequence converging in \(C\). Uniqueness follows because for two different minimizers, the squared distance to their midpoint is strictly less than the common minimum. The closest point is characterized by \[\langle y-x,z-x\rangle\le0\qquad(z\in C).\] Indeed, for \(0\le t\le1\), the segment \(x+t(z-x)\) belongs to \(C\). The right derivative of \(\|y-x-t(z-x)\|_2^2\) at \(t=0\) must be nonnegative, which gives the inequality. Conversely, expanding \(\|y-z\|_2^2\) shows it is at least \(\|y-x\|_2^2\). Supporting hyperplane at a boundary point. Given \(x\in\partial K\), take \(y_\ell\notin K\) with \(y_\ell\to x\). If \(z_\ell\) is the closest point in \(K\) to \(y_\ell\), then \(\|y_\ell-z_\ell\|_2\le\|y_\ell-x\|_2\), so \(z_\ell\to x\). A subsequence of the unit vectors \((z_\ell-y_\ell)/\|z_\ell-y_\ell\|_2\) converges to a unit vector \(n\). The projection inequality then gives \(\langle z-x,n\rangle\ge0\) for every \(z\in K\). Thus \(n\) is an inward normal of a supporting hyperplane through \(x\). Preservation argument. Let \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). Choose a unit inward normal \(n_i\) at each \(x_i\) and put \(y_i=x_i+n_i\). Apply Johnson–Lindenstrauss to the set \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_m\}\). Write \(x'_i=f(x_i)\) and \(n'_i=f(n_i)\). For each \(i,j\) the three squared distances of the triangle \(x_i,y_i,x_j\) are preserved within factors \(1\pm\varepsilon\). Polarization gives \[\begin{aligned} \langle n'_i,x'_j-x'_i\rangle &=\tfrac12\bigl(\|f(y_i-x_i)\|_2^2+\|f(x_j-x_i)\|_2^2-\|f(y_i-x_j)\|_2^2\bigr)\\ &\ge (1+\varepsilon)\langle n_i,x_j-x_i\rangle -\varepsilon\bigl(1+\|x_j-x_i\|_2^2\bigr)\\ &\ge -(1+D^2)\varepsilon. \end{aligned}\] Set \(C_D=1+D^2\). Each \(x'_j\) is strictly inside every half-space \[H_i=\{z:\langle z-x'_i,n'_i\rangle\ge -(C_D+1)\varepsilon\}.\] Intersect the \(H_i\) with a closed ball large enough to contain all \(x'_j\) in its interior. This gives a compact convex body \(K'\) with nonempty interior. In direction \(n'_i\), its actual supporting plane is attained at the minimum of \(z\mapsto\langle z-x'_i,n'_i\rangle\) on \(K'\). That minimum lies between \(-(C_D+1)\varepsilon\) and \(0\) because \(K'\subseteq H_i\) and \(x'_i\in K'\). Since \(\|n'_i\|_2\ge\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}>1/2\), the plane is within \(2(C_D+1)\varepsilon\) of \(x'_i\). The segment from \(x'_i\) to its orthogonal projection onto the plane meets \(\partial K'\) no later than it meets the plane. This yields the desired distance bound. Normalizing \(n'_i\) to unit length changes the half-space error by at most a factor of two. \(\square\) Exercises1. Independent sets by the probabilistic methodLet \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and \(d(v)\) the degree of \(v\). Prove that \(G\) has an independent set of size at least \(\sum_{v\in V}1/(d(v)+1)\). Hint. Order the vertices uniformly at random and keep those that come before every neighbor. If \(|V|=n\) and \(|E|=m\), deduce a lower bound of \(n^2/(2m+n)\). 2. Where the mass of a Euclidean ball liesLet \(X\) be uniform in \(B_2^n\), so \(\Pr(X\in A)=\operatorname{Vol}(A)/\operatorname{Vol}(B_2^n)\) for measurable \(A\subseteq B_2^n\). Prove that the shell \(1-5/n\le\|X\|_2\le1\) contains at least \(99\%\) of the mass. Prove that \(\mathbb E\|X\|_2=n/(n+1)\). 3. The chi-square distribution and random projectionLet \(X=\sum_{i=1}^k Z_i^2\), where the \(Z_i\) are independent standard Gaussians. Compute \(\mathbb EX\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\). Derive \(\mathbb E e^{tX}=(1-2t)^{-k/2}\) for \(t<1/2\). Use the moment generating function and the logarithm’s Taylor bound to show that for \(0<\varepsilon<1\), \[\Pr\bigl(|X-\mathbb EX|>\varepsilon\mathbb EX\bigr) \le2\exp\left(-\frac{k}{4}(\varepsilon^2-\varepsilon^3)\right).\] Show also that the probability is at most \(2e^{-Ck\varepsilon^2}\) for an absolute \(C>0\) over this range. Hint. For the second bound, use \(\varepsilon-\log(1+\varepsilon)=\int_0^\varepsilon t/(1+t)\,dt\).4. Combine this estimate with a union bound to derive the Johnson–Lindenstrauss dimension order. 4. A dimension lower bound by packing If \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^k\) satisfy \(1<\|z_i-z_j\|_2\le2\) for all \(i\ne j\), show that \(n\le5^k\). Hint. Pack disjoint open balls of radius \(1/2\) around the points inside a ball of radius \(5/2\). Find \(n\) vectors in \(\mathbb R^n\) for which no map into \(\mathbb R^k\) preserves every distance to relative error \(0.01\) when \(k<\tfrac12\log n\). Hint. Try the standard basis vectors and use part 1. 5. Characterizing a closest pointGiven a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) and \(x\in C\), prove that \(x\) is the projection of \(y\) onto \(C\) if and only if \(\langle y-x,z-x\rangle\le0\) for all \(z\in C\). Try proving both directions before checking the argument above. 6. A deterministic greedy constructionLet \(T\subseteq B_2^n\) and \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(T)\). Construct a sequence \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\in T\) such that for every \(k\ge1\), its empirical mean \(p_k=k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^k x_i\) satisfies \[\|x-p_k\|_2^2\le 4/k.\] Hint. Set \(e_k=x-p_k\). Express \(x\) as a convex combination from \(T\) and choose \(x_{k+1}\) with \(\langle e_k,x-x_{k+1}\rangle\le0\). Then bound the change in the squared norm of \(ke_k\). The choice of a point by a linear objective also appears in Frank–Wolfe optimization. In this exercise the iterates retain a sparse convex representation. 7. Sparse strategies in a large zero-sum gameLet \(A\in[-1,1]^{m\times n}\) be the payoff matrix and let \(y\in\Delta_n\) be a mixed strategy for the column player. Here \(\Delta_n=\{u\in\mathbb R^n:u_i\ge0,\ \sum_i u_i=1\}\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), show that a strategy \(\widehat y\in\Delta_n\) supported on at most \[k=\left\lceil\frac{2\log(2m)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\rceil\] columns can satisfy \(\|A\widehat y-Ay\|_\infty\le\varepsilon\). Hint. Sample columns independently according to \(y\). Apply Hoeffding’s inequality coordinate by coordinate and count the possible payoff deviations. 8. Coresets for an SVM marginLet \(P,Q\subset B_2^n\) be two point sets whose convex hulls attain a minimum distance \(\gamma>0\). Prove that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there are subsets \(P'\subseteq P\) and \(Q'\subseteq Q\), each of size at most \(\lceil4/\varepsilon^2\rceil\), such that \[\gamma\le\min_{\substack{p\in\operatorname{conv}(P')\\q\in\operatorname{conv}(Q')}}\|p-q\|_2 \le\gamma+\varepsilon.\] Hint. Approximate one closest pair \(p_\star,q_\star\) by averages of \(k\) points from the respective sets, with \(k=\lceil4/\varepsilon^2\rceil\), and apply the triangle inequality. The result gives a dimension-independent coreset for the optimal margin value.

title: ML 14: Model Interpretability and Feature Attribution
summary: Derive the weighted fit in LIME and prove completeness for Integrated Gradients and efficiency for Shapley values.
body:
Derive the weighted fit in LIME and prove completeness for Integrated Gradients and efficiency for Shapley values. The model is locally flat at the input, but the path from the baseline crosses a segment of slope one. Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic ExplanationsLecture 14, slides 4–12. Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin, Sections 3.1–3.3. A human-readable explanation should fit the reader’s working memory and state a claim that can be checked. A sufficiently large decision tree can be difficult to inspect. Attribution methods simplify a single prediction to a collection of feature contributions. The feature representation, the score to explain, and the reference used to measure contribution all belong to the problem definition. For an input \(x\), sample nearby or masked inputs \(z_j\) and compute the black box’s scores \(f(z_j)\). Fit an interpretable model \(g\) on human-readable representations \(z'_j\) via \[\min_g \sum_j \pi_x(z_j)(f(z_j)-g(z'_j))^2+\Omega(g).\] In the slide formulation, \(\pi_x(z)=\exp(-D(x,z)^2/\sigma^2)\). It emphasizes nearby inputs according to the selected distance \(D\). A mask \(z'\) might encode present words in a text or visible superpixels in an image. The inverse mapping from the mask to an input determines what the black box actually evaluates. The penalty \(\Omega\) limits complexity, for example the number of nonzero coefficients. On a fixed feature set and without the penalty, write the design as \(A\), weights as a diagonal matrix \(W\), and responses as \(f\). Differentiating \((A eta-f)^	op W(A eta-f)\) gives the normal equation \(A^	op WA eta=A^	op Wf\). Kernel width and the distribution of perturbed examples determine the fitting problem. For a direction \(h\), the derivative of the weighted squared loss is \(2h^	op A^	op W(A eta-f)\). Its quadratic term in \(h\) is \(\|W^{1/2}Ah\|^2\), so the normal equation suffices for a minimizer, and full column rank of \(W^{1/2}A\) gives uniqueness. A fixed support lets us use this unconstrained calculation on just its active columns. An \(\ell_1\) penalty is a soft surrogate for selecting at most \(k\) nonzeros and changes the optimum; it is not an algebraic conversion of the hard constraint. A model flat near \(x\) can have near-zero fitted slopes even when its output differs substantially from a meaningful baseline. For example, \(\operatorname{ReLU}(x)\) is zero in a neighborhood of \(x=-5\), while the output changes by one relative to baseline \(x'=1\). The slide’s black-image example sets an explicit comparison point. Two different baselines can yield different allocations because they define different output differences and paths. Integrated Gradients along a baseline pathLecture 14, slides 12–16. Sundararajan, Taly, and Yan, Sections 2–4. Set \(\gamma(t)=x'+t(x-x')\) for baseline \(x'\). The attribution for coordinate \(i\) is \[\operatorname{IG}_i(x;x')=(x_i-x'_i)\int_0^1\partial_iF(\gamma(t))\,dt.\] When \(F\circ\gamma\) is absolutely continuous and the chain rule holds almost everywhere along the path, summing the attributions gives \[\sum_i\operatorname{IG}_i =\int_0^1
abla F(\gamma(t))^	op (x-x')\,dt =\int_0^1 (F\circ\gamma)'(t)\,dt=F(x)-F(x').\] This is completeness. If only coordinate \(i\) differs from baseline and the output changes, every other factor \(x_j-x'_j\) is zero, so all nonzero difference is assigned to \(i\) (sensitivity a). If \(F\) is independent of coordinate \(i\), its partial derivative there is zero wherever defined, and the attributed integral is zero (sensitivity b). Implementation invariance follows on paths where the relevant derivatives exist almost everywhere: any two mathematical implementations of the same function have the same partial derivatives at those points. An autodiff choice at a kink along the whole path needs special care. A componentwise finite-difference ratio cannot in general be propagated like a Jacobian: there is no single secant gradient canonically determined by two points in multiple dimensions. Linearity follows by taking partial derivatives and integrals of \(aF_1+bF_2\). For symmetry, suppose swapping features \(i\) and \(j\) leaves \(F\) unchanged, and the baseline and input each have equal coordinates in the two positions. At every point on the straight path those coordinates agree. Differentiating the equality under the swap gives \(\partial_iF=\partial_jF\) on that path wherever both derivatives exist. The prefactors also agree, so both attributions are equal. For \(F(x)=\min\{\max(x,0),1\}\) from baseline 0 to input 2, the path lies in the unit-slope region for half its duration. The contribution is \(2(1/2)=1\) despite zero endpoint derivative. Numerical quadrature can be checked by the residual in completeness. Which single path preserves symmetry?The slide’s example uses \(F(u,v)=uv\) from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\). A path moving \(u\) first and then \(v\) attributes all one to \(v\), because the integral for \(u\) runs where \(v=0\). A straight path gives \((1/2,1/2)\). More generally, on the normalized two-coordinate problem, a continuous coordinatewise-monotone, piecewise smooth single path preserves symmetry for every smooth symmetric \(F\) only if it stays on the diagonal, up to reparameterization. This is the symmetry test underlying the paper’s path result. To see necessity, path attribution to the first coordinate is \(\int_0^1 F_u(u,v(u))\,du\), where \(v(u)\) is the height of the path at horizontal position \(u\) for almost every \(u\). Vertical segments have zero first-coordinate contribution. Its difference from the diagonal attribution is \[\int_0^1\int_u^{v(u)}F_{uv}(u,s)\,ds\,du.\] If the path goes above the diagonal, there is an open region with \(u<s<v(u)\), away from vertical endpoints. Its reflection across the diagonal cannot lie in the region between path and diagonal: monotonicity gives \(v(s)\ge v(u)>s\), so the reflected height \(u<s\) is below both. Pick a smooth nonnegative bump within this open region and add its reflected bump. Let this symmetric sum be \(F_{uv}\), integrating once in each variable from zero to obtain a smooth symmetric \(F\). The double integral is strictly positive, while its reflected bump gives no contribution. A path below the diagonal is treated by swapping coordinates. By completeness the two attributions deviate in opposite directions from their equal diagonal shares. For the normalized problem from \(\mathbf0\) to \(\mathbf1\) in \(n\) dimensions, apply the same argument to every pair of coordinates and choose test functions depending only on that pair. If any projected pair leaves the diagonal, its two attributions differ for one such symmetric test function. Thus all coordinate paths agree and the full path is \(\gamma(t)=\lambda(t)\mathbf1\) for a common nondecreasing parameter \(\lambda\). Changing variables in the line integrals gives exactly Integrated Gradients. For inputs with unequal coordinate increments, the same characterization applies to single-path rules that are equivariant under independently translating and scaling the coordinate intervals. Normalize each nonconstant coordinate to \([0,1]\), use the pairwise argument with common endpoints, then undo the normalization. A constant coordinate gives zero under a coordinatewise-monotone path. This states the hypotheses under which the straight path is determined by the symmetry argument. Averaging several paths can also preserve symmetry, as the permutation construction below illustrates. Shapley values as averages over permutationsLecture 14, slides 18–21. Lundberg and Lee, Sections 2–4. Let \(v(S)\) be the prediction-related value for a coalition of available features \(S\) from feature set \(N\). The Shapley attribution is \[\phi_i=\sum_{S\subseteq N\setminus\{i\}}  rac{|S|!(|N|-|S|-1)!}{|N|!}\,[v(S\cup\{i\})-v(S)].\] The coefficient is the probability that exactly \(S\) precedes \(i\) in a uniform random permutation: order these predecessors arbitrarily, then order all successors. For any fixed permutation, the marginal contributions telescope to \(v(N)-v(\varnothing)\). Averaging proves efficiency. Symmetric participants exchange positions through a bijection of permutations and hence receive the same average. A dummy with zero marginal contribution receives zero, and linearity follows by taking expectations. For a pure interaction \(v_T(S)=\mathbf1\{T\subseteq S\}\), an element of \(T\) receives the unit contribution exactly when it is last among \(T\). Its attribution is therefore \(1/|T|\). These pure interactions also span all games with \(v(\varnothing)=0\) by subset inclusion–exclusion, which gives uniqueness under these axioms. SHAP specifies a value function and an approximation or evaluation procedure. Examples include filling missing features with a fixed baseline, integrating over background features, or conditioning the missing features on observed ones. Correlation means these choices answer different questions. In a conditional game, a feature can get credit for information about another feature on which the model directly depends. Why Shapley weights give the unique additive attributionWrite \(v(\varnothing)=0\) after subtracting the baseline. For nonempty \(T\subseteq[d]\), let \(u_T(S)=\mathbf1\{T\subseteq S\}\). Every set function has a unique expansion \(v=\sum_{T
e\varnothing}a_Tu_T\): recursively take \(a_T=v(T)-\sum_{U\subsetneq T}a_U\) starting with singletons. For the game \(u_T\), the null-player axiom gives zero to players outside \(T\) and symmetry forces equal shares inside \(T\). Efficiency makes those shares sum to one, so each player in \(T\) gets \(1/|T|\). The additivity and homogeneity axioms then determine every share for \(v\). The permutation formula yields exactly these values: in \(u_T\), the marginal contribution is one precisely when the player is last among the elements of \(T\), an event of probability \(1/|T|\). This proves existence and uniqueness under the axioms. The last slide shows why efficiency determines the sum of the attributions without identifying the score change when one feature is removed. The displayed word “very” is attributed 19.9 percentage points, while its deletion changes the displayed prediction from 97.8% to 88.7%, a 9.1-point difference. The deletion is one coalition’s marginal contribution, whereas Shapley averages all predecessor coalitions. A smaller example is \(v(\{1,2\})=1\) and \(v(S)=0\) otherwise: each attribution is \(1/2\), even though removing either feature from the full coalition loses the entire unit. For two features the argument gives \[\phi_1=	frac12(v(\{1\})-v(\varnothing))+	frac12(v(\{1,2\})-v(\{2\})).\] A symmetric interaction visible only when both features are present is divided in half. The definition of \(v(S)\) determines which interaction is being explained: averaging missing features independently and taking a conditional expectation can produce different coalition values. ChallengeFor \(F(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2 x_2\), compare Integrated Gradients and baseline Shapley at \((2,3)\) relative to \((0,0)\). Explain the discrepancy. Show solution Along \((2t,3t)\) the partials are \(12t^2\) and \(4t^2\), giving Integrated Gradients \((8,4)\). The baseline game is zero unless both features are present, in which case its value is 12. Each variable is last in one of the two permutations and receives attribution 6. Along the straight path the two factors of \(x_1\) give it twice the attribution of \(x_2\). In the baseline game both features are equally necessary, and arrival order splits the payoff evenly. Both totals are 12. Second challenge. For \(F(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2x_2\), compare Integrated Gradients from zero with Shapley values from zero masking. Show solution to the second challenge On the straight path \(tx\), the first partial derivative is \(2t^2x_1x_2\) and the second is \(t^2x_1^2\). The Integrated Gradients are \((2/3,1/3)F(x)\) after integrating \(t^2\) from zero to one. Under zero masking neither feature alone yields any value and the two-feature coalition yields \(F(x)\), so Shapley gives \((1/2,1/2)F(x)\). Both satisfy completeness, with different allocations of the interaction because one measures increments along a continuous path and the other averages discrete coalition orders. Research challenge — why KernelSHAP’s regression uses that kernelLet \(N\) have \(n\ge2\) features, and assume \(v(\varnothing)=0\). Fit an additive model \(g_\phi(S)=\sum_{i\in S}\phi_i\) by minimizing the coalition residuals \[\sum_{0<|S|<n} w_{|S|} igl(g_\phi(S)-v(S) igr)^2,\qquad w_s= rac{n-1}{ inom ns\,s(n-s)},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n\phi_i=v(N).\] Prove that the unique minimizer gives the exact Shapley values. Use the unanimity games \(u_T(S)=\mathbf1\{T\subseteq S\}\) and derive why summing over coalition sizes with these weights yields the factor \(1/|T|\). Show research challenge solution The quadratic form is positive definite because every singleton is observed with positive weight and its model score is \(\phi_i\). The constraint is feasible, and strict convexity gives a unique minimizer. With the constraint enforced by a Lagrange multiplier, the solution is linear in the vector of game values, including \(v(N)\) on the right of the constraint. It suffices to prove the result for \(u_T\), since those games span all normalized games. Write \(t=|T|\). The candidate is \(\phi_i=1/t\) on \(T\) and zero outside. It is feasible. At a constrained optimum all coordinates of the objective gradient agree. The candidate and the objective are symmetric separately within \(T\) and its complement, so it remains to compare the gradients of \(i\in T\) and \(j
otin T\) when \(t<n\). Coalitions containing both or neither cancel in that difference. Pair a coalition of size \(s\) containing \(i\) and omitting \(j\) with the coalition obtained by swapping them. The model difference in each pair is \(1/t\). The value difference is one exactly when all \(t-1\) remaining elements of \(T\) lie among the \(s-1\) other members. Its mean over all such pairs is \[p_{s,t}= rac{ inom{s-1}{t-1}}{ inom{n-2}{t-1}},\] where the numerator is zero if \(s<t\). There are \( inom{n-2}{s-1}\) pairs, and multiplying this number by the regression weight \(w_s\) gives \(1/n\) for each size. Thus the gradient difference divided by two is \((1/n)\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}(1/t-p_{s,t})\). The identity \(\sum_{s=1}^{n-1} inom{s-1}{t-1}= inom{n-1}{t}\) follows by grouping \(t\)-subsets of \([n-1]\) by their largest element. Therefore \(\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}p_{s,t}=(n-1)/t\) and the gradient difference is zero. When \(T=N\), every gradient coordinate agrees by symmetry. In both cases the candidate is the unique optimum. These \(\phi_i\) agree with the Shapley values on every \(u_T\), so linearity extends the result. In practice there are \(2^n-2\) interior coalitions. Sampling them approximates this regression and need not yield the full-coalition minimizer. Challenge source: Lundberg and Lee, Theorem 2, Shapley kernel. title: ML 13: Hyperparameter Optimization and Resource Allocation
summary: Derive Gaussian-process posteriors, Expected Improvement, and hypergradients, then compare resource allocation under successive halving.
body:
Derive Gaussian-process posteriors, Expected Improvement, and hypergradients, then compare resource allocation under successive halving. The synthetic example picks the unobserved location that maximizes Expected Improvement for a minimization problem. Training and model selectionLecture 13, slides 4–11 and 33. The black-box setting allows discrete choices such as layer count and continuous choices such as learning rate. Each query can require a full training run. The lecture’s egg example has the same structure: the quality measurement comes after trying a combination of boiling time, cooling time, and seasoning. Grid search fixes a schedule, random search draws configurations independently, and Bayesian optimization conditions its next query on earlier outcomes. Hypergradients require a differentiable dependence on the hyperparameter. Bandit allocation can exploit cheaper partial evaluations. The inner procedure produces weights \(w_T(\lambda)\) for hyperparameters \(\lambda\). The outer optimization minimizes \(F(\lambda)=L_{m val}(w_T(\lambda),\lambda)\). Fixed training time and full convergence can rank configurations differently. Random seeds make single runs noisy, so comparisons can use common seeds or repeated runs. Keep the final test set separate from the choice of hyperparameters. A grid with \(m\) values per dimension uses \(m^d\) evaluations. If one coordinate dominates, it tests just \(m\) distinct values for that coordinate. Sampling \(m^d\) configurations from a continuous distribution generally tests a different value each time along that coordinate. Distributions on positive scales that span orders of magnitude are often defined in log space. Gaussian-process predictionLecture 13, slides 12 and 14–20. Rasmussen and Williams, Chapter 2. A Gaussian process is a consistent prior on function values: for any finite list of inputs, the corresponding values form a joint Gaussian vector, with mean given by the mean function and covariance given by the kernel. This finite-vector statement is enough for prediction. Let \(F\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) and observe \(y_j=F(\lambda_j)+e_j\), where independent \(e_j\sim N(0,\sigma_n^2)\). Define \(K_{ij}=k(\lambda_i,\lambda_j)\), \(\Sigma=K+\sigma_n^2I\), and \(k_\star=(k(\lambda_i,\lambda_\star))_i\). Consider the residual \[r=F(\lambda_\star)-m(\lambda_\star)-k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}(y-m_\Lambda).\] The cross-covariance of \(F(\lambda_\star)\) with \(y\) is \(k_\star^	op\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(y)=\Sigma\). Hence \(\operatorname{Cov}(r,y)=k_\star^	op-k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma=0\). The jointly Gaussian pair \((r,y)\) has a block-diagonal covariance matrix, so its joint characteristic function factors and \(r\) is independent of \(y\). The residual variance expansion subtracts \(2k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}k_\star\) through the cross term and adds \(k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma\Sigma^{-1}k_\star\) through the predictor’s variance. This yields \[\mu_\star=m(\lambda_\star)+k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}(y-m_\Lambda),\qquad s_\star^2=k(\lambda_\star,\lambda_\star)-k_\star^	op\Sigma^{-1}k_\star.\] To predict a future noisy observation, add \(\sigma_n^2\) to the latent variance. Expected ImprovementFor a reference value \(b\) to beat in minimization, define \(\mathrm{EI}=\mathbb E[(b-F)_+]\). Write \(F=\mu+s Z\) for standard normal \(Z\), and set \(z=(b-\mu)/s\). The integral is \[\mathrm{EI}=\int_{-\infty}^z(b-\mu-su)\phi(u)\,du =(b-\mu)\Phi(z)+s\phi(z),\] because \(\phi'(u)=-u\phi(u)\). When \(s=0\), the limit is \((b-\mu)_+\). Low mean and high uncertainty can both make a point worth evaluating. Noisy evaluations may favor basing \(b\) on predicted latent values. The successive plots on slides 14–20 show this closed loop: evaluate the maximizer of the current acquisition function, insert the observation into the GP, then recompute the mean, uncertainty, and acquisition. Low posterior variance near evaluated points makes large improvement there less likely. Sequential conditioning is the reason the simplest version needs a different acquisition rule for parallel batches. Differentiating through the training trajectoryLecture 13, slides 21–31. Maclaurin, Duvenaud, and Adams, Sections 2.1–2.3. For learning rate \(\eta\) and \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta
abla L_{m train}(w_t)\), assume \(w_0\) is independent of \(\eta\). Differentiating both the multiplication by \(\eta\) and the gradient’s input gives \[u_{t+1}=(I-\eta H_t)u_t-
abla L_{m train}(w_t),\qquad u_t=\partial_\eta w_t,\quad H_t=
abla^2 L_{m train}(w_t),\quad u_0=0.\] The outer derivative is \(
abla_wL_{m val}(w_T,\eta)^	op u_T+\partial_\eta L_{m val}(w_T,\eta)\). For the slides’ two-step least-squares example \(L(w)=\|Xw-y\|^2/2\), let \(g_t=X^	op(Xw_t-y)\) and \(H=X^	op X\). Then \(u_1=-g_0\), so \(u_2=-g_0-g_1+\eta Hg_0\). If the outer objective is \(L(w_2)\) as in the example, the two-step hypergradient is \(g_2^	op(-g_0-g_1+\eta Hg_0)\). Reconstructing momentum SGD and reversing its derivativesUse the fresh velocity in the position update. This convention is consistent with reversing the position before recomputing its gradient. Write \(g_t=
abla_w L_t(w_t,	heta)\), where \(t\) also fixes the batch and other training inputs. The forward map is \[v_{t+1}=\gamma_t v_t-(1-\gamma_t)g_t,\qquad w_{t+1}=w_t+\alpha_t v_{t+1}.\] The update for \(v_{t+1}\) contains an exponentially weighted history of gradients. To recover the previous state in exact arithmetic, compute \(w_t=w_{t+1}-\alpha_t v_{t+1}\), recompute \(g_t\) at \(w_t\), and recover \(v_t=(v_{t+1}+(1-\gamma_t)g_t)/\gamma_t\) for \(\gamma_t
e0\). Let \(a=\partial F/\partial w_{t+1}\) and \(b=\partial F/\partial v_{t+1}\) be column adjoints arriving from future steps. The position update contributes \(a^	op v_{t+1}\) to the derivative with respect to \(\alpha_t\), contributes \(a\) directly to the adjoint for \(w_t\), and changes the velocity adjoint to \(\widetilde b=b+\alpha_t a\). Differentiating the first equation gives the remaining updates: \[ egin{aligned} \partial_{\gamma_t}F&\mathrel{+}=\widetilde b^	op(v_t+g_t),\ \partial_	heta F&\mathrel{+}=-(1-\gamma_t)(D_	heta g_t)^	op\widetilde b,\ a_t&=a-(1-\gamma_t)(D_w g_t)^	op\widetilde b,\qquad b_t=\gamma_t\widetilde b. \end{aligned}\] Initialize with \(a_T=
abla_w F(w_T)\) and \(b_T=0\) if \(F\) is independent of the final velocity. For shared hyperparameters, sum their contributions over steps. In particular, \((D_w g_t)^	op\widetilde b\) is a Hessian-vector product obtained by differentiating \(g_t^	op\widetilde b\) at fixed \(\widetilde b\). A full Hessian is unnecessary. Reversible fixed-point momentum decayFloating-point rounding breaks the exact inverse. Even when only a velocity rounding error is considered, a reverse decay multiplies it by \(1/\gamma_t\). Repeating this for constant \(0<\gamma<1\) can magnify an existing error by \(\gamma^{-T}\). In the paper’s fixed-point scheme, let \(c\) be an integer encoding a velocity coordinate, \(B\ge0\) an information buffer, and \(\gamma=n/d\) with positive integers \(n<d\). Euclidean division writes \(c=dq+r\) with \(0\le r<d\). Put \(S=dB+r\), and divide it as \(S=nB'+a\) with \(0\le a<n\). The new pair is \((c',B')=(nq+a,B')\). Inverting, first divide \(c'\) by \(n\) to recover \(q,a\). Then recover \(S=nB'+a\), divide by \(d\) to get \(B,r\), and set \(c=dq+r\). The final digit \(a\) uses the space left by multiplying \(q\) by \(n\). It frees up roughly \(\log_2 n\) bits per step compared with storing the remainder without this transfer. For constant \(n/d\), \(B'\le(d/n)B+(d-1)/n\). Iterating that inequality gives \(B_T=O((d/n)^T)\), so the buffer needs at most \(T\log_2(d/n)+O(1)\) bits for an integer coordinate, up to the fixed initial/setup cost. At \(\gamma=0.98\), \(\log_2(1/\gamma)\approx0.0291\), compared with 32 bits for a full per-step snapshot of one coordinate. Practical overhead also depends on integer representation, overflow management, and whether the same gradient and batch can be reconstructed. The bit logic reverses the chosen discrete arithmetic. The adjoint equations describe the underlying real-valued training updates. Successive halving and HyperbandLecture 13, slides 34–41. Jamieson and Talwalkar, Algorithm 1, and Li et al., Section 2. The fixed-budget stationary version in the slides begins with \(S_0=[n]\), spends approximately \(B/\log_2 n\) pulls each round, and divides those pulls equally among active arms. It then retains the half with largest empirical reward. For eight arms, slides 36–41 show the first round retaining A3, A5, A6, and A7, the second retaining A5 and A7, and the third selecting A7. The shown fourth value is a check of the final arm, since the elimination algorithm terminates when one arm remains. Allocation in training uses resource levels rather than repeated draws from a fixed reward distribution. Start \(n\) candidates with \(r\) units of resource. Rank their scores, retain roughly a fraction \(1/\eta_{\mathrm{sh}}\), and multiply the resource per survivor by \(\eta_{\mathrm{sh}}\). With 16 candidates, resource 1, and elimination factor 2, the round totals from scratch are \(16,16,16,16,16\) epochs. Continuing from checkpoints makes the increments \(16,8,8,8,8\), totaling 48 epochs. The saving assumes earlier training can be reused. Learning curves that cross can eliminate a slow-starting eventual winner. Hyperband distributes its budget among brackets with different initial candidate counts and starting budgets. In a stationary best-arm model, each configuration \(i\) has reward mean \(\mu_i\). If every arm is sampled \(m\) times with independent rewards in \([0,1]\) and the unique best mean exceeds the others by at least \(\Delta\), Hoeffding bounds the chance of any empirical mean deviating by at least \(\Delta/2\) by \(2n e^{-m\Delta^2/2}\). On the complementary event the empirical best is the genuine best. The same argument yields a conservative guarantee for the slide’s fixed-budget elimination scheme with fresh independent samples. At round \(r\), condition on the entire prior history and on the unique best arm surviving. With \(m_r\) new samples per remaining arm and gap at least \(\Delta\), the probability of any current estimate deviating by at least \(\Delta/2\) is at most \(2|S_r|e^{-m_r\Delta^2/2}\) by a union bound. Otherwise the true best has a strictly higher estimate than every other arm and survives. Sum this bound over the possible round of its first elimination. This bound does not require independence across survival events, only fresh samples within the round. Early-training scores generally evolve with allocation, so a stationary gap guarantee does not transfer automatically. ChallengeLet the inner objective be \(L_{m train}(w,\lambda)=	frac12(w-a)^2+	frac{\lambda}{2}w^2\) and the outer objective \(	frac12(w^\star(\lambda)-b)^2\), with \(a>b>0\) and \(\lambda\ge0\). Derive the exact minimizing regularization and verify the derivative by implicit differentiation. Show solution Stationarity is \((1+\lambda)w^\star=a\), so \(w^\star=a/(1+\lambda)\). It decreases from \(a\) to 0, so the squared loss is minimized when \(w^\star=b\), at \(\lambda=a/b-1\). Implicit differentiation of stationarity gives \((1+\lambda)\partial_\lambda w^\star+w^\star=0\). The hypergradient is \(-(w^\star-b)w^\star/(1+\lambda)\), negative below the optimum and positive above it. Second challenge. Show that Expected Improvement is nondecreasing in predictive standard deviation when the mean and current best are fixed. Show solution to the second challenge Write \(a\) for the incumbent minus the mean in minimization, \(z=a/s\), and \(\mathrm{EI}(s)=a\Phi(z)+s\phi(z)\). Differentiate for \(s>0\). The derivatives through \(z\) cancel because \(\phi'(z)=-z\phi(z)\) and \(a=sz\). Hence \(\mathrm{EI}'(s)=\phi(z)>0\). Continuity at \(s=0\) gives \(\max(a,0)\), so uncertainty increases this acquisition value even at fixed predicted mean. Research challenge — GP-UCB regret from information gainLet \(D\) be a finite domain of \(N\) configurations, and maximize \(f\) drawn from a known GP with \(k(x,x)\le1\). At step \(t\) observe \(y_t=f(x_t)+\epsilon_t\), with independent \(\epsilon_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(\sigma^2>0\). Let \(x_t\) maximize \(\mu_{t-1}(x)+\sqrt{ eta_t}s_{t-1}(x)\), with \( eta_t=2\log(N\pi^2t^2/(3\delta))\) for \(0<\delta<1\). Define \[\gamma_T=\max_{x_{1:T}\in D^T}	frac12\log\det(I+\sigma^{-2}K_T).\] Here \(K_T\) is the covariance matrix at a list of \(T\) points and repeats are allowed. Prove that with probability at least \(1-\delta\), the cumulative regret satisfies \[\sum_{t=1}^T[f(x^\star)-f(x_t)] \le\sqrt{ rac{8T eta_T\gamma_T}{\log(1+\sigma^{-2})}}\] simultaneously for every \(T\ge1\). Show research challenge solution Conditional on the history, the residual at each fixed \(x\) has standard deviation \(s_{t-1}(x)\). When this is positive, a Gaussian tail bounds violation of the interval \(\mu_{t-1}(x)\pm\sqrt{ eta_t}s_{t-1}(x)\) by \(2e^{- eta_t/2}\). At zero variance the interval is exact. This conditional bound also holds unconditionally. A union bound over \(D\) and all \(t\) sums to \(\sum_t 6\delta/(\pi^2t^2)=\delta\). On the common event, optimism gives \(f(x^\star)\le\mu_{t-1}(x_t)+\sqrt{ eta_t}s_{t-1}(x_t)\) and \(f(x_t)\ge\mu_{t-1}(x_t)-\sqrt{ eta_t}s_{t-1}(x_t)\). The instantaneous regret is at most \(2\sqrt{ eta_t}s_{t-1}(x_t)\). Fix any realized list of query locations when forming its covariance matrix. Successive Schur complements of the noisy covariance \(K_T+\sigma^2 I\) give \[\log\det(I+\sigma^{-2}K_T) =\sum_{t=1}^T\log(1+\sigma^{-2}s_{t-1}^2(x_t)).\] This is a deterministic matrix identity at each list, even though the list came from a random adaptive procedure. For a fixed list, half the determinant logarithm is also the mutual information between its latent values and observations, by subtracting the entropy of the independent noise from the entropy of the observations. Since \(s_{t-1}^2(x_t)\in[0,1]\), concavity of \(q\mapsto\log(1+\sigma^{-2}q)\) places it above the chord \(q\log(1+\sigma^{-2})\). Thus the sum of posterior variances is at most \(2\gamma_T/\log(1+\sigma^{-2})\). Cauchy–Schwarz now bounds the squared cumulative regret by \(4T eta_T\sum_t s_{t-1}^2(x_t)\), proving the claim. Minimization follows by using a lower confidence bound or applying this result to \(-f\). Challenge source: Srinivas, Krause, Kakade, and Seeger, Gaussian Process Optimization in the Bandit Setting, Theorem 1 and Lemmas 5.1–5.4. Rasmussen and Williams, Chapter 2, Snoek et al., Section 2, Maclaurin et al., Algorithms 1–3, Jamieson and Talwalkar, Algorithm 1, and Li et al., Section 2. title: ML 12: Robust Learning and Randomized Smoothing
summary: Derive exact robust margins for linear classifiers and prove a Gaussian-smoothing certificate for bounded input changes.
body:
Derive exact robust margins for linear classifiers and prove a Gaussian-smoothing certificate for bounded input changes. A shift in the input changes the probability assigned to either side of the classifier’s decision boundary. Robust risk and the envelope derivativeLecture 12, slides 4–21. The examples motivate measuring model behavior under bounded input changes as well as accuracy on unchanged inputs. A perturbation set \(\Delta\) models allowable input changes. The worst-case training objective is \[\min_	heta\mathbb E_{X,Y}\!\left[\max_{\delta\in\Delta}\ell(f_	heta(X+\delta),Y)ight].\] An \(\ell_\infty\) ball bounds each coordinate change, whereas an \(\ell_2\) ball bounds total squared magnitude. Robustness depends on the selected input metric. For a differentiable inner loss \(g_	heta(\delta)=\ell(f_	heta(x+\delta),y)\), its first-order change is \(
abla_\delta g_	heta(0)^	op\delta\). On the box \(\|\delta\|_\infty\le r\), each coordinate contributes at most \(r|\partial_i g_	heta(0)|\), attained by choosing that coordinate’s sign to match the derivative. This derives the first-order sign rule on slide 11. Its value is exact for the linearized loss. Projected ascent updates a current \(\delta\) and projects it back to \(\Delta\). For the box, the squared Euclidean projection objective separates by coordinates, and each minimizer is a clipping operation. With a nonconcave loss, this generally solves only a local problem. Let \(F(	heta)=\max_{z\in\Delta}g(	heta,z)\), with \(\Delta\) compact and \(g,
abla_	heta g\) continuous. Write \(M(	heta)\) for its set of maximizers. For any \(z\in M(	heta)\), evaluating it at \(	heta+tv\) gives the lower bound \(\liminf_{t\downarrow0}(F(	heta+tv)-F(	heta))/t\ge 
abla_	heta g(	heta,z)^	op v\). For the upper bound choose a maximizer \(z_t\) at \(	heta+tv\). Since \(F(	heta)\ge g(	heta,z_t)\), the difference quotient is bounded above by the directional change in \(g\) at \(z_t\). Compactness gives a convergent subsequence of maximizers, continuity puts its limit in \(M(	heta)\), and the uniform first-order remainder yields \[F'(	heta;v)=\max_{z\in M(	heta)}
abla_	heta g(	heta,z)^	op v.\] For a unique maximizer \(z_\star\), the gradient of \(F\) is \(
abla_	heta g(	heta,z_\star)\). For differentiability, take \(h	o0\). By compactness and uniqueness every maximizing sequence \(z_{	heta+h}\) tends to \(z_\star\). The first-order expansions at \(z_\star\) and \(z_{	heta+h}\) sandwich \(F(	heta+h)-F(	heta)\) between two linear terms differing by \(o(\|h\|)\). Several maximizers can make the directional derivative nonlinear in \(v\), as for \(\max(	heta,-	heta)\) at zero. For a minibatch, compute an approximate inner maximizer for each example and differentiate the outer average at the selected inputs. The exact envelope identity is a statement about true inner maximizers. Each feasible input evaluated during a numerical search gives a lower bound on worst-case loss. In accuracy, a finite check gives an upper bound on worst-case accuracy, while prediction invariance gives the lower bound used for certification. If unlike labels have overlapping perturbation sets, one deterministic classifier cannot give the correct label throughout both sets. For instance, two points at \(\ell_p\) distance at most \(2r\) share their midpoint inside both radius-\(r\) sets. Linear robust margins are exactFor a linear score \(w^	op x+b\) and \(y\in\{-1,1\}\), let \(m=y(w^	op x+b)\). The dual-norm identity gives \[\min_{\|\delta\|_p\le r}y(w^	op(x+\delta)+b)=m-r\|w\|_q,\quad 1/p+1/q=1.\] Hölder’s inequality gives the lower bound, and compactness of the unit ball and the definition of the dual norm give equality. The whole closed ball is classified correctly when \(m>r\|w\|_q\). At \(p=2\) the limiting radius agrees with the geometric distance from the SVM lecture. Evaluating robustness with nonsmooth or random componentsLecture 12, slides 19–28. Athalye et al., Sections 2–4. An inaccurate or uninformative gradient can make a numerical lower bound particularly loose. The slides distinguish shattered gradients from nonsmooth computations, stochastic gradients from randomized transformations, and badly scaled gradients through long chains of operations. A bounded prediction check measures the full forward model. In a differentiable approximation to a composition, every replaced derivative changes the product of Jacobians. Through randomness, differentiating an expected loss gives the expected derivative when a local integrable bound justifies differentiation under the integral. A single random gradient need not characterize the expected model. The Gaussian smoothing proofLecture 12, slides 29–37. Cohen, Rosenfeld, and Kolter, Section 3 and Appendix A. For base classifier \(f\), smooth by class probabilities \(p_c(x)=P(f(x+Z)=c)\) with \(Z\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I)\) and choose the most likely class. Suppose the leading class \(A\) has probability at least \(\underline p_A\) at \(x\) and any other class has probability at most \(\overline p_B<\underline p_A\). Greedy filling for a general noise kernelThe slides start with a binary problem. Let \(E=\{z:f(z)=A\}\) be the region assigned to the leading class, and let \(P,Q\) be the laws of noisy inputs at \(x\) and \(x+\delta\). Given only the histogram entry \(P(E)=a\), seek the smallest possible \(Q(E)\). In a discretized space with cell weights \(p_i,q_i\), choose fractions \(0\le u_i\le1\) of cells assigned to \(A\) to minimize \(\sum_i q_i u_i\) subject to \(\sum_i p_i u_i=a\). A cell with \(p_i=0<q_i\) can be left unfilled. Among the others, if a cell with ratio \(q_i/p_i\) larger than another is filled before that cheaper one is full, transfer a small amount of \(P\)-mass to the cheaper cell. The change in \(Q\)-mass is that amount times the difference of ratios, and is negative. Thus the optimum fills in increasing \(Q/P\) order, taking a fraction of a threshold cell if necessary. Slide 36 uses the reciprocal \(P/Q\) in decreasing order. For the uniform ball illustration, write \(C\) for the overlap of the two equal-volume balls, and \(t=P(C)=Q(C)\). The region exclusive to the first ball contributes up to \(1-t\) units of \(P\)-mass and zero \(Q\)-mass. If \(a>1-t\), the remaining \(a-1+t\) must come from the overlap, where the densities agree. The smallest possible \(Q(E)\) is \(\max\{0,a+t-1\}\). A binary guarantee based on this histogram requires that lower bound to exceed \(1/2\). Gaussian likelihood ratios and the certified radiusLet \(P=N(x,\sigma^2I)\), \(Q=N(x+\delta,\sigma^2I)\) and \(L(z)=dQ/dP(z)\). Given fixed \(P\)-mass, a set of low likelihood ratio minimizes \(Q\)-mass. To prove it, choose \(H=\{L\le c\}\) with the desired mass, and compare any set \(E\) of equal mass: \[Q(E)-Q(H)=\int (\mathbf1_E-\mathbf1_H)(L-c)\,dP\ge0.\] Both products on the symmetric difference are nonnegative. Reversing the threshold proves the upper-bound version. For nonzero \(\delta\), the logarithm of \(L\) is \(\delta^	op(z-x)/\sigma^2-\|\delta\|^2/(2\sigma^2)\), monotone along \(\delta\). Consequently the extremal sets are halfspaces in that direction. Projection onto \(\delta/\|\delta\|\) shifts the mean by \(\|\delta\|\) and preserves standard deviation \(\sigma\). For any class \(A\) event with the stated lower bound, its \(Q\)-mass is at least \[\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\underline p_A)-\|\delta\|/\sigma),\] and every other class has \(Q\)-mass at most \(\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\overline p_B)+\|\delta\|/\sigma)\). Therefore the prediction is unchanged for \[\|\delta\|< rac{\sigma}{2} ig(\Phi^{-1}(\underline p_A)-\Phi^{-1}(\overline p_B) ig).\] Comparing the two bounds is equivalent, by strict monotonicity of \(\Phi\), to the displayed strict radius inequality. When \(P(E_A)>\underline p_A\), the same threshold comparison has an extra term \(c(P(E_A)-\underline p_A)\ge0\). For an upper bound on a rival, take the upper tail of \(L\), reverse the signs, and use \(P(E)\le\overline p_B\). A class boundary of the base model inside the radius is compatible with the guarantee because the certified output is the maximum of the smoothed probabilities. If estimates come from sampling, use valid confidence bounds. Selecting \(A\) on an independent batch and taking a one-sided exact binomial lower bound on a fresh batch permits the conservative bound \(p_B\le1-p_A\). A larger \(\sigma\) increases the prefactor but may shrink the class-probability gap. ChallengeFor a binary halfspace base classifier with nonzero normal \(w\) and a point at positive signed geometric distance \(d\), derive its smoothed probability and show that the certified radius is exact. Show solution Gaussian projection along \(w/\|w\|\) has variance \(\sigma^2\), so the smoothed positive probability is \(\Phi(d/\sigma)\) and the negative probability is \(\Phi(-d/\sigma)\). The certificate radius is \(\sigma(\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(d/\sigma))-\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(-d/\sigma)))/2=d\). Smoothing leaves this halfspace’s decision boundary in place, because positive probability exceeds \(1/2\) precisely on its positive side. A shift along the negative normal of magnitude greater than \(d\) therefore switches the prediction. Second challenge. Find the exact Gaussian smoothing certificate for a binary base classifier whose decision boundary is a hyperplane. Show solution to the second challenge Let \(h(z)=\mathbf1\{w^	op z\ge b\}\) and \(w
e0\). With isotropic Gaussian noise, the positive class probability at \(x\) is \(p=\Phi((w^	op x-b)/(\sigma\|w\|))\). The runner-up has probability \(1-p\), so on the positive side the certificate is \(\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p)=(w^	op x-b)/\|w\|\). Moving against the unit normal reaches the hyperplane at exactly this distance. The averaged classifier retains the original boundary. Research challenge — sharpness of certification from class probabilitiesTake \(0<p_B<p_A<1\) and \(p_A+p_B\le1\). Suppose there are enough classes to divide the leftover mass \(1-p_A-p_B\) into pieces at most \(p_B\). Prove Cohen et al.’s Theorem 2 in this setting. If \[r> rac{\sigma}{2}(\Phi^{-1}(p_A)-\Phi^{-1}(p_B)),\] construct a deterministic base classifier with leading mass \(p_A\) and runner-up mass \(p_B\) at \(x\) whose smoothed class at \(x+ru\) differs from \(A\), for any unit direction \(u\). Explain what the inequality says about a particular trained model. Show research challenge solution Write \(t(z)=u^	op(z-x)/\sigma\). Assign class \(A\) to the half-space \(t(z)\le a\), with \(a=\Phi^{-1}(p_A)\), and class \(B\) to \(t(z)\ge b\), with \(b=\Phi^{-1}(1-p_B)=-\Phi^{-1}(p_B)\). Under the noise law at \(x\), \(t\) is standard normal. Since \(p_A\le1-p_B\), we have \(a\le b\) and the two half-spaces are disjoint up to a null boundary. Divide \((a,b)\) by normal quantiles into the remaining classes, assigning each a mass at most \(p_B\). The resulting classifier has the stated histogram and unique leading class \(A\) at \(x\). At \(x+ru\), \(t\) is normal with mean \(r/\sigma\) and variance one. Class \(A\) has mass \(\Phi(a-r/\sigma)\) and class \(B\) has mass \(\Phi(r/\sigma-b)\). The second is strictly larger precisely when \(2r/\sigma>a+b\). The construction attains the likelihood-ratio lower and upper bounds simultaneously. Thus a certificate based only on this histogram cannot reach farther in general. A particular classifier can have a larger actual radius because its class regions may differ from these extremal half-spaces. Challenge source: Cohen, Rosenfeld, and Kolter, Theorem 2 and Appendix A.
