title: ML 11: SimCLR, t-SNE, and Rotary Position Embeddings
summary: Derive the contrastive and t-SNE gradients, connect augmentation pairs to graph energy, and prove why RoPE depends explicitly on relative position.
body:
Derive the contrastive and t-SNE gradients, connect augmentation pairs to graph energy, and prove why RoPE depends explicitly on relative position. A two-dimensional query and key rotate at a shared frequency. Their relative angle changes by the difference of the position rotations. SimCLR and positive-pair graphsLecture 11, slides 3–7 and 10–15. The full-vocabulary model below follows Tan et al., Sections 3–4. Recall why spectral clustering uses the eigenvectors of smallest eigenvalue. For a symmetric nonnegative weight matrix \(A\) and \(L=\operatorname{diag}(A\mathbf 1)-A\), write \(L=V\Lambda V^	op\), with \(\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n\). For \(U^	op U=I_k\), let \(r_\ell\) be the squared norm of row \(\ell\) of \(V^	op U\). Then \(0\le r_\ell\le1\) because \(V^	op UU^	op V\) is an orthogonal projection, \(\sum_\ell r_\ell=k\) by its trace, and \(\operatorname{tr}(U^	op LU)=\sum_\ell\lambda_\ell r_\ell\). Moving mass from any larger occupied \(\lambda_\ell\) to a smaller unsaturated one cannot increase this sum. Its minimum is \(\sum_{\ell=1}^k\lambda_\ell\), attained by taking the corresponding eigenvectors. The row of \(U\) for object \(i\) is a \(k\)-dimensional embedding. Apply \(k\)-means to those rows and transfer the resulting labels to the original objects. Apply two independent random augmentations to each image. Each such pair consists of positive views, while the other images in the batch supply negative views. An encoder provides \(h_i\), and a projection head provides unit embeddings \(z_i\). For anchor \(i\) and its positive partner \(j\), define \[\ell_{i,j}=-\log rac{\exp(z_i^	op z_j/	au)}{\sum_{k
e i}\exp(z_i^	op z_k/	au)}.\] Write \(s_{ik}=z_i^	op z_k\) and \(p_{ik}\) for the temperature softmax. Differentiating the positive linear term and the log normalizer gives \(\partial\ell_{i,j}/\partial s_{ik}=(p_{ik}-\mathbf1\{k=j\})/	au\). High-similarity negative examples receive a larger repulsive derivative. The actual encoder gradient couples many pairs through shared parameters. SimCLR uses both directions of each positive pair and commonly uses the encoder’s pre-projection representation downstream. In a finite vocabulary of possible augmented views, put a symmetric edge weight on each positive pair proportional to its frequency. With embedding matrix \(Z\) and Laplacian \(L\), expanding squared edge differences gives \[	frac12\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}\|z_i-z_j\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(Z^	op LZ).\] With unit embeddings, minimizing this term is equivalent to maximizing the weighted dot products over positive edges. The InfoNCE normalizer adds a second term. For example, with ordered positive-pair probabilities \(\pi_{ij}\) and marginals \(\pi_i=\sum_j\pi_{ij}\), the full-vocabulary loss is \(-	au^{-1}\sum_{ij}\pi_{ij}s_{ij}+\sum_i\pi_i\log\sum_{k
e i}e^{s_{ik}/	au}\). The graph energy accounts for the attraction term. Spectral equivalence for a complete contrastive objective depends on how subgraphs, kernel probabilities, and normalization are modeled. Image–text contrastive learning instead uses a bipartite positive graph. From an RKHS Gram matrix to a subgraph distributionLet \(K_{ij}=k(z_i,z_j)=\langle\varphi(z_i),\varphi(z_j)angle_{\mathcal H}\) for a positive semidefinite kernel \(k\). In its RKHS one can take \(\varphi(z)=k(z,\cdot)\), since reproducing function evaluation gives \(\langle k(z,\cdot),k(z',\cdot)angle=k(z,z')\). For any coefficient vector \(c\), \(c^	op Kc=\|\sum_i c_i\varphi(z_i)\|_{\mathcal H}^2\ge0\). The finite Gram matrix remains computable even when \(\mathcal H\) is infinite-dimensional. The graph probability also requires nonnegative allowed edge weights. Positive semidefiniteness alone does not ensure nonnegative entries. For the Gaussian weights used here, nonnegativity is immediate. Positive semidefiniteness follows from \[e^{-\|z-z'\|^2/(2	au)} =e^{-\|z\|^2/(2	au)}e^{-\|z'\|^2/(2	au)} \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} rac{\langle z,z'angle^r}{r!	au^r}.\] Each dot-product power is the inner product of \(r\)-fold tensor powers, and scaling a feature vector by the leading exponential gives the outside factors. Directly summing these weighted tensor features proves the Gram property. SimCLR uses unit vectors, so \(\exp(-\|z-z'\|^2/(2	au))=\exp(-1/	au)\exp(z^	op z'/	au)\). The constant cancels in each ratio. Deriving InfoNCE from the graph cross-entropyFor each directed edge from \(i\) to \(j\), let \(w_{ij}\) be its nonnegative score and exclude self-edges. Impose the constraint that every row selects one outgoing edge. A graph is then determined by its choices \(j(i)\), and its unnormalized probability is \(\prod_i w_{i,j(i)}\). Since the constraint on one row is independent of the other rows, summing this product over all graphs gives \(\prod_i\sum_{k
e i}w_{ik}\). The resulting probability of the graph factors into the product of its row probabilities. Take the positive-pair weights to be \(\pi_{ij}\) and the embedding weights to be \(w_{ij}=\exp(z_i^	op z_j/	au)\). Write \(\pi(j\mid i)=\pi_{ij}/\sum_{k
e i}\pi_{ik}\) for every row with positive total weight. The negative log probability under the embedding distribution, averaged over the positive-pair graph, is \[-\sum_i\sum_{j
e i}\pi(j\mid i) \log rac{\exp(z_i^	op z_j/	au)}{\sum_{k
e i}\exp(z_i^	op z_k/	au)}.\] This is the sum of per-anchor InfoNCE objectives, averaged over each anchor’s positives. Weighting the rows by their anchor frequencies gives the ordered-pair objective above. The derivation requires the one-outgoing-edge constraint and these exponential weights. For a graph model that couples row choices, the partition function need not factor. Recovering the Laplacian term and the role of the partition functionFor either graph, write the full law as \[P_B(W)= rac{\Omega(W)\prod_{i,j
e i}B_{ij}^{W_{ij}}}{\mathcal Z_B}, \qquad \mathcal Z_B=\prod_i\sum_{j
e i}B_{ij}.\] Here \(B=\pi\) produces the augmentation graph, \(B=K\) produces the embedding graph, and \(\Omega\) enforces one outgoing edge per row. Only used edges enter the product. Put \(P_{ij}=\mathbb E_{\pi} W_{ij}=\pi(j\mid i)\), and use Gaussian \(K_{ij}\). Taking the negative logarithm and then expectation under \(P_\pi\) gives \[H(P_\pi,P_K)= rac{1}{2	au}\sum_{i,j
e i}P_{ij}\|z_i-z_j\|^2 +\sum_i\log\sum_{k
e i}e^{-\|z_i-z_k\|^2/(2	au)}.\] The distance is symmetric in the edge endpoints, hence we may replace \(P\) in the first sum by \(A=(P+P^	op)/2\). Expanding the square gives that sum as \(2\operatorname{tr}(Z^	op L_A Z)\), so the first term is \(\operatorname{tr}(Z^	op L_A Z)/	au\). For symmetric \(P\), \(A=P\) exactly. This is Tan et al.’s regularized spectral formulation in the finite full-vocabulary setting. The log partition function still depends on \(Z\), and ordinary Laplacian eigendecomposition minimizes only a relaxed trace objective. At collapse the trace term is zero, but every row predicts a uniform neighbor and its loss is \(\log(n-1)\). CLIP uses a bipartite candidate graphLecture 11, slide 16. Tan et al., Section 5. Let \(M_{ij}\) count the observed pairings of image \(i\) and text \(j\). Image anchors draw texts with probabilities \(M_{ij}/\sum_j M_{ij}\). Text anchors use \(M_{ij}/\sum_i M_{ij}\). Use kernel weights only between the two modalities. On each image row the kernel partition sums over all texts, and on each text row it sums over all images. The graph cross-entropy therefore splits into the two directional contrastive losses. On a batch of \(N\) paired and indexed image/text views, averaging their \(2N\) row losses gives CLIP’s symmetric contrastive objective. A vocabulary of deduplicated objects can have unequal degrees. Uniform objects and uniform edges induce different anchor frequencies, so the finite theory needs the sampling convention stated. t-SNE preserves a distribution over neighborsLecture 11, slides 18–25. The original objective and gradient are in van der Maaten and Hinton, Sections 2–3. For high-dimensional inputs use \[p_{j\mid i}=  rac{e^{-\|x_i-x_j\|^2/(2\sigma_i^2)}}{\sum_{k
e i}e^{-\|x_i-x_k\|^2/(2\sigma_i^2)}},\qquad p_{ij}= rac{p_{j\mid i}+p_{i\mid j}}{2n}.\] Tune \(\sigma_i\) so that the row perplexity, \(2\) raised to its base-2 entropy, matches the desired effective neighborhood size. For low-dimensional coordinates let \(w_{ij}=(1+\|y_i-y_j\|^2)^{-1}\) and \(q_{ij}=w_{ij}/Z\), \(Z=\sum_{a
e b}w_{ab}\). Self-pairs have probability zero. The heavy tail leaves room for moderate and large distances and reduces crowding in the embedding. To differentiate \(D_{m KL}(P\|Q)\), omit the constant \(\sum p_{ij}\log p_{ij}\) and write the remainder as \(\log Z-\sum p_{ij}\log w_{ij}\). For \(j
e i\), \(
abla_{y_i}\log w_{ij}=-2w_{ij}(y_i-y_j)\). Each unordered pair appears twice. The two terms therefore combine to \[
abla_{y_i}D_{m KL}(P\|Q)=4\sum_{j
e i}(p_{ij}-q_{ij})w_{ij}(y_i-y_j).\] A pair with \(p_{ij}>q_{ij}\) attracts under gradient descent. Distances between clusters and relative cluster areas can vary considerably with the initialization and perplexity. For the original SNE, the low-dimensional conditional distribution uses Gaussian weights \(q_{j\mid i}\propto e^{-\|y_i-y_j\|^2}\), and the loss is \(\sum_i D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\cdot\mid i}\|q_{\cdot\mid i})\). In symmetric t-SNE each conditional row sums to one, so summing the displayed \(p_{ij}\) over ordered distinct pairs gives \((n+n)/(2n)=1\). This is why the symmetric KL and its derivative use a single global normalizer. To see the geometric source of crowding, note that a radius-\(r\) ball in \(D\) dimensions has volume proportional to \(r^D\) by the Jacobian of scaling. Doubling radius multiplies local capacity by \(2^{10}\) in ten dimensions and by \(4\) in two. Uniform local density is an illustration, and the exponent describes how rapidly available space expands. At distance \(r\), t-SNE’s unnormalized weight is asymptotic to \(r^{-2}\), while the Gaussian weight decays as \(e^{-r^2}\). Thus a distant pair can move much farther for a given small relative weight under the heavy-tailed kernel. At the origin \((1+r^2)^{-1}=1-r^2+O(r^4)\) has finite weight and zero slope. The distribution works for a chosen embedding dimension above two as well. RoPE is a representation of position offsetsLecture 11, slides 26–33. Su et al., Sections 3.2–3.4. Represent a real block \((a,b)\) by \(a+ib\). Then \[\overline{(a+ib)}(c+id)=(ac+bd)+i(ad-bc),\] so the ordinary dot product is its real part. Multiplying by \(e^{im	heta}=\cos(m	heta)+i\sin(m	heta)\) acts on real coordinates via the rotation matrix below. For complex query and key blocks \(q,k\), their rotated Euclidean dot product is \(\operatorname{Re}(\overline q\,k\,e^{i(n-m)	heta})\) because conjugation reverses the query rotation. This derives the relative-offset form without losing the distinction between the complex product and the real score. In each two-dimensional coordinate block, apply \(R(m	heta_j)\) to query at position \(m\) and \(R(n	heta_j)\) to key at position \(n\). Here \(R(\alpha)\) is the rotation with rows \((\cos\alpha,-\sin\alpha)\) and \((\sin\alpha,\cos\alpha)\). Since \(R(\alpha)^	op=R(-\alpha)\) and \(R(a)R(b)=R(a+b)\), \[(R(m	heta_j)q)^	op R(n	heta_j)k=q^	op R((n-m)	heta_j)k.\] Thus the positional action on the dot product is a function of the relative position. The content vectors can still depend on the surrounding context. Multiple blocks use different frequencies, for example \(	heta_j=10000^{-2j/d}\), so they encode different offset scales. In dimension \(d\) even, let \(\mathcal R_m=\operatorname{diag}(R(m	heta_1),\dots,R(m	heta_{d/2}))\) and \(	heta_j=10000^{-2(j-1)/d}\). Matrices in different blocks act independently, so \(\mathcal R_m^	op\mathcal R_n=\mathcal R_{n-m}\). The full score is \(x_m^	op W_q^	op\mathcal R_{n-m}W_kx_n\) and each rotation preserves norm. With \(d=100\), the first three frequencies are \(1\), approximately \(0.8318\), and approximately \(0.6918\). Large frequencies change quickly with position, and small frequencies have longer periods. An individual block wraps modulo \(2\pi\). Multiple frequencies can still distinguish offsets after a single block wraps, and even a single irrational frequency need not repeat exactly on integer offsets. ChallengeProve row perplexity is nondecreasing as Gaussian bandwidth grows. Under what conditions is it strictly increasing? Show solution Write \( eta=1/(2\sigma_i^2)\), \(a_j=\|x_i-x_j\|^2\), and \(p_j=e^{- eta a_j}/Z\). In natural units \(H=\log Z+ eta\mathbb E_pa\). Differentiate: \((\log Z)'=-\mathbb E_pa\) and \((\mathbb E_pa)'=-\operatorname{Var}_p(a)\). Therefore \(dH/d eta=- eta\operatorname{Var}_p(a)\). Increasing \(\sigma_i\) decreases \( eta\), so \(e^H\) is nondecreasing. For finite positive bandwidth and at least two unequal distances the variance is positive, making the increase strict. If all distances are equal, the distribution is always uniform. Second challenge. Suppose a single RoPE block uses angle \(	heta\) with \(	heta/2\pi\) irrational. Can two integer offsets give exactly the same rotation? Can their rotations be arbitrarily close? Show solution to the second challenge Equality would require \((m-n)	heta\in2\pi\mathbb Z\), which is impossible for different integer offsets. For closeness, divide the circle into \(N\) intervals and place the \(N+1\) angles \(0,	heta,\ldots,N	heta\) into them modulo \(2\pi\). Two fall into the same interval, so the nonzero difference has angular distance at most \(2\pi/N\) from zero. Exact injectivity therefore gives no uniform numerical separation over unbounded positions. Research challenge — the large-negative limit of contrastive learningIn Wang and Isola’s Theorem 1, embeddings lie on the unit sphere. In this exercise the encoder and temperature \(	au>0\) are fixed. Draw \((X,Y)\) from a positive-pair distribution with common marginal \(\mu\), and draw \(X_1^-,\ldots,X_M^-\) independently from \(\mu\), independent of the pair. Let \(s(x,y)=f(x)^	op f(y)/	au\). Prove that \[\lim_{M	o\infty}\left[ \mathbb E\left(-s(X,Y)+\log\left(e^{s(X,Y)}+ \sum_{j=1}^M e^{s(X,X_j^-)}ight)ight)-\log M ight] =-\mathbb E s(X,Y)+\mathbb E_X\log\mathbb E_{Z\sim\mu} e^{s(X,Z)}.\] Give a direct \(O(M^{-1/2})\) bound at fixed \(	au\) and rewrite the two limiting terms using squared distances. Why does the second term contain an expectation of a logarithm? Show research challenge solution Condition on \(X,Y\) and write \(Y_j=e^{s(X,X_j^-)}\), \(m(X)=\mathbb E[Y_j\mid X]\). All these random variables lie in \([a,b]\) where \(a=e^{-1/	au}\) and \(b=e^{1/	au}\). The normalized sum \(Q_M=M^{-1}\sum_jY_j+e^{s(X,Y)}/M\) is at least \(a\), as is \(m(X)\). The derivative of \(\log\) is bounded by \(1/a\) on this interval. Independence gives \[\mathbb E\left| rac1M\sum_jY_j-m(X)ight| \le\sqrt{\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}\!\left(M^{-1}\sum_jY_j\mid Xight)} \le rac{b-a}{2\sqrt M}.\] The variance bound uses that the squared deviation from the midpoint of \([a,b]\) is at most \((b-a)^2/4\), and variance minimizes mean squared deviation from a constant. Therefore \[\left|\mathbb E\log Q_M-\mathbb E\log m(X)ight| \le a^{-1}\left( rac{b-a}{2\sqrt M}+ rac bMight).\] The positive-pair term is independent of \(M\). This proves convergence and its rate. For unit embeddings \(s=1/	au-\|f(x)-f(y)\|^2/(2	au)\). The constants cancel, leaving \[ rac{\mathbb E\|f(X)-f(Y)\|^2}{2	au} +\mathbb E_X\log\mathbb E_Z e^{-\|f(X)-f(Z)\|^2/(2	au)}.\] The negative sample average converges for each anchor first. Jensen’s inequality gives \(\mathbb E_X\log m(X)\le\log\mathbb E_X m(X)\), with equality precisely when \(m(X)\) is almost surely constant. A pooled negative average inside a single logarithm therefore changes the objective in general. Source of the challenge: Wang and Isola, Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning through Alignment and Uniformity on the Hypersphere, Theorem 1 and Appendix A.1. Original paper Sources Derivation Lecture 11 slides Supplement Graph Laplacian relaxation and embedding 3 Tan et al., Definition 3.6 RKHS, subgraph partition functions, InfoNCE, and repulsion 4–7, 10–15 Tan et al., Lemmas 3.3–3.5 and Theorem 4.1 Bipartite contrastive objective 16 Tan et al., Theorem 5.2 Perplexity, crowding, and symmetric KL gradient 18–25 van der Maaten and Hinton, Sections 2–3 Complex rotations and relative offsets 26–33 Su et al., Sections 3.2–3.4 Large-negative asymptotics Paper exercise Wang and Isola, Theorem 1 and Appendix A.1 Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, Lecture 11, slides 3–16 (SimCLR and CLIP), 18–25 (SNE and t-SNE), and 26–33 (RoPE). SimCLR, Section 2, Tan et al., Lemmas 3.3–3.5 and Theorems 4.1 and 5.2, t-SNE, Sections 2–3, and RoFormer, Sections 3.2–3.4. Previous lecture · Course notes · Next lecture

title: ML 10: K-means and Spectral Clustering
summary: Derive Lloyd’s updates, prove the graph Laplacian’s spectral properties, and obtain a clustering algorithm by relaxing RatioCut.
body: Derive Lloyd’s updates, prove the graph Laplacian’s spectral properties, and obtain a clustering algorithm by relaxing RatioCut. The bridge is weak relative to the triangle edges. The second eigenvector places the two triangles on opposite sides of zero. Lloyd’s alternating updatesK-means minimizes \(\sum_i\|x_i-\mu_{c_i}\|^2\) over assignments and centers. With centers fixed, each point chooses its closest center independently. For a fixed nonempty cluster \(S\), expansion about its mean gives \[\sum_{i\in S}\|x_i-\mu\|^2 =\sum_{i\in S}\|x_i-\bar x_S\|^2+|S|\|\mu-\bar x_S\|^2.\] The cross term vanishes because the centered points sum to zero. Therefore the optimal center is the cluster mean. Exact alternating updates cannot increase the objective. With ties assigned to the previous cluster whenever possible, every changed assignment strictly decreases the cost at the current centers. Reoptimizing the nonempty centers decreases it further or leaves it unchanged. The value after optimizing centers depends only on the partition, since empty centers contribute zero. A strict decrease cannot revisit a partition, so the algorithm stabilizes after finitely many assignment changes. If empty centers are needed for later assignments, one possible choice is to leave them at their previous positions. Slides 14–15 illustrate how a stable Lloyd partition can have arbitrarily poor cost. Consider the six points \((\pm M,j)\) for \(j=0,1,2\) and \(M>0\). Initialize three centers at \((0,0),(0,1),(0,2)\). Each point is uniquely closest to the center in its own row and each center is already its row mean, so Lloyd is at a fixed point of cost \(6M^2\). Partition by vertical columns, splitting one column into a singleton and an adjacent pair to use three centers. That cost is \(2+1/2\), independent of \(M\), giving an unbounded approximation ratio. Nearest centers partition Euclidean space into convex Voronoi cells, which are also a poor fit for the concentric rings on slide 18. Graph Laplacian energy and null spaceLet \(W\) be a symmetric nonnegative weight matrix, \(D_{ii}=\sum_jW_{ij}\), and \(L=D-W\). Symmetry gives \[u^\top Lu=\sum_iD_{ii}u_i^2-\sum_{ij}W_{ij}u_iu_j =\tfrac12\sum_{ij}W_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2.\] Thus \(L\) is positive semidefinite. The energy is zero exactly when every edge of positive weight joins two equal coordinates. This means \(u\) is constant on each connected component, so the multiplicity of eigenvalue zero is the number of components. In particular, \(L\mathbf1=0\). The graph can use an \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood rule, a symmetrized \(k\)-nearest-neighbor rule, or a dense similarity function. For the nearest-neighbor construction on slide 20, include an edge if either endpoint appears in the other’s neighbor list. If a point belongs to a different connected component, the corresponding entry of \(W\) is zero, so after ordering vertices by component the Laplacian becomes block diagonal with exactly one constant null vector on each block. Zero-degree vertices count as singleton components. Compute the smallest eigenspace by shiftingIf \(A\) is symmetric with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n\), any upper bound \(c\ge\lambda_n\) makes \(B=A-cI\) share its eigenvectors and have only nonpositive eigenvalues. The negative eigenvalue \(\lambda_1-c\) has greatest magnitude. Thus power iteration on \(B\) finds a direction in the smallest eigenspace of \(A\), given a nonzero initial projection onto it. Apply the Rayleigh quotient to recover the signed shifted eigenvalue, then add \(c\). For a simple smallest eigenvalue and \(c>\lambda_1\), the relative error decays with ratio \((c-\lambda_2)/(c-\lambda_1)\). Because the dominant shifted eigenvalue is negative, the signed iterates can alternate while their spans converge. To find subsequent vectors, use orthogonal deflation or a block eigensolver. This is the shift argument of slide 29. RatioCut as a relaxationDefine \(W(A,B)=\sum_{i\in A,j\in B}W_{ij}\). For a partition \(A,B\), take \(u_i=\sqrt{|B|/(n|A|)}\) on \(A\) and \(u_i=-\sqrt{|A|/(n|B|)}\) on \(B\). Then \(\|u\|=1\) and \(u\perp\mathbf1\). All internal edges have zero energy. A crossing edge contributes its weight times \((1/|A|+1/|B|)\), so \(u^\top Lu=\operatorname{RatioCut}(A,B)\). Removing the two-level constraint permits any unit vector perpendicular to \(\mathbf1\). Expand in an eigenbasis with \(\mathbf1/\sqrt n\) first. The minimum is \(\lambda_2(L)\), achieved by a Fiedler vector, and is a lower bound on the discrete optimum. A threshold or one-dimensional two-means converts its real coordinates into a cut. For \(k\) nonempty groups, set \(H_{ij}=\mathbf1\{i\in A_j\}/\sqrt{|A_j|}\). Then \(H^\top H=I\) and \[\operatorname{tr}(H^\top LH)=\sum_j\frac{W(A_j,\overline{A_j})}{|A_j|}.\] To solve the relaxation over all \(H^\top H=I\), let \(u_i\) be Laplacian eigenvectors and write the trace as \(\sum_i\lambda_i c_i\) where \(c_i=\|H^\top u_i\|^2\). Since \(HH^\top\) is a rank-\(k\) orthogonal projector, \(0\le c_i\le1\) and \(\sum_i c_i=k\). Moving weight from a larger eigenvalue to a smaller one until the smallest \(k\) have weight one gives the lower bound \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\). Taking their eigenvectors as columns attains it. This is the trace minimization proof used for the spectral embedding; each row is a node’s embedding, and k-means rounds the points to clusters. The same trace argument, applied to the largest eigenvalues, gives the PCA characterization from Lecture 9. Replacing the size of a group by its total degree \(\operatorname{vol}(A_j)=\sum_{i\in A_j}D_{ii}\) gives normalized cut. For positive degrees, define \(H_{ij}=\mathbf1\{i\in A_j\}/\sqrt{\operatorname{vol}(A_j)}\). Direct expansion gives \(H^\top DH=I\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(H^\top LH)=\sum_j W(A_j,\overline{A_j})/\operatorname{vol}(A_j)\). Substitute \(U=D^{1/2}H\) to get the orthogonality constraint \(U^\top U=I\) and minimize the trace of \(U^\top L_{\rm sym}U\), where \(L_{\rm sym}=I-D^{-1/2}WD^{-1/2}\). Its bottom \(k\) eigenvectors solve the relaxation. The equivalent generalized equation is \(L H = DH\Lambda\), or \(D^{-1}LH=H\Lambda\). In a random walk with transition matrix \(P=D^{-1}W\), the stationary probability of vertex \(i\) is proportional to its degree by detailed balance. Conditional on starting in group \(A\) with that distribution, the probability of stepping out is \(W(A,\overline A)/\operatorname{vol}(A)\). This gives each normalized cut term a transition interpretation. Von Luxburg, “A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering,” §§5–6 The Birkhoff proof in the lectureComplete \(H\) to an orthogonal basis and express its columns in an eigenbasis of \(L\), obtaining an orthogonal matrix \(Q\). The matrix \(B\) with entries \(Q_{ij}^2\) is doubly stochastic because each row and column of \(Q\) has squared norm one. By Birkhoff’s theorem, \(B\) is a convex combination of permutation matrices. The objective is the linear expression \(\sum_i\lambda_i\sum_{j\le k}B_{ij}\). At each permutation this is the sum of some \(k\) distinct eigenvalues, at least \(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k\). The same is true of their convex combination. The first \(k\) eigenvectors give equality. Two supplementary proofs of the trace minimumPCA and best low-rank approximation. Choose \(c>\lambda_{\max}(L)\) and set \(A=cI-L=XX^\top\) using the symmetric square root. Minimizing \(\operatorname{tr}(H^\top LH)\) over \(H^\top H=I_k\) is equivalent to maximizing \(\operatorname{tr}(H^\top XX^\top H)\), since their sum is \(ck\). For a fixed column subspace, the best approximation of \(X\) in that subspace is the projection \(HH^\top X\). Its squared error is \(\|X\|_F^2-\operatorname{tr}(H^\top XX^\top H)\). Every matrix of rank at most \(k\) has columns in such a subspace, so the problem is exactly best rank-\(k\) approximation. Here is the singular value argument from Zeyang Zhang’s supplement. For \(n\)-column matrices \(B,C\), take the subspaces orthogonal to the leading \(i-1\) right singular vectors of \(B\) and leading \(j-1\) of \(C\). Their intersection has dimension at least \(n-i-j+2\), and \(\|(B+C)v\|\le(\sigma_i(B)+\sigma_j(C))\|v\|\) there. The variational formula for singular values, which minimizes the maximal stretch over subspaces of this dimension, gives \(\sigma_{i+j-1}(B+C)\le\sigma_i(B)+\sigma_j(C)\). This variational formula follows by choosing the trailing right singular vectors for the upper bound and intersecting any candidate subspace with the span of the first \(i+j-1\) right singular vectors for the lower bound. Set \(B=X-M\), \(C=M\), and \(j=k+1\). Since \(\sigma_{k+1}(M)=0\) for rank at most \(k\), summing squares gives \[\|X-M\|_F^2=\sum_i\sigma_i(X-M)^2\ge\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i(X)^2.\] The rank-\(k\) truncated singular value decomposition attains the bound. The largest eigenvalues of \(XX^\top=cI-L\) correspond to the smallest ones of \(L\), giving the desired trace minimum. Lagrange multipliers and the determinant argument. This follows Wenjie Huang’s supplement. For any symmetric \(A\), use the Lagrangian \(\operatorname{tr}(H^\top AH)-\operatorname{tr}(M(H^\top H-I))\), with \(M\) symmetric. The derivative of the constraint is onto the symmetric \(k\times k\) matrices, because the perturbation \(HS/2\) gives derivative \(S\) for any symmetric \(S\). Thus at a minimizer \(AH=HM\). To see the determinant step, form the block matrix \(D\) with commuting entries \(D_{ij}=\delta_{ij}A-M_{ij}I\). The cofactor identity \(\operatorname{adj}(D)D=\det(D)I\) holds over the commutative ring generated by \(A\) and \(I\): an off-diagonal entry is the expansion of a determinant with two equal columns and vanishes. Applying it to the column vectors of \(H\) gives \(p(A)h_j=0\) with \(p(t)=\det(tI_k-M)\). For simple spectrum, \(p(A)\) has at least \(k\) linearly independent null vectors, so \(p(t)\) vanishes at \(k\) distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_{i_1},\ldots,\lambda_{i_k}\) of \(A\). Since \(p\) is monic of degree \(k\), comparing the coefficient of \(t^{k-1}\) gives \(\operatorname{tr}(M)=\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_{i_j}\). The objective is \(\operatorname{tr}(M)\) at the stationary point and is at least the sum of the smallest \(k\) eigenvalues. Choosing their eigenvectors attains equality. For repeated eigenvalues diagonalize \(M=Q\Lambda Q^\top\): \(AHQ=HQ\Lambda\), so the \(k\) orthonormal columns select eigenvalues with multiplicity at most their eigenspace dimensions. The same lower bound follows. Compactness of \(H^\top H=I\) ensures the minimum is attained. ChallengeSuppose \(G\) has exactly \(k\) connected components. Show that k-means on the rows of any orthonormal basis of the bottom-\(k\) eigenspace has a unique zero-loss grouping up to label order. Show solution The normalized component indicators form an orthonormal basis \(B\) of the null space. Every other orthonormal basis is \(BQ\) for an orthogonal \(Q\). The rows of \(B\) are constant within each component, and different components use nonzero multiples of distinct standard basis vectors, so have distinct rows. Orthogonal rotation preserves these distances. There are exactly \(k\) distinct embedded points. A zero-loss solution requires all rows assigned to a center to be identical, so its \(k\) centers must be the \(k\) distinct points and recover the components. Second challenge. For a connected weighted graph, show the normalized Laplacian has spectrum in \([0,2]\). When does the largest eigenvalue reach 2? Show solution to the second challenge For \(v=D^{-1/2}u\), the energy is \(\tfrac12\sum_{ij}W_{ij}(v_i-v_j)^2\). The bound \((a-b)^2\le2(a^2+b^2)\) makes it at most \(2\sum_iD_{ii}v_i^2=2\|u\|^2\). Equality requires \(v_i=-v_j\) on every positive-weight edge, so a connected graph has a nonzero equality vector exactly when its edges respect a bipartition. On a bipartite graph take \(v=1\) on one side and \(-1\) on the other. Paper challenge · Recover two clusters after a weak bridgeDevelop the perturbation argument in von Luxburg, “A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering,” §7.1. Let \(L_0\) be the unnormalized Laplacian of two disconnected, internally connected components of sizes \(a,b\). Its third eigenvalue is \(\gamma>0\). Add one bridge of weight \(\varepsilon\) between them. Prove an angle bound for the new unit Fiedler vector and give a sufficient condition for its signs to recover both components exactly. Show paper solution Write \(L=L_0+E\), with \(E=\varepsilon(e_i-e_j)(e_i-e_j)^\top\) for the bridge endpoints. The rank-one update satisfies \(\|E\|_{\rm op}=2\varepsilon\). Let \(u\) be the unit two-level null vector of \(L_0\) perpendicular to \(\mathbf1\), with entries \(\sqrt{b/(a(a+b))}\) on one component and \(-\sqrt{a/(b(a+b))}\) on the other. If \(v\) is a unit Fiedler eigenvector of \(L\) perpendicular to \(\mathbf1\), its eigenvalue satisfies \[\lambda_2(L)\le u^\top Lu=\varepsilon(1/a+1/b)\le2\varepsilon .\] Let \(P\) project orthogonally onto the complement of \(\ker L_0\). Since \(P\) commutes with \(L_0\), projecting \(Lv=\lambda_2v\) gives \((L_0-\lambda_2 I)Pv=-PEv\). For \(2\varepsilon<\gamma\), the restriction of \(L_0-\lambda_2I\) on this space has eigenvalues at least \(\gamma-\lambda_2>0\). Therefore \[\|Pv\|_2\le\frac{2\varepsilon}{\gamma-\varepsilon(1/a+1/b)}.\] Choose the sign of \(v\) with \(u^\top v\ge0\). Since both are orthogonal to \(\mathbf1\), \(\|Pv\|_2\) is the sine of their angle and \(\|v-u\|_\infty\le\|v-u\|_2\le\sqrt2\|Pv\|_2\). Every coordinate retains its sign when \[\frac{2\sqrt2\varepsilon}{\gamma-\varepsilon(1/a+1/b)} < \min\left\{\sqrt{\frac{b}{a(a+b)}},\sqrt{\frac{a}{b(a+b)}}\right\}.\] The sufficient bound deteriorates when the smallest magnitude of the ideal coordinate shrinks. The spectral gap alone bounds the angle, while an entrywise margin is needed to conclude exact sign recovery. Sources Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, legacy Lecture 10, slides 5–17 for Lloyd’s algorithm and the bad fixed-point geometry, 18–26 for graph construction and the null-space proof, 29 for the spectral shift, 30–37 for RatioCut and its relaxation, and 38–40 for Birkhoff’s proof and the two supplement pointers. Wenjie Huang, A Linear Algebra Optimization Problem, pp. 1–2 in the local Cramer supplement. Zeyang Zhang, local PCA derivation and Eckart–Young–Mirsky proof. The two arguments appear in the trace-minimization section above. Ulrike von Luxburg, A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering, §§3, 5–7. Paper Previous lecture · Course notes · Next lecture

title: ML 09: PCA, Nearest Neighbors, and Metric Learning
summary: Prove the equivalence of PCA’s variance and reconstruction objectives, derive locality-sensitive hashing guarantees, and learn distances from labels.
body:
Prove the equivalence of PCA’s variance and reconstruction objectives, derive locality-sensitive hashing guarantees, and learn distances from labels. Each thin segment represents a reconstruction residual. Squaring and averaging its length gives the reconstruction loss of the chosen direction. PCA and orthogonal reconstructionCenter the columns of \(X=[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\in\mathbb R^{d	imes n}\) and form \(C=XX^	op/n\). A unit vector \(v\) maximizes retained variance \(v^	op Cv\) exactly when it minimizes the mean squared reconstruction error. By orthogonality, \[n^{-1}\sum_i\|x_i-vv^	op x_i\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(C)-v^	op Cv.\] Writing \(v=\sum_j a_j u_j\) in the eigenbasis gives \(v^	op Cv=\sum_j\lambda_j a_j^2\) with \(\sum_j a_j^2=1\). The maximum is the largest eigenvalue. More generally, for \(k\) orthonormal columns \(V\), the retained variance is \(\sum_j\lambda_j\|V^	op u_j\|^2\). Each weight is in \([0,1]\) and their sum is \(k\), so the largest \(k\) eigenvalues give the best possible total. The omitted eigenvalues sum to the minimum residual. For \(\lambda_1>\lambda_2\) and initial \(v_0\) with nonzero first eigencoordinate, the normalized power iteration gives a vector parallel to \(C^tv_0\). Each eigencoordinate relative to the first is multiplied by \((\lambda_j/\lambda_1)^t\), establishing convergence to the leading eigendirection. Orthogonal projection away from an exactly known leading eigenvector preserves the other eigendirections, which permits orthogonal deflation. Scaling features changes the covariance geometry, so the units of the data affect the principal directions. More quantitatively, write \(v_0=\sum_j a_j u_j\) with \(a_1
e0\). The tangent of the angle from \(u_1\) to the \(t\)th iterate, ignoring its sign, is at most \((\lambda_2/\lambda_1)^t\sqrt{\sum_{j\ge2}a_j^2}/|a_1|\). This follows by taking the ratio between the perpendicular component and the \(u_1\) projection of \(C^tv_0\). If \(a_1=0\) and \(a_2
e0\), the iteration remains in \(u_1^\perp\) and can converge to \(u_2\) when \(\lambda_2\) is the simple largest eigenvalue in that subspace. With a repeated top eigenvalue it converges to the direction of the initial projection onto the whole top eigenspace, assuming that projection is nonzero. Slides 12–23 illustrate compression using \(12	imes12\) image patches. Treat each patch as a vector in \(\mathbb R^{144}\), subtract the mean patch, and keep coefficients along the chosen \(k\) principal directions. At reconstruction, multiply the coefficients by the basis and add back the mean. The relative squared reconstruction error is \(\sum_{j>k}\lambda_j/\sum_j\lambda_j\), provided total centered variance is positive. The displayed PCA basis resembles several low-frequency cosine patterns, whereas a DCT basis is fixed before seeing the image. Gaussian Johnson–Lindenstrauss projection, discussed in Lecture 6, instead preserves a finite set’s pairwise distances with high probability at dimension \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)\). From neighbor search to locality-sensitive hashingThe \(k\) nearest labeled examples vote in a kNN classifier. Search is the separate problem of finding candidates quickly. In the \((R,cR)\) decision version, if there is an item within \(R\) of a query, an item within \(cR\) qualifies. Every returned candidate can be checked using its actual distance. The slide sequences on Iris data (26–45) and overlapping Gaussian classes (46–68) vary \(k\) while holding the training sample fixed. With a small neighborhood, a single unusual point can create a separate decision region. A larger neighborhood stabilizes the votes in these examples, but it can also erase a small genuine cluster. A simple model explains the variance side: if the \(k\) selected labels were conditionally independent Bernoulli draws with common probability \(p\), their class proportion would have variance \(p(1-p)/k\). The common-\(p\) approximation gets worse as the neighborhood crosses regions where the true class probabilities differ. Exact nearest-neighbor search answers an exact radius query by one distance comparison. In the other direction, suppose positive nearest distance \(r_\star\) is bracketed by known positive scales. Query independent approximate radius structures at a geometric sequence with ratio \(1+\zeta>1\) and return the smallest-distance verified answer. The first tested radius \(R\) with \(R\ge r_\star\) is at most \((1+\zeta)r_\star\), so successful analysis at that radius yields a \(c(1+\zeta)\) approximation. An earlier valid return after testing increasing radii has the same guarantee. An exact point lookup handles distance zero. The radius search in slide 72 uses doubling, which gives a factor \(2c\). Repetition over independently drawn structures reduces the per-query failure probability geometrically. An \((R,cR,p_1,p_2)\)-sensitive hash family offers collision probability at least \(p_1\) for near points and at most \(p_2<p_1\) for far points. For Hamming distance, a uniformly chosen coordinate agrees with probability \(1-d_H(x,y)/d\). Concatenate \(k\) independent hashes so the near and far collision probabilities become at least \(p_1^k\) and at most \(p_2^k\). Then use \(L\) independent tables. A fixed near point is missed with probability at most \((1-p_1^k)^L\le e^{-Lp_1^k}\). The tables store \(O(nL)\) point references. The success proof combines the probability of seeing a distinguished near neighbor with a budget on how many far collisions the query can examine. Learning a useful metricA linear representation \(Ax\) gives squared distance \((x_i-x_j)^	op A^	op A(x_i-x_j)\). Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA) replaces a hard neighbor choice by \[p_{ij}= rac{e^{-\|A(x_i-x_j)\|^2}}{\sum_{k
e i}e^{-\|A(x_i-x_k)\|^2}},\quad j
e i,\qquad p_{ii}=0.\] The expected number of correct leave-one-out predictions is \(\sum_i\sum_{j:y_j=y_i}p_{ij}\). Excluding self-neighbors ensures that training fits relationships between distinct examples. Another approach uses a triplet objective to prefer a positive neighbor over a negative one by a margin. Under a matrix metric \(M\succeq0\), a fixed triplet yields the hinge of an affine function of \(M\), hence a convex penalty in that variable. Euclidean locality-sensitive hashingFor the \(p\)-stable construction at \(p=2\), let \(a\sim N(0,I_d)\) and \(b\) be uniform on \([0,w)\), independently, and hash \(h_{a,b}(x)=\lfloor(a^	op x+b)/wfloor\). Conditional on projection separation \(t=|a^	op(x-z)|\), the random shift places a bin boundary between the projections with probability \(\min(1,t/w)\). This follows because a boundary lies between them for exactly \(t\) out of \(w\) shift values when \(t<w\), and at least one boundary always lies between them when \(t\ge w\). The variance of \(a^	op(x-z)\) is \(\sum_i(x_i-z_i)^2\), so \(t\overset{d}{=}\|x-z\|_2|Z|\) for \(Z\sim N(0,1)\). The collision probability at distance \(r>0\) is \[p(r)=\mathbb E\!\left[(1-r|Z|/w)_+ight] =\int_0^w \left(1- rac twight) rac2r\,\phi(t/r)\,dt,\] where \(\phi\) is the standard Gaussian density. The second expression is the scaling calculation from slides 86–87. The same offset proof works with a symmetric \(p\)-stable random projection and \(r=\|x-z\|_p\), replacing the Gaussian density by its \(p\)-stable counterpart.For \(0\le r_1<r_2\), use the same \(|Z|\) in both expectations. The integrand for \(r_1\) is larger on the positive-probability event \(0<|Z|<w/r_2\), and never smaller. Thus the \((R,cR)\) near and far probabilities satisfy \(p(R)>p(cR)\) for \(R>0,c>1\). Why the LMNN objective is convex in the metricFix the same-class target neighbors in advance and put \(D_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^	op\). A positive semidefinite matrix \(M\) gives squared distance \(d_M(i,j)=\operatorname{tr}(MD_{ij})\). The large-margin nearest neighbor objective combines the sum of target-neighbor distances and a hinge penalty \(\max(0,1+d_M(i,j)-d_M(i,k))\) on differently labeled \(k\). Both distance expressions are affine in \(M\). The maximum of two affine functions is convex, sums with nonnegative weights preserve convexity, and the positive semidefinite cone is convex since each inequality \(z^	op Mz\ge0\) is linear in \(M\). Factoring \(M=T^	op T\) gives the resulting Euclidean embedding. A bounded-work query guaranteeFor a fixed query, suppose at least one data point is within \(R\). Let \(k=\lceil\log n/\log(1/p_2)ceil\), concatenate \(k\) independent hashes per table, and let \(ho=\log(1/p_1)/\log(1/p_2)\). A far point collides in one table with probability at most \(p_2^k\le1/n\). Linearity of expectation bounds the number of far candidate occurrences across \(L\) tables by \(L\), whether or not different data points collide independently. With \(L=\lceil p_1^{-k}ceil=O(n^ho/p_1)\), independence across tables makes the distinguished near point absent with probability at most \(e^{-1}\). By Markov, the probability of more than \(2L\) far occurrences is at most \(1/2\). On the complement of both bad events, testing \(2L+1\) candidates suffices to return a point within \(cR\). A union bound gives the lecture’s \(1/2-e^{-1}\) success rate. For success at least \(1/2\), use \(L=\lceil p_1^{-k}\log 4ceil\) and a budget \(4L+1\): each of the two failure probabilities is now at most \(1/4\). Duplicates can count as occurrences in this argument. Any scanned point within \(cR\) already qualifies, whether it is the designated near point or another candidate. ChallengeFind the behavior of Gaussian bucket hashing when the projected spacing parameter \(w\) is tiny compared with the original distance \(d=\|x-y\|\). Show \(P(h(x)=h(y))\sim w/(d\sqrt{2\pi})\). Show solution The density of \(t=d|Z|\) is \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\exp(-t^2/(2d^2))/d\) for \(t\ge0\). Thus \[P=\sqrt{ rac2\pi} rac wd\int_0^1(1-u)e^{-w^2u^2/(2d^2)}\,du.\] As \(w/d	o0\), dominated convergence gives an integral tending to \(1/2\), proving the result. Second challenge. Suppose each query uses \(L\) independent tables from the proved constant-success LSH construction. How many independent copies are required to answer \(Q\) fixed queries with total failure probability at most \(\delta\)? Show solution to the second challenge For a query with a near neighbor, each fresh copy fails with probability at most \(1/2\). Trying \(r\) copies independently reduces this to \(2^{-r}\). A union bound over queries gives at most \(Q2^{-r}\) even though different queries reuse the copies. It suffices to take \(r=\lceil\log_2(Q/\delta)ceil\). This argument assumes the queries are fixed independently of the randomized tables. Paper challenge · Derive NCA’s gradient and test a collapseFor the NCA objective \(F(A)=\sum_i p_i\), where \(p_i=\sum_{j:y_j=y_i}p_{ij}\), derive the exact matrix gradient. Show that the fully collapsed map \(A=0\) is stationary by parameterization. Then suppose there is a feature direction along which all examples in each class project to their class constant and all class constants are distinct. If there are two or more classes and at least one class has more than one point, prove that collapse is locally improvable. Goldberger et al., “Neighbourhood Components Analysis,” §2 Show paper solution Let \(D_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^	op\), \(s_{ij}=-\operatorname{tr}(A D_{ij}A^	op)\), and \(C_i=\{j
e i:y_j=y_i\}\). Differentiating the softmax gives \(dp_{ij}=p_{ij}(ds_{ij}-\sum_{k
e i}p_{ik}ds_{ik})\). The score derivative is \(
abla_A s_{ij}=-2AD_{ij}\). Summing first over \(j\in C_i\), then over \(i\), yields \[
abla_A F= 2A\sum_i\left( p_i\sum_{j
e i}p_{ij}D_{ij}-\sum_{j\in C_i}p_{ij}D_{ij} ight).\] In particular it vanishes at \(A=0\). This conclusion does not say whether the point optimizes the objective. Let \(v\) be the stated feature direction and choose \(A=t v^	op\) in one embedding dimension. For anchor \(i\) in class \(c\), the numerator of \(p_i\) is \(|C_i|\) because all its correct neighbors are at zero distance. The denominator is \(|C_i|+\sum_{j:y_j
e c}\exp(-t^2(\mu_c-\mu_{y_j})^2)\) with distinct class constants \(\mu\). At any nonzero \(t\), each cross-class term strictly decreases relative to \(t=0\). Thus \(p_i\) strictly increases for every anchor with at least one correct neighbor, while the singleton-class probabilities remain zero. Arbitrarily small nonzero \(t\) therefore improves \(F\). The claim in slide 91 relies on a separable perturbation of this kind. With identical features and conflicting labels, such a direction need not exist. The metric-learning references also discuss learned search embeddings. A spherical embedding can separate relevant pairs while spreading all items across directions to reduce crowding in an index. A triplet margin, a leave-one-out classification score, and an embedding-uniformity term optimize different objectives. Sablayrolles et al., “Spreading Vectors for Similarity Search” Sources Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, legacy Lecture 9, slides 4–11 for PCA and power iteration, 12–23 for patch compression, 24–69 for nearest-neighbor classification examples, 70–84 for the search reduction and LSH query proof, 85–87 for Gaussian collision probabilities, and 88–94 for NCA and LMNN. Piotr Indyk and Rajeev Motwani, Approximate Nearest Neighbors, and Alexandr Andoni and Piotr Indyk, Near-Optimal Hashing Algorithms for Approximate Nearest Neighbor in High Dimensions. Original ANN paper Mayur Datar, Nicole Immorlica, Piotr Indyk, and Vahab Mirrokni, Locality-Sensitive Hashing Scheme Based on p-Stable Distributions, §3. Paper Jacob Goldberger, Sam Roweis, Geoff Hinton, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Neighbourhood Components Analysis, §2. title: ML 08: Decision Trees, Random Forests, and Boosting
summary: Compute a greedy tree split, derive AdaBoost’s training and margin bounds, and connect gradient boosting to functional descent.
body: Compute a greedy tree split, derive AdaBoost’s training and margin bounds, and connect gradient boosting to functional descent. The weighted post-split impurity is about 0.317, below the parent impurity of 0.480. Greedy splits and baggingFor class proportions \(p_c\), Gini impurity is \(I(p)=1-\sum_c p_c^2\), the chance of different labels in two independent draws. A split maximizes parent impurity minus the sample-count weighted impurity of its children. The illustrated root has 6 blue and 4 orange examples. Its left child has 5 blue and 1 orange, giving \(5/18\), and its right child has 1 blue and 3 orange, giving \(3/8\). The weighted child value is \((6/10)(5/18)+(4/10)(3/8)=19/60\). Each node optimizes one split. Depth limits, minimum leaf counts, and pruning control the eventual tree size. Replacing Gini by entropy gives information gain. A bootstrap sample draws \(n\) times with replacement from \(n\) cases. A specific case is absent with probability \((1-1/n)^n\to e^{-1}\), so the trees that leave it out can supply its out-of-bag prediction. A random forest also samples feature candidates at each split. For conditional prediction variance \(\sigma^2\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\) in an ensemble model, expanding the variance of the mean over \(B\) trees gives \(\sigma^2(\rho+(1-\rho)/B)\). The correlation term survives as the number of trees increases. For the ten observations on slides 6–9, the root’s up/down counts are \((4,6)\) and its Gini impurity is \(12/25\). The three candidates have the following root scores: Split Child up/down counts Weighted Gini Past trend \((4,2)\) and \((0,4)\) \(4/15\) Open interest \((2,2)\) and \((2,4)\) \(7/15\) Trading volume \((4,3)\) and \((0,3)\) \(12/35\) Past trend therefore gives the lowest weighted impurity, equivalently the greatest gain. Its negative branch is pure. On the positive branch, open interest gives \((2,0)\) and \((2,2)\), with weighted impurity \(1/3\). Volume gives \((4,0)\) and \((0,2)\), both pure. The finished tree predicts up exactly when trend is positive and volume high. Splitting on a continuous feature works similarly after sorting its distinct values and trying thresholds between successive values. For \(C\) classes, Gini is maximized at the uniform distribution with value \(1-1/C\), by Cauchy–Schwarz. AdaBoost from exponential lossFor labels and weak predictions in \(\{-1,1\}\), write \(F_t=F_{t-1}+\alpha_t h_t\). At round \(t\), set \(D_t(i)\propto e^{-y_iF_{t-1}(x_i)}\) and let \(\epsilon_t\) be the error of \(h_t\) under \(D_t\). For fixed \(h_t\), adding the new learner multiplies the empirical exponential loss by \[Z_t(\alpha)=(1-\epsilon_t)e^{-\alpha}+\epsilon_t e^\alpha.\] Differentiation gives the minimum at \(\alpha_t=\tfrac12\log((1-\epsilon_t)/\epsilon_t)\) when \(0<\epsilon_t<1/2\). Substituting gives \(Z_t=2\sqrt{\epsilon_t(1-\epsilon_t)}\). The new sample weight is \(D_{t+1}(i)=D_t(i)e^{-\alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i)}/Z_t\). A perfect weak rule can terminate boosting, and error \(1/2\) gives zero coefficient. With \(F_0=0\), unrolling the weight recurrence gives \(D_{T+1}(i)=e^{-y_iF_T(x_i)}/(n\prod_t Z_t)\), since the initial weight is \(1/n\). Summing over \(i\) gives the empirical exponential loss \(\prod_t Z_t\). Misclassification implies \(y_iF_T(x_i)\le0\), and then its exponential term is at least 1. Writing \(\epsilon_t=1/2-\gamma_t\) gives \[\widehat R(\operatorname{sign}F_T)\le\prod_t\sqrt{1-4\gamma_t^2}\le e^{-2\sum_t\gamma_t^2}.\] Moreover, for the normalized margin \(m_i=y_iF_T(x_i)/\sum_t\alpha_t\), a threshold \(\theta\) gives \[\widehat P(m_i\le\theta) \le e^{\theta\sum_t\alpha_t}\prod_t Z_t =\prod_t 2\,\epsilon_t^{(1-\theta)/2}(1-\epsilon_t)^{(1+\theta)/2}.\] The first inequality compares an indicator at threshold \(\theta\) with \(\exp(\theta\sum_t\alpha_t-y_iF_T(x_i))\). Suppose \(\epsilon_t\le1/2-\gamma\) for all \(t\), with \(0<\gamma<1/2\). The factor on the right is increasing in \(\epsilon_t\) for \(\epsilon_t<(1-\theta)/2\), as differentiating its logarithm shows. For \(0\le\theta<\gamma\), each factor is thus bounded by \((1-2\gamma)^{(1-\theta)/2}(1+2\gamma)^{(1+\theta)/2}<1\). To see the strict inequality, set \(u=2\gamma\). The log of this upper bound is \(\tfrac12\log(1-u^2)+\theta\operatorname{atanh}(u)\). The inequality \(-\log(1-u^2)\ge u\operatorname{atanh}(u)\) follows since their difference has derivative \(u/(1-u^2)-\operatorname{atanh}(u)\ge0\) and vanishes at zero. Since \(\theta<u/2\), the log is negative. This gives the exponential decay in slides 33–35. For the zero-margin bound, \(\sum_t\gamma_t^2=\infty\) suffices for convergence to zero, in particular when every edge is at least \(\gamma>0\). The weight update is also mirror descent on the sample simplex, as asked on slide 19. Fix \(h_t\) and put \(g_i=y_i h_t(x_i)\). The update minimizes \(\alpha_t g^\top D+D_{\rm KL}(D\|D_t)\). Its interior stationarity condition is \(\alpha_t g_i+\log(D_i/D_t(i))+1+\nu=0\), where \(\nu\) enforces \(\sum_iD_i=1\). Exponentiating and normalizing gives the AdaBoost weights. Thus correctly classified examples lose relative weight and mistakes gain it. On slides 20–24, the first of three stumps misses 3 of 10 samples, giving \(\epsilon_1=3/10\) and \(\alpha_1=\log(7/3)/2\). Under \(D_2\), those three each weigh \(1/6\) and the remaining seven each weigh \(1/14\). The second stump misses three of the latter, so \(\epsilon_2=3/14\) and \(\alpha_2=\log(11/3)/2\). The update divides correct weights by \(2(1-\epsilon_2)=11/7\) and incorrect weights by \(2\epsilon_2=3/7\). The third stump misses three samples of weight \(1/22\) each, giving \(\epsilon_3=3/22\) and \(\alpha_3=\log(19/3)/2\). Since the three positive coefficients satisfy the strict triangle inequalities, every pair’s total exceeds the third coefficient. Their final weighted vote therefore agrees with the majority of the three stumps in this example. Functional gradient boostingTreat the predictions \(F(x_i)\) as coordinates. With squared loss, the negative gradient is the observed residual \(y_i-F(x_i)\). With a general differentiable loss, set \[r_i=-\left.\frac{\partial\ell(y_i,u)}{\partial u}\right|_{u=F(x_i)}.\] Fit a weak regressor to \((x_i,r_i)\), line-search its coefficient, and update the predictions. A tree fits an allowable approximation to the descent direction. For squared loss and a fixed tree partition, minimizing \(\sum_{i\in A}(r_i-c_A)^2/2\) on a leaf gives \(c_A=\sum_{i\in A}r_i/|A|\) by differentiation. The normal equations for that orthogonal projection also give \(r^\top h=\|h\|_2^2\). Hence shrinking the tree by \(0<\eta\le1\) decreases the squared loss by \(\eta(1-\eta/2)\|h\|_2^2\) unless \(h=0\). The lecture’s sample predictions \((0.8,1.4)\) and targets \((0.9,1.3)\) give residual targets \((0.1,-0.1)\) for the next tree. A uniform margin bound, with constantsFix a margin threshold \(0<\theta\le1\). For a normalized vote \(f\), draw \(N\) independent base hypotheses from its weights, and write \(g\) for their average. When \(yf(x)\le0\), Hoeffding gives \(\Pr_g(yg(x)>\theta/2)\le a=e^{-N\theta^2/8}\). When \(yf(x)>\theta\), it gives \(\Pr_g(yg(x)\le\theta/2)\le a\). Therefore \[P(yf\le0)\le \mathbb E_g P(yg\le\theta/2)+a,\qquad \mathbb E_g P_S(yg\le\theta/2)\le P_S(yf\le\theta)+a.\] For every one of the at most \(|\mathcal H|^N\) possible ordered sampled votes, apply the one-sided Hoeffding bound to its binary thresholded loss over \(n\) independent training examples. A union bound gives, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), \(P(yg\le\theta/2)\le P_S(yg\le\theta/2)+b\) simultaneously, where \(b=\sqrt{(N\log|\mathcal H|+\log(1/\delta))/(2n)}\). The event does not depend on the vote weights. Combining the two displays yields the uniform gap \(2a+b\). For \(n\ge2\), choose \(N=\lceil4\log n/\theta^2\rceil\) so \(a\le1/\sqrt n\). Slide 32 states the result simultaneously for all margins. To recover that quantifier, first apply the bound at \(\theta_j=2^{-j}\) for \(j\ge0\), giving the \(j\)th event failure budget \(\delta/((j+1)(j+2))\). These budgets sum to \(\delta\). For an arbitrary \(0<\theta\le1\), choose \(\theta_j\le\theta<2\theta_j\). Then \(P_S(yf\le\theta_j)\le P_S(yf\le\theta)\), and \(\theta_j^{-2}\le4\theta^{-2}\). For \(\theta\ge n^{-1/2}\) the extra confidence cost is only \(O(\log(1+\log n))\), absorbed by the leading term when \(|\mathcal H|\ge2\). For smaller \(\theta\) the displayed big-\(O\) bound is already at least one with a universal constant. The single-base-rule case is ordinary Hoeffding. This proves the margin theorem with order \(\sqrt{(\log|\mathcal H|\log n/\theta^2+\log(1/\delta))/n}\). Schapire et al., “Boosting the Margin,” Theorem 1 ChallengeShow that for finite base class, the first AdaBoost round is a greedy coordinate minimization of exponential loss, and give the exact objective improvement when the selected rule has weighted error \(\epsilon\). What changes if the class contains each sign-flipped rule? Show solution For coordinate \(h\), the minimized multiplicative ratio is \(2\sqrt{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}\) when the new coefficient is unconstrained. If coefficients may only increase, its optimum is at zero whenever \(\epsilon\ge1/2\). On \([0,1/2]\) the ratio increases with \(\epsilon\), so the best permitted coordinate is the lowest-error rule. The decrease is current loss times \(1-2\sqrt{\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}\). With a closed-under-sign-flip class, a negative coefficient on \(h\) has the same effect as a positive coefficient on \(-h\), whose weighted error is \(1-\epsilon\). Second challenge. Derive the optimal second-order score for a new tree split when leaf weights have an \(\ell_2\) penalty. Show solution to the second challenge For a leaf let \(G\) and \(H\) be the sums of sample gradients and Hessians at the current predictions. Its quadratic term is \(Gw+\tfrac12(H+\lambda)w^2\). If \(H+\lambda>0\), the minimizer is \(-G/(H+\lambda)\) and the fitted contribution is \(-G^2/(2(H+\lambda))\). Thus split gain is half the sum of the two new \(G^2/(H+\lambda)\) scores minus half the old score and minus the extra leaf penalty. A large Newton weight alone gives no guarantee of a large gain. Paper challenge · When a Newton split improves the treeIn the XGBoost quadratic fit, let the two child nodes have gradient sums \(G_L,G_R\) and positive Hessian sums \(H_L,H_R\). First set the leaf ridge penalty \(\lambda=0\) and prove that the unpenalized gain before the extra leaf cost is a weighted square of the difference of the two Newton steps. Then construct a split with \(\lambda>0\) that has strictly negative gain even when the extra leaf cost vanishes. Chen and Guestrin, “XGBoost,” §2.2, equations (5)–(7) Show paper solution Put \(a=G_L/H_L\) and \(b=G_R/H_R\). These ratios are the negatives of the separate Newton steps. Twice the score improvement at \(\lambda=0\) equals \[H_L a^2+H_R b^2-\frac{(H_La+H_Rb)^2}{H_L+H_R} =\frac{H_LH_R}{H_L+H_R}(a-b)^2.\] This is nonnegative, with equality exactly when one weight fits both child Newton steps. For \(\lambda>0\), choose identically sized children with \(G_L=G_R=1\) and \(H_L=H_R=1\). Twice the gain is \(2/(1+\lambda)-4/(2+\lambda)\), which is strictly negative. Duplicating a nonzero fitted parent weight on its children incurs the ridge penalty twice, so the two-leaf model has a different regularized objective even before the split cost is included. Sources Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, legacy Lecture 8, slides 4–12 for tree split calculations and bootstrap aggregation, 14–24 for boosting and its example, 25–28 for training error, 31–35 for margin bounds, and 37–43 for functional descent. Robert E. Schapire, Yoav Freund, Peter Bartlett, and Wee Sun Lee, Boosting the Margin: A New Explanation for the Effectiveness of Voting Methods, Theorems 1–2. Annals of Statistics paper Leo Breiman, Random Forests. Jerome H. Friedman, Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine, §§2–4. Tianqi Chen and Carlos Guestrin, XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System, §2.2. Random Forests · Gradient Boosting · XGBoost Previous lecture · Course notes · Next lecture

title: ACG 07: Ray Intersection, Acceleration, and Light Transport
summary: Ray tracing separates two questions. An intersection query finds the first surface hit along a ray. A transport calculation determines the radiance that surface sends toward the camera. Primary visibility, shad
body: Ray tracing separates two questions. An intersection query finds the first surface hit along a ray. A transport calculation determines the radiance that surface sends toward the camera. Primary visibility, shadows, and mirror reflections use the same intersection machinery with different directions and parameter intervals. Primary and secondary raysA ray is \(r(t)=o+td\), evaluated on a permitted interval. With unit direction \(d\), \(t\) is distance. For a shadow query from \(x\) to a point light at \(\ell\), choose direction \(\ell-x\) and check for an occluder strictly between \(t=0\) and \(t=1\). A closest-hit query returns the smallest permitted intersection, while an any-hit query can stop after finding an occluder. Whitted-style recursion adds mirror reflections and refractions to direct lighting. For a unit incident direction \(d\) pointing toward a surface with unit normal \(n\), reflecting flips its normal component and keeps the tangent component, yielding \(d_r=d-2(d\cdot n)n\). Snell’s law gives the transmitted direction when refraction is possible. Recursion depth bounds the workload and truncates longer paths. Diffuse interreflection involves many incident directions rather than a single secondary ray. Sphere, plane, and triangle intersectionsFor a sphere centered at \(c\) with radius \(R\), substitute \(o+td\) into \(\|r(t)-c\|^2=R^2\) and put \(m=o-c\): \[(d\cdot d)t^2+2(m\cdot d)t+(m\cdot m-R^2)=0.\] The discriminant tests for real roots. Pick the smallest root in the allowed interval, which may be the larger quadratic root when the origin is inside the sphere. For a general implicit surface \(F(x)=0\), substitution similarly reduces the search to the scalar equation \(F(o+td)=0\). For a plane through \(A\) with normal \(n\), solve \(n\cdot(o+td-A)=0\) to obtain \(t=n\cdot(A-o)/(n\cdot d)\). A zero denominator indicates a parallel ray. The numerator then determines whether the ray lies in the plane. Möller–Trumbore combines triangle plane intersection and barycentric tests. For \(e_1=B-A\) and \(e_2=C-A\), solve \[[-d\quad e_1\quad e_2] \begin{pmatrix}t\\u\\v\end{pmatrix}=o-A.\] Set \(s=o-A\), \(p=d\times e_2\), \(q=s\times e_1\), and \(D=e_1\cdot p\). Cramer’s rule gives \(u=(s\cdot p)/D\), \(v=(d\cdot q)/D\), and \(t=(e_2\cdot q)/D\). For a nonsingular system, accept only \(u,v\ge0\), \(u+v\le1\), and a parameter \(t\) within the ray interval. Acceleration structuresTo intersect an axis-aligned bounding box, solve \(b_i^-\le o_i+t d_i\le b_i^+\) for each axis with \(d_i\ne0\). The two crossing parameters have to be sorted when the direction is negative. Intersect the resulting intervals with the ray interval: \[t_{\mathrm{enter}}=\max_i t_i^-, \qquad t_{\mathrm{exit}}=\min_i t_i^+.\] When \(d_i=0\), the ray’s fixed coordinate either excludes the whole ray or imposes no additional limit. Allow a singleton interval to retain tangential intersections and zero-thickness bounds. A uniform grid stores primitive references in cells. Its DDA traversal advances to the next crossing by comparing the candidate times for each axis, updating a crossed axis by its cell width divided by the absolute direction component. A kd-tree partitions space recursively and clips the ray interval at each split. A primitive may overlap both halves. A BVH partitions primitives instead. Its child bounding boxes may overlap, but the primitive groups in a basic BVH are disjoint. PBRT, “Bounding Volume Hierarchies” Implement near-first BVH traversalA stack stores candidate nodes and their box-entry parameters. The current best hit provides a shrinking far bound. 1234567891011121314closest = no hitfar = ray.t_maxpush root if its box intersects [ray.t_min, far]while the stack is not empty: pop node, entry if entry > far: continue if node is a leaf: test its primitives against [ray.t_min, far] update closest and far for each closer hit else: intersect each child box with [ray.t_min, far] push valid children in descending entry orderreturn closest The first child popped has the nearest box entry, so its hits can prune farther boxes early. Box entry is only a lower bound. Returning immediately from the first hit leaf can be wrong when boxes overlap. For a shadow query that needs any opaque hit, an immediate return is valid. Radiometry Quantity Definition Unit Radiant flux \(\Phi\) Energy per unit time W Radiant intensity \(I\) Flux per unit solid angle W/sr Irradiance \(E\) Incoming flux per unit surface area W/m² Radiance \(L\) Flux per projected area and unit solid angle W/(m²·sr) A patch at distance \(r\) with area \(dA\) and normal angle \(\theta\) subtends \(dA\cos\theta/r^2\) at a point source facing its front. This gives irradiance \(I\cos\theta/r^2\). Integrating general incoming radiance gives \[E(x)=\int_{\Omega^+(n)} L_i(x,\omega)(n\cdot\omega)\,d\omega.\] For uniform incident radiance \(L\), write \(d\omega=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi\). The hemisphere integral of the cosine is \(\pi\), so the irradiance is \(\pi L\). PBRT, “Radiometry” The rendering equationA BRDF \(f_r\) relates outgoing radiance to irradiance from one incoming direction. Conservation of energy bounds the directional reflected fraction, \[\int_{\Omega^+(n)} f_r(x,\omega_i,\omega_o) (n\cdot\omega_o)\,d\omega_o\le1 .\] The Lambertian function \(\rho/\pi\) integrates to \(\rho\). For an opaque reflective surface, adding emission and summing reflected contributions gives the rendering equation, \[L_o(x,\omega_o)=L_e(x,\omega_o)+ \int_{\Omega^+(n)}f_r(x,\omega_i,\omega_o) L_i(x,\omega_i)(n\cdot\omega_i)\,d\omega_i .\] Under the outward direction convention, if the ray along \(\omega_i\) reaches \(y\) first through vacuum, then \(L_i(x,\omega_i)=L_o(y,-\omega_i)\). This couples outgoing radiance at different surfaces. Path tracing estimates the integral by sampling directions. Given a sample density \(p(\omega)\) in solid-angle units, each sample contributes its integrand divided by \(p(\omega)\), assuming the density is positive wherever the integrand is nonzero. Exercises Prune a BVH without discarding the nearest hit. Child boxes intersect the ray over \([2,8]\) and \([4,6]\). The first child reports a primitive hit at \(t=7\). Can the traversal skip the second child? What if the first hit were at \(t=3\)? Answer With a hit at \(7\), the second box begins at \(4\) and may contain a closer surface. With a hit at \(3\), its lower bound \(4\) is already farther away, so the second child can be skipped. Keep the exit root. A ray starts at \((0,0,1)\) with direction \((0,0,2)\) inside a sphere of radius \(3\) at the origin. Find the valid hit and its world-space distance. Answer Solve \((1+2t)^2=9\), giving \(t=1,-2\). The forward hit is at \((0,0,3)\), two world units from the ray origin. The direction is nonunit, so the valid parameter \(1\) is not the distance. Choose a sampling measure. For a Lambertian patch with constant incoming radiance \(L\), compare one-sample estimates from cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling and uniform hemisphere sampling. Answer With \(f_r=\rho/\pi\) and \(p(\omega)=\cos\theta/\pi\), the factor of cosine cancels and every sample gives \(\rho L\). Uniform hemisphere sampling uses \(p=1/(2\pi)\) and yields \(2\rho L\cos\theta\). Since a uniform hemisphere draw has \(\cos\theta\) uniform on \([0,1]\), the latter has mean \(\rho L\) and variance \((\rho L)^2/3\). ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 7, “Ray Tracing I,” November 4, 2026, slides 10–39 for rays and intersections, 40–100 for acceleration, and 101–136 for radiometry and transport. title: ML 07: Support Vector Machines and Kernels
summary: Derive hard- and soft-margin SVMs, use KKT conditions to recover the classifier, and prove positive semidefiniteness of the Gaussian kernel.
body:
Derive hard- and soft-margin SVMs, use KKT conditions to recover the classifier, and prove positive semidefiniteness of the Gaussian kernel. The closest points lie on the dashed support hyperplanes. The full margin is twice the distance from either hyperplane to the decision boundary. From distance to a convex programFor \(f(x)=w^	op x+b\), the signed distance of a labeled point to the separating hyperplane is \(y_i f(x_i)/\|w\|\). Its formula follows by moving \(x_i\) along the unit normal until \(f\) is zero. Rescaling \((w,b)\) by a positive scalar leaves that geometric distance unchanged. On separated data, normalize \(\min_i y_if(x_i)=1\). Maximizing the minimum distance becomes \[\min_{w,b}	frac12\|w\|^2 \quad	ext{s.t. } y_i(w^	op x_i+b)\ge1\quad orall i.\] The supporting hyperplanes \(f=\pm1\) are \(2/\|w\|\) apart. For nonseparable data, introduce \(\xi_i\ge0\) and require \(y_if(x_i)\ge1-\xi_i\). Minimize \(\|w\|^2/2+C\sum_i\xi_i\). With \(w,b\) fixed, the best slack is \(\xi_i=(1-y_if(x_i))_+\), which yields the hinge-loss objective. Comparing with an average hinge loss plus \(\lambda\|w\|^2/2\) gives \(\lambda=1/(nC)\). Deriving the dualConsider first \(\min_{x\ge b} x^2\). For \(\alpha\ge0\), the Lagrangian \(x^2+\alpha(b-x)\) is at most \(x^2\) on the feasible set. Its infimum over all \(x\) is \(b\alpha-\alpha^2/4\), attained at \(x=\alpha/2\). Maximizing this concave function over \(\alpha\ge0\) gives \(\alpha^\star=\max(2b,0)\) and optimal value \(\max(b,0)^2\), matching the primal minimum at \(x^\star=\max(b,0)\). The KKT conditions are \(x\ge b\), \(\alpha\ge0\), \(2x=\alpha\), and \(\alpha(x-b)=0\). When \(b=0\), the constraint is active at zero even though its optimal multiplier vanishes. With inequality multipliers \(\alpha_i, eta_i\ge0\) for the margin and slack constraints, respectively, the Lagrangian is \[\mathcal L=	frac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i+ \sum_i\alpha_i(1-\xi_i-y_i(w^	op x_i+b))-\sum_i eta_i\xi_i.\] For feasible primal variables, the added terms are nonpositive, so \(\inf_{w,b,\xi}\mathcal L\) is a lower bound on the primal optimum. Its infimum in \(b\) and \(\xi\) is finite only if their linear coefficients vanish. Minimizing in \(w\) completes the square. These calculations give \[w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i x_i,\qquad \sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0,\qquad C-\alpha_i- eta_i=0.\] Substitution gives \[\max_{0\le\alpha_i\le C,\,\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0} \left\{\sum_i\alpha_i-	frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j x_i^	op x_jight\}.\] Soft-margin strict feasibility follows from \(w=b=0,\xi_i=2\). Hard-margin strict feasibility follows by scaling any separator by a sufficiently large factor. Slater’s condition yields strong duality in either case. For the hard-margin problem there is no slack coefficient to impose an upper bound on \(\alpha_i\). Complementary slackness gives \(\alpha_i(1-\xi_i-y_if(x_i))=0\) and \((C-\alpha_i)\xi_i=0\). Strictly outside the margin, \(\alpha_i=0\). An interior multiplier \(0<\alpha_i<C\) has zero slack and \(y_if(x_i)=1\), hence \(b=y_i-w^	op x_i\). At \(\alpha_i=C\), the point may be inside the margin or misclassified. If there are no interior multipliers, use the corresponding KKT inequalities to find the allowable interval for \(b\). If strong duality holds and the optima are attained, \(d(\alpha^\star)\le\mathcal L(x^\star,\alpha^\star)\le f(x^\star)\) has equal endpoints. The first equality makes \(x^\star\) an unconstrained minimizer of the Lagrangian in the primal variables. The second makes each nonpositive product of a multiplier with its inequality vanish. This derives stationarity and complementary slackness without differentiating with respect to a multiplier at the boundary of its admissible range. In the bias-free hard-margin case of slide 13, minimizing over \(w\) gives \(\sum_i\alpha_i-\|\sum_i\alpha_i y_i x_i\|^2/2\). The constraints are only \(\alpha_i\ge0\) because there is no free intercept. For a free intercept, let \(r_i=y_i-w^	op x_i\). If \(\alpha_i=0\), KKT requires \(b\ge r_i\) for \(y_i=1\) and \(b\le r_i\) for \(y_i=-1\). If \(\alpha_i=C\), these inequalities reverse because the point’s margin is at most one. Their intersection gives the allowable intercepts when there is no interior multiplier. Kernels and finite Gram matricesA feature map induces \(K(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)angle\). For any finite sample and real vector \(a\), the Gram matrix satisfies \[a^	op K a=\left\|\sum_i a_i\phi(x_i)ight\|^2\ge0.\] Conversely, a symmetric kernel whose every finite Gram matrix is positive semidefinite induces a feature space. Start with finitely supported formal sums of symbols \(\delta_x\), set \(\langle\delta_x,\delta_zangle=K(x,z)\), and extend bilinearly. Cauchy–Schwarz for this semidefinite form follows by requiring \(\|u+tv\|^2\ge0\) for all \(t\). Therefore zero-norm vectors are orthogonal to the whole space. Quotient them out, take the Hilbert completion, and map \(x\) to the equivalence class of \(\delta_x\). This construction suffices for the kernel trick. Mercer expansions additionally impose conditions on the integral operator and its domain. The SVM dual replaces dot products by \(K\). The quadratic term has matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(y)K\operatorname{diag}(y)\), which remains positive semidefinite, so the maximization remains concave. The prediction is \(f(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i K(x_i,x)+b\). The inhomogeneous quadratic feature map of slides 19–20 is \[\phi(x)=\left(1,\,(\sqrt2 x_i)_i,\,(x_i^2)_i,\,(\sqrt2 x_ix_j)_{i<j}ight).\] Its inner product expands to \(1+2\sum_i x_i z_i+\sum_i x_i^2z_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}x_ix_jz_iz_j\). The last two sums are \((x^	op z)^2\), so the whole expression equals \((1+x^	op z)^2\). Evaluating the latter takes \(O(d)\) operations despite the \(1+2d+d(d-1)/2\) explicit features. A dense Gram matrix evaluates at most \(n(n+1)/2\) distinct pairs by symmetry. Evaluation at a new point uses only kernels against support vectors. For the Gaussian, write \[K(x,z)=e^{-\|x\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}e^{-\|z\|^2/(2\sigma^2)} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} rac{(x^	op z)^m}{m!\sigma^{2m}}.\] Each power is a kernel because \((x^	op z)^m=\langle x^{\otimes m},z^{\otimes m}angle\), including the constant kernel for \(m=0\). Partial sums have nonnegative Gram quadratic forms, and their finite-entry limits do also. Multiplying by the point factors applies the same diagonal scaling to both sides of the Gram matrix. This proves the Gaussian is a valid kernel. ChallengesProblem 1Strengthen the Gaussian proof: show its Gram matrix is positive definite for any finite set of pairwise distinct points and any finite \(\sigma>0\). Show solution If a quadratic form is zero, the preceding expansion expresses it as a sum of nonnegative squared norms. Writing \(b_i=a_i e^{-\|x_i\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), every tensor moment \(\sum_i b_i x_i^{\otimes m}\) must vanish. Pick a vector \(v\) such that the numbers \(s_i=v^	op x_i\) are all distinct. This is possible because the forbidden vectors lie in a finite union of proper hyperplanes. Contracting with \(v^{\otimes m}\) gives \(\sum_i b_is_i^m=0\) for \(m=0,\ldots,n-1\). The Vandermonde determinant is \(\prod_{i<j}(s_j-s_i)
e0\), so all \(b_i\) and hence all \(a_i\) vanish. Problem 2Solve the one-dimensional soft-margin SVM for \((-1,-1)\) and \((1,1)\) at arbitrary \(C>0\). Which intercepts are optimal? Show solution The balance constraint gives \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha\), and the dual objective is \(2\alpha-2\alpha^2\). Hence \(\alpha=\min(C,1/2)\) and \(w=2\alpha\). If \(C>1/2\), both multipliers are interior, so the margin equalities force \(b=0\). If \(C\le1/2\), the positive multipliers give \(\xi_1=1-w+b\) and \(\xi_2=1-w-b\). The feasible interval is \(|b|\le1-w\), reducing to zero at \(C=1/2\). All intercepts in the interval have the same total slack and satisfy KKT. Paper challenge · Dual coordinates for squared hinge lossWork in the bias-free linear formulation of Hsieh et al., “A Dual Coordinate Descent Method for Large-Scale Linear SVM,” §3. Starting from \(\min_w \|w\|_2^2/2+C\sum_i(1-y_iw^	op x_i)_+^2\), derive the dual diagonal correction, the exact projected coordinate update, and a certificate that every coordinate is optimal simultaneously. Explain how one sparse dot product and one sparse vector update replace a dense Gram row. Finally, prove geometric convergence in expectation when each coordinate is chosen uniformly at random. Show paper solution Introduce slack \(\xi_i\) with \(\xi_i\ge 1-y_iw^	op x_i\). Minimizing \(\xi_i^2\) over this half-line chooses \((1-y_iw^	op x_i)_+\), so a separate positivity constraint is unnecessary. With margin multipliers \(\alpha_i\ge0\), the unconstrained minimizers in the Lagrangian are \(w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i x_i\) and \(\xi_i=\alpha_i/(2C)\). Thus the dual in minimization form is \[F(\alpha)=	frac12\alpha^	op\left(Q+	frac1{2C}Iight)\alpha-\mathbf1^	op\alpha, \qquad Q_{ij}=y_i y_j x_i^	op x_j,\quad \alpha_i\ge0.\] Strong duality follows from strict primal feasibility. Set \(D=Q+I/(2C)\). Along coordinate \(i\), the objective variation for change \(d\) is \(G_i d+D_{ii}d^2/2\), with \(G_i=y_iw^	op x_i+\alpha_i/(2C)-1\) and \(d\ge-\alpha_i\). Completing the square gives \(\alpha_i^+=\max(0,\alpha_i-G_i/D_{ii})\) with \(D_{ii}=\|x_i\|_2^2+1/(2C)>0\). Apply the update \(w^+=w+(\alpha_i^+-\alpha_i)y_i x_i\). Each operation visits only the nonzero entries of \(x_i\). For all coordinates define the projected derivative as \(G_i\) if \(\alpha_i>0\) and \(\min(G_i,0)\) at zero. Its simultaneous vanishing is necessary by feasible one-dimensional derivatives. It is sufficient because then \(
abla F(\alpha)^	op( eta-\alpha)\ge0\) for every \( eta\ge0\), and convexity gives \(F( eta)\ge F(\alpha)\). The diagonal correction also makes \(F\) strongly convex and its dual optimizer unique. For ordinary hinge loss, the slack term is linear, yielding \(0\le\alpha_i\le C\), zero diagonal correction, and clipping at both endpoints. A free intercept imposes \(\sum_i y_i\alpha_i=0\) and generally requires coordinated changes to two multipliers. For the convergence proof, let \(\mu=1/(2C)>0\), \(L_{\max}=\max_i D_{ii}\), and \(s=\alpha^\star-\alpha\). For \(0\le t\le1\), \(\alpha+t s_i e_i\) is a feasible coordinate step, so the exact coordinate update at \(i\) achieves at least as much decrease. Conditional on the current iterate and averaging the quadratic expansions over uniform \(i\) gives \[\mathbb E_i[F(\alpha^+)-F(\alpha)] \le rac tn
abla F(\alpha)^	op s+ rac{t^2L_{\max}}{2n}\|s\|^2.\] Strong convexity implies \(
abla F(\alpha)^	op s\le F(\alpha^\star)-F(\alpha)-\mu\|s\|^2/2\). Choose \(t=\mu/L_{\max}\le1\) so the squared terms cancel. The gap contracts in conditional expectation by \(1-\mu/(nL_{\max})\) per step, and repeated expectations give geometric convergence. This proof uses the positive diagonal correction in the squared-hinge dual. Sources Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, Lecture 7. Legacy and 2026 slides 3–7 for margins and slack, 9–15 for Lagrangian examples and SVM duality, and 16–22 for feature maps and positive semidefinite kernels. Baxter Tyson Smith, Lagrange Multipliers Tutorial in the Context of Support Vector Machines, §§4–5. CMU 10-315, Support Vector Machines: Dual Formulation and Kernel, local lecture supplement. Cho-Jui Hsieh, Kai-Wei Chang, Chih-Jen Lin, Sathiya Keerthi, and S. Sundararajan, A Dual Coordinate Descent Method for Large-Scale Linear SVM, §3.
