title: ACG 06: Shading, Texture Filtering, and Shadows
summary: Shading computes the appearance of a visible sample. Its result depends on the local surface orientation, the attributes interpolated across the projected triangle, the area of the texture seen by the sample, a
body: Shading computes the appearance of a visible sample. Its result depends on the local surface orientation, the attributes interpolated across the projected triangle, the area of the texture seen by the sample, and whether the light reaches the surface. Lambert and Blinn–PhongLet \(n\) be the unit normal, \(\ell\) the direction toward the source, and \(v\) the direction toward the viewer. A patch of physical area \(dA\) presents projected area \(dA\max(0,n\cdot\ell)\) to incoming light. For a point source with radiant intensity \(I\) in the direction toward the surface and distance \(r\), the resulting irradiance is \[E=\frac I{r^2}\max(0,n\cdot\ell).\] A Lambertian surface gives a direction-independent outgoing radiance \(kE\). The total outgoing flux per surface area is \(kE\int_{\Omega^+}\cos\theta\,d\omega=\pi kE\). Therefore a diffuse reflectance \(\rho\) gives \(k=\rho/\pi\). This normalization connects the classroom cosine term to a physically defined BRDF. Blinn–Phong estimates a specular lobe via \(\max(0,n\cdot h)^p\), where \(h\) is the normalized \(\ell+v\) and the exponent \(p\) controls the lobe width. Local models can include ambient light as a constant approximation to unresolved transport. Flat shading uses one normal per face. Gouraud shading interpolates colors computed at the vertices and can miss a highlight entirely if it lies between them. Phong shading interpolates normals, renormalizes them, and evaluates lighting per fragment. Perspective-correct interpolationConsider clip positions \(c_i\) with fourth components \(w_i\) and affine weights \(\mu_i\) before projection. For the covered screen point, the perspective divide gives \[\frac{\sum_i\mu_i(c_i)_{xy}}{\sum_i\mu_iw_i} =\sum_i\frac{\mu_iw_i}{\sum_j\mu_jw_j} \frac{(c_i)_{xy}}{w_i}.\] By uniqueness of barycentric coordinates, screen weights \(\lambda_i\) are \(\mu_iw_i/\sum_j\mu_jw_j\). Solving for the original weights gives the rule for vertex attribute \(a\), \[a=\frac{\sum_i\lambda_i a_i/w_i}{\sum_i\lambda_i/w_i}.\] In a rasterizer, compute \(a_i/w_i\) and \(1/w_i\) at the vertices, interpolate both independently in screen space, then take the quotient. In texture coordinates, this produces the correct texture motion when a surface tilts relative to the camera. UV seams may duplicate a geometric vertex in the attribute buffer so adjacent triangles can use different UV values. Filtering texturesMagnification calls for reconstruction between texels. With fractional offsets \(s,t\in[0,1]\), bilinear interpolation produces \[c(s,t)=(1-t)\left[(1-s)c_{00}+sc_{10}\right] +t\left[(1-s)c_{01}+sc_{11}\right].\] Minification calls for an average across the texture footprint. A mipmap filters and halves both texture dimensions at each level. The full chain for a large square power-of-two texture approaches \(1+1/4+1/16+\cdots=4/3\) times the base storage. Select a mip level from derivativesEstimate texel-space footprint vectors from the derivatives of normalized UV coordinates. Convert normalized coordinates to texel units with the base width and height before taking vector lengths. 123456789101112from math import floor, hypot, log2def sample_trilinear(texture, uv, grad_x, grad_y): w, h = texture.base_size a = hypot(grad_x[0]*w, grad_x[1]*h) b = hypot(grad_y[0]*w, grad_y[1]*h) lod = min(log2(max(1.0, a, b)), texture.last_level) low = floor(lod) high = min(low + 1, texture.last_level) s = lod - low return ((1 - s)*texture.bilinear(low, uv) + s*texture.bilinear(high, uv)) A derivative magnitude of one texel per screen pixel uses level zero. A magnitude of eight selects level three. Averaging neighboring mip levels reduces transitions between discrete estimates. An elongated anisotropic footprint still calls for more sampling along its long axis than along its short axis. Isotropic mip selection based on the larger length can blur details across the short axis. Texture channels may also store normals, volume densities, or displacements. For a local height field \((u,v,h(u,v))\), crossing the two partial derivatives gives the normal \((-h_u,-h_v,1)\). Bump and normal mapping change the direction used for shading. Displacement moves surface positions and therefore can change the silhouette or cast shadows. Two-pass shadow mappingFirst, rasterize from the light and store the nearest depth for each sample. Then rasterize from the eye. Project each camera-visible fragment into the light’s clip coordinates, divide by its fourth component, and compare the result with the shadow depth in that light-space sample. If the query is farther by more than a tolerance, a surface lies between it and the source. Too little bias reveals artifacts from finite precision and resolution. Too much moves the shadow away from its caster. An area light requires integrating visibility over its surface; one shadow view samples only one position. Exercises Quantify interpolation drift. Triangle vertices have clip \(w=(1,2,4)\), scalar attributes \((0,1,1)\), and screen weights \((1/2,1/4,1/4)\). Calculate the correct scalar and the screen-linear error. Answer The denominator is \(1/2+1/8+1/16=11/16\). The numerator is \(1/8+1/16=3/16\), giving \(3/11\). The direct estimate is \(1/2\), an overestimate of \(5/22\). Select the filtering footprint. For a \(1024\times512\) base map, normalized derivatives along screen \(x\) and \(y\) are \((1/256,0)\) and \((0,1/64)\). Find the mip level and estimate the ratio between the two footprint axes. Answer The vectors in texel units are \((4,0)\) and \((0,8)\), so max-length mip selection yields \(\log_2 8=3\). These orthogonal footprint axes are in a ratio of \(2:1\). An isotropic level covers approximately eight texels on both axes and filters across twice the short-axis length. Compare diffuse normalization. A surface with \(\rho=0.7\) receives irradiance \(E=10\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\). Compare outgoing radiance and total flux per unit area for the expressions \(\rho E\) and \(\rho E/\pi\) interpreted as radiance. Answer The normalized radiance is \(7/\pi\,\mathrm{W/(m^2\,sr)}\) and its hemisphere integral is \(7\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\). Taking the radiance as \(7\,\mathrm{W/(m^2\,sr)}\) yields \(7\pi\,\mathrm{W/m^2}\), more than twice the incident power density. ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 6, “Shading,” October 28, 2026, slides 5–44 for local shading, 45–95 for interpolation and texture queries, and 96–124 for texture applications and shadows. title: ML 06: Linear Models, Sparsity, and Compressed Sensing
summary: Derive least squares, perceptron convergence, logistic curvature, and soft thresholding, then prove when sparse signals can be recovered.
body:
Derive least squares, perceptron convergence, logistic curvature, and soft thresholding, then prove when sparse signals can be recovered. The diamond has a minimizer on a coordinate axis. The disk has a minimizer with two nonzero coordinates. Least squares and ridgeFor a design matrix \(X\) and responses \(y\), stationarity of \(\|Xw-y\|^2/2\) gives \(X^	op Xw=X^	op y\). The fitted response is the orthogonal projection of \(y\) onto \(\operatorname{col}(X)\), even when several parameter vectors attain it. Ridge adds \(\lambda\|w\|^2/2\). With \(\lambda>0\) and thin SVD \(X=U\Sigma V^	op\), \[w_\lambda=(X^	op X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^	op y =\sum_i rac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2+\lambda}\langle u_i,yangle v_i.\] This follows by diagonalizing \(X^	op X\) in the right-singular basis. In a direction with small positive singular value, least squares uses a large inverse gain \(1/\sigma_i\). Ridge shrinks that gain. The normal equation is a linear system that can be solved without forming the inverse. For the mean loss \(\ell(w)=\|Xw-y\|_2^2/(2n)\), differentiation gives \(
abla\ell=X^	op(Xw-y)/n\) and \(
abla^2\ell=X^	op X/n\). Adding \(\lambda\|w\|_2^2/2\) shifts every Hessian eigenvalue by \(\lambda\), so the new objective is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex. Its exact gradient step is \(w^+=(1-\eta\lambda)w-\eta
abla\ell(w)\). Shrinking after a data-gradient step also scales that gradient, producing a difference of \(\eta^2\lambda
abla\ell(w)\). An intercept can be absorbed by a constant feature. Remove it from the regularizer if the intercept should remain unpenalized. Let \(R(w)\) be either \(\|w\|_2^2/2\) or \(\|w\|_1\). If \(w_\lambda\) minimizes \(\ell+\lambda R\) with \(\lambda\ge0\), it minimizes \(\ell\) over \(R(w)\le R(w_\lambda)\), since a feasible point with smaller loss would improve the penalized objective. Conversely, for a radius \(c>0\), \(w=0\) is strictly feasible for \(R(w)\le c\). Slater’s condition gives a multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\) with \(0\in
abla\ell(w)+\lambda\partial R(w)\) and \(\lambda(R(w)-c)=0\), so a constrained minimizer also minimizes the penalized loss. For \(\lambda_2>\lambda_1\), add the two penalized optimality inequalities with their competitors swapped to get \((\lambda_2-\lambda_1)(R(w_{\lambda_2})-R(w_{\lambda_1}))\le0\). The origin constraint \(c=0\) may require a limiting penalty. Why the perceptron terminates on separated dataTake labels \(\pm1\), norms \(\|x_i\|\le R\), and a unit vector \(w^\star\) with \(y_i(w^\star)^	op x_i\ge\gamma>0\). Starting at zero, update \(w\gets w+y_ix_i\) on a mistake or tie. After \(M\) updates, \((w^\star)^	op w_M\ge M\gamma\) by summing the projected increments. Each update also satisfies \[\|w+y_ix_i\|^2=\|w\|^2+2y_iw^	op x_i+\|x_i\|^2\le\|w\|^2+R^2.\] Thus \(M\gamma\le\|w_M\|\le R\sqrt M\), proving \(M\le(R/\gamma)^2\). A bias is handled by augmenting the vectors with a constant feature and recomputing the radius and margin. Logistic likelihood and cross-entropyFor \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), a Bernoulli model uses \(p_i=\sigma(s_i)\), where \(s_i=w^	op x_i\). Its negative log likelihood equals \(\log(1+e^{s_i})-y_i s_i\). Since \(\sigma'(s)=\sigma(s)(1-\sigma(s))\), \[
abla_w\ell_i=(p_i-y_i)x_i,\qquad 
abla_w^2\ell_i=p_i(1-p_i)x_ix_i^	op.\] The Hessian is positive semidefinite and bounded by \(x_ix_i^	op/4\). The loss equals cross-entropy. At a fixed input, cross-entropy between the true Bernoulli parameter \(q\) and prediction \(p\) is \(H(q)+D_{m KL}(q\|p)\), minimized at \(p=q\) by nonnegativity of KL. For separable training data the unregularized empirical loss approaches zero along a growing separating direction and has no finite minimizer. For general probability vectors, subtracting the entropy \(-\sum_iq_i\log q_i\) from the cross-entropy \(-\sum_iq_i\log p_i\) gives \(\sum_{i:q_i>0}q_i\log(q_i/p_i)\). If \(p_i=0<q_i\) the divergence is infinite. Otherwise \(\log z\le z-1\) at \(z=p_i/q_i\) gives \(D_{m KL}(q\|p)\ge1-\sum_{i:q_i>0}p_i\ge0\). Equality forces \(p=q\). For a one-hot class \(c\), the derivative of \(-\log p_c\) with respect to \(p_c\) is \(-1/p_c\). Differentiating through softmax yields the logit gradient \(p-q\). The binary threshold \(p=1/2\) corresponds to score zero. On a two-element probability vector the lecture’s alternative \(\ell_1\) loss is \(2|p-y|\). LASSO and proximal gradientWith \(X^	op X=I\), the LASSO objective \(\|Xw-y\|^2/2+\lambda\|w\|_1\) separates into \(	frac12(u-z)^2+\lambda|u|\) with \(z=(X^	op y)_j\). Stationarity gives \(u=z-\lambda\) when \(u>0\) and \(u=z+\lambda\) when \(u<0\). At zero, the subgradient interval contains zero exactly when \(|z|\le\lambda\). Therefore \[S_\lambda(z)=\operatorname{sign}(z)(|z|-\lambda)_+.\] For general \(X\), minimize the first-order loss model plus a quadratic proximity penalty and the \(\ell_1\) term. Completing the square gives the proximal update \(w^+=S_{\eta\lambda}(w-\eta X^	op(Xw-y))\) coordinatewise. The same threshold determines which coordinates become exactly zero. Sparse recovery and restricted geometryFrom measurements \(y=Aw\), basis pursuit solves \(\min_z\|z\|_1\) subject to \(Az=y\). Uniform unique recovery of every \(s\)-sparse \(w\) is equivalent to the null-space property \[\|h_S\|_1<\|h_{S^c}\|_1\qquad(0
e h\in\ker A,\ |S|\le s).\] Sufficiency follows from \(\|w+h\|_1\ge\|w\|_1-\|h_S\|_1+\|h_{S^c}\|_1>\|w\|_1\) for \(S=\operatorname{supp}(w)\). If the inequality fails, take \(w=-h_S\) and competitor \(h_{S^c}=w+h\). Both have the same measurements and the competitor has norm no greater. The order-\(k\) restricted isometry property (RIP) asks that \((1-\delta_k)\|z\|^2\le\|Az\|^2\le(1+\delta_k)\|z\|^2\) for every \(k\)-sparse vector. The difference of two \(s\)-sparse candidates is \(2s\)-sparse. If both have residual at most \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta_{2s}<1\), their distance is at most \(2\varepsilon/\sqrt{1-\delta_{2s}}\) by the lower RIP inequality and the triangle inequality. Exact measurements give uniqueness within the sparse class. This argument concerns sparse candidates. A basis-pursuit guarantee needs to control differences that may be dense. Why the order-\(2s\) RIP can recover dense but compressible signalsSuppose \(A\) has order-\(2s\) RIP constant \(\delta<1/(1+\sqrt2)\) and \(\hat x\) solves basis pursuit from \(Ax\). Let \(h=\hat x-x\), and let \(S_0\) index the \(s\) largest coordinates of \(x\) in magnitude. Since \(\|\hat x\|_1\le\|x\|_1\), the triangle inequality on \(S_0\) and its complement gives \[\|h_{S_0^c}\|_1\le\|h_{S_0}\|_1+2\|x_{S_0^c}\|_1.\] Break \(S_0^c\) into blocks \(S_1,S_2,\ldots\) of size \(s\) in decreasing order of \(|h_i|\), except possibly the final block. Each entry in \(S_j\) is bounded by the average absolute entry in \(S_{j-1}\) for \(j\ge2\), so \(\sum_{j\ge2}\|h_{S_j}\|\le\|h_{S_0^c}\|_1/\sqrt s\). For disjointly supported, unit, \(s\)-sparse vectors \(u,v\), the sum and difference are \(2s\)-sparse and have squared norms \(2\). Polarization and the two-sided RIP give \[4|\langle Au,Avangle| =\left|\|A(u+v)\|_2^2-\|A(u-v)\|_2^2ight|\le4\delta.\] Rescaling gives \(|\langle Au,Avangle|\le\delta\|u\|\|v\|\) for nonunit vectors. Set \(H=S_0\cup S_1\). Because \(Ah=0\), \(\|Ah_H\|^2=-\sum_{j\ge2}\langle Ah_H,Ah_{S_j}angle\). Split \(h_H\) into its two blocks. The bound \(\|h_{S_0}\|+\|h_{S_1}\|\le\sqrt2\|h_H\|\) then gives \[(1-\delta)\|h_H\|^2 \le\sqrt2\delta\|h_H\|\sum_{j\ge2}\|h_{S_j}\|.\] With \(ho=\sqrt2\delta/(1-\delta)<1\) and \(\sigma=\|x_{S_0^c}\|_1/\sqrt s\), these estimates give \(\|h_H\|\leho(\|h_H\|+2\sigma)\) and hence \(\|h_H\|\le2ho\sigma/(1-ho)\). Finally \(\|h\|\le\|h_H\|+\sum_{j\ge2}\|h_{S_j}\|\le2\|h_H\|+2\sigma\), so \[\|\hat x-x\|_2\le rac{2(1+ho)}{1-ho} rac{\|x_{S_0^c}\|_1}{\sqrt s}.\] The right-hand side vanishes for an \(s\)-sparse signal. With measured noise the equality \(Ah=0\) is replaced by a residual bound and contributes an additional error term. Why Gaussian measurements workFor a matrix with independent \(N(0,1/m)\) entries, any fixed unit vector has squared measured norm distributed as \(\chi^2_m/m\). Its deviation outside \(1\pm t\) has probability at most \(2e^{-mt^2/8}\) for \(0<t<1\). Indeed, the moment-generating function of \(\chi^2_m\) is \((1-2s)^{-m/2}\). Markov’s inequality with \(s=t/(2(1+t))\) on the upper side gives \(\exp[-m(t-\log(1+t))/2]\). With \(s=-t/(2(1-t))\) on the lower side it gives \(\exp[-m(-t-\log(1-t))/2]\). The quantities \(t-\log(1+t)=\int_0^t u/(1+u)\,du\) and \(-t-\log(1-t)=\int_0^t u/(1-u)\,du\) are at least \(t^2/4\) and \(t^2/2\), respectively. On one support of size \(k\), take a maximal \(1/4\)-separated set of unit vectors. Maximality gives a \(1/4\)-net, and the disjoint radius-\(1/8\) balls about its points all fit in a radius-\(9/8\) ball, giving at most \(9^k\) points by volume. For \(B=A_S^	op A_S-I\), if all net values satisfy \(|v^	op Bv|\le\delta/2\), then \(\|B\|\le\delta\): approximate a maximizing unit vector by a net vector and bound the quadratic-form difference by \(2\|B\|/4\). The union bound over at most \((ed/k)^k\) supports and \(9^k\) net points per support gives \(m\gtrsim\delta^{-2}(k\log(ed/k)+\log(1/\alpha))\) for failure probability at most \(\alpha\). In particular, the preceding tail estimate shows the failure probability is at most \(2 inom dk9^ke^{-m\delta^2/32}\), so \(m\ge32\delta^{-2}[k\log(9ed/k)+\log(2/\alpha)]\) suffices. The slides state the sufficient condition \(m\ge216k\log(120d/(\alpha\delta))/\delta^2\). Both describe the standard Gaussian scaling. Applying the fixed-vector estimate directly to normalized pairwise differences of a finite set proves the Gaussian Johnson–Lindenstrauss bound with \(O(\delta^{-2}(\log n+\log(1/\alpha)))\) measurements for \(n\) points. For a fixed orthogonal basis \(\Psi\), the transpose of each row of \(A\Psi\) is a linear transform of a jointly Gaussian vector, with covariance \(\Psi^	op(I/m)\Psi=I/m\). Zero covariance gives independence for Gaussian coordinates, and the rows remain independent. Thus \(A\Psi\) has the same law as \(A\), giving the same high-probability guarantee for signals sparse in that basis. Recovery with a nonlinear generatorLet \(S=\{G(z):z\in\mathbb R^k\}\) and \(y=Ax^\star+\eta\). Suppose \(A\) has a lower secant bound \(\|A(u-v)\|\ge(2/3)\|u-v\|\) for all \(u,v\in S\). Choose a nearest comparator \(u\) in the closure of \(S\), which exists because the distance to \(x^\star\) has bounded sublevel sets. The secant and residual inequalities extend to the closure by continuity. For this fixed comparator, suppose \(\|A(u-x^\star)\|\le(5/3)\|u-x^\star\|\). If \(\hat x=G(\hat z)\) has measured residual within \(\varepsilon\) of the infimum, then \[	frac23\|\hat x-u\| \le\|A(\hat x-u)\| \le2\|A(u-x^\star)\|+2\|\eta\|+\varepsilon.\] Divide by \(2/3\) and add \(\|u-x^\star\|\) to obtain a reconstruction error at most \(6\inf_z\|G(z)-x^\star\|+3\|\eta\|+2\varepsilon\). For a fixed depth-\(D\) ReLU generator of layer width at most \(c\), the Gaussian sample bound is order \(kD\log c\). Each feasible activation pattern gives an affine output on the corresponding latent region. A layer cuts such a region by at most \(c\) hyperplanes in \(\mathbb R^k\), creating at most \(\sum_{j=0}^k{c\choose j}\) pieces (add one hyperplane and count its induced regions inductively). Across all layers the number of pieces is at most \((c+1)^{O(kD)}\). Secants lie in a union of subspaces of dimension at most \(2k+1\), one for each pair of affine images. Apply Gaussian concentration and the net argument to each and union bound. This yields the lower secant inequality with probability \(1-e^{-\Omega(m)}\) for sufficiently many measurements. The upper comparator bound also follows from fixed-vector concentration. The argument assumes approximate minimization of the measured residual and keeps that error explicit. ChallengesProblem 1Suppose all columns of \(A\) have unit Euclidean norm and mutual coherence \(\mu=\max_{i
e j}|a_i^	op a_j|\). Prove basis pursuit recovers every \(s\)-sparse vector if \((2s-1)\mu<1\). Show solution For \(h\in\ker A\), take the inner product of \(\sum_jh_ja_j=0\) with \(a_i\). This gives \(|h_i|\le\mu\sum_{j
e i}|h_j|\), hence \((1+\mu)|h_i|\le\mu\|h\|_1\). Sum over any \(S\) of size at most \(s\) to obtain \(\|h_S\|_1\le s\mu\|h\|_1/(1+\mu)<\|h\|_1/2\). This is exactly the strict null-space inequality for nonzero \(h\). Problem 2For least squares penalized by \(\lambda_1\|w\|_1+\lambda_2\|w\|^2/2\), derive the solution when \(X^	op X=I\). Prove uniqueness for arbitrary \(X\) when \(\lambda_2>0\). Show solution Put \(z=X^	op y\). Each coordinate minimizes \((1+\lambda_2)u^2/2-z_ju+\lambda_1|u|\), giving \(S_{\lambda_1}(z_j)/(1+\lambda_2)\) by its three subgradient cases. For arbitrary \(X\), the quadratic Hessian obeys \(X^	op X+\lambda_2I\succeq\lambda_2I\). Adding the convex penalty preserves strong convexity, and coercivity gives existence, hence the minimizer is unique. Paper challenge · Basis pursuit with noisy measurementsIn the noisy model \(y=Ax+e\) with \(\|e\|_2\le\varepsilon\), replace exact feasibility by \(\|Az-y\|_2\le\varepsilon\) and minimize \(\|z\|_1\). Prove a bound with the same \(\delta_{2s}<\sqrt2-1\) as the noiseless theorem, and give explicit coefficients of \(\varepsilon\) and the sparsity tail. This develops the noisy recovery theorem from Candès’s RIP analysis. Candès, “The Restricted Isometry Property and Its Implications for Compressed Sensing” Show paper solution Both \(x\) and \(\widehat x\) are feasible, so \(\|Ah\|_2\le2\varepsilon\) for \(h=\widehat x-x\). The cone inequality and block tail estimates above still hold because \(x\) is a valid competitor in the norm minimization. Keep \(H=S_0\cup S_1\), let \(\sigma=\|x_{S_0^c}\|_1/\sqrt s\), and write \(Ah_H=Ah-\sum_{j\ge2}Ah_{S_j}\). Taking its inner product with \(Ah_H\) gives \[(1-\delta)\|h_H\|^2 \le2\varepsilon\sqrt{1+\delta}\|h_H\| +\sqrt2\delta\|h_H\|\sum_{j\ge2}\|h_{S_j}\|.\] The first term uses Cauchy–Schwarz and the upper RIP bound. Divide by \(\|h_H\|\) when positive, use \(\sum_{j\ge2}\|h_{S_j}\|\le\|h_H\|+2\sigma\), and take \(ho=\sqrt2\delta/(1-\delta)\). Rearranging gives \(\|h_H\|\le[2\varepsilon\sqrt{1+\delta}/(1-\delta)+2ho\sigma]/(1-ho)\). This bound also holds when the head is zero. Adding the tail yields \[\|\widehat x-x\|_2\le  rac{4\sqrt{1+\delta}}{1-(1+\sqrt2)\delta}\,\varepsilon + rac{2(1+ho)}{1-ho}\,\sigma .\] The two terms separately control measurement noise and the departure from exact sparsity. Sources Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, Lecture 6 and Problem Set 4. Both decks, slides 3–16 for linear methods, 19–29 for regularization, and 31–43 for sparse measurements. Legacy slides 44–59 give the block proof of RIP recovery, 61–62 the Gaussian result and basis change, and 64–67 the generator guarantee. Their 2026 counterparts are slides 42–43, 45–46, and 48–52. Michael Collins, Convergence Proof for the Perceptron Algorithm, pp. 1–2. Shai Shalev-Shwartz, Compressed Sensing: Basic Results and Self-Contained Proofs, Theorems 1–4 and §§3.1–3.3. title: ACG 05: Rasterization, Sampling, and Visibility
summary: Rasterization converts projected geometry into samples on a finite grid. Triangle edge tests decide which samples are covered, filtering limits aliasing, and the depth buffer resolves opaque visibility at each
body:
Rasterization converts projected geometry into samples on a finite grid. Triangle edge tests decide which samples are covered, filtering limits aliasing, and the depth buffer resolves opaque visibility at each sample. Sampling a projected triangleA pixel indexed by \((i,j)\) can be represented by the square \([i,i+1]	imes[j,j+1]\). Center sampling tests the continuous triangle at \((i+	frac12,j+	frac12)\). A covered sample initially says nothing about the rest of the pixel. A triangle can cross a pixel without touching its center. For counterclockwise vertices \(A,B,C\) in a coordinate system with \(y\) pointing upward, use the directed edge function \[E_{AB}(P)=(B_x-A_x)(P_y-A_y)-(B_y-A_y)(P_x-A_x).\] The function is a signed area scaled by two. The inside of a counterclockwise triangle lies to the left of all three oriented edges. Equivalently, \(E_{AB}(P)/E_{AB}(C)\) is the barycentric weight for \(C\), and the other two come from cyclic permutations. The three nonnegative weights sum to one and give a convex combination of the vertices. Incremental edge evaluationFor fixed vertices, \(E(x,y)\) is affine. Moving one coordinate unit to the right changes it by \(-(B_y-A_y)\), and moving up changes it by \(B_x-A_x\). Initialize once at the first sample center of the triangle’s bounding box, cache a row start for each edge, and step across the row by addition. With an integer grid of \(S\) subpixel units per pixel, the increments for one pixel are \(-S(B_y-A_y)\) horizontally and \(S(B_x-A_x)\) vertically. Choose even \(S\) so pixel centers are representable and quantize shared vertices consistently. 1234567for each scanline y in the bounding box: e0, e1, e2 = saved values at the first pixel center for each x in the scanline: if all three edges accept their current values: emit the covered sample with barycentric weights e0, e1, e2 += horizontal increments saved values += vertical increments In this \(y\)-up, counterclockwise convention, accept equality on an edge with \(B_y<A_y\), or on a horizontal edge with \(B_x<A_x\). A reversed shared edge has exactly the opposite tie classification. This fills the left and top boundaries consistently and leaves the bottom and right boundaries for their neighbors. With \(y\) pointing down, derive the rule again from the winding convention. A tile can be rejected when the maximum of an edge function over its four corners fails that edge test. Why sampling aliases frequenciesSampling step \(T\) is equivalent to multiplying by \(\sum_k\delta(t-kT)\). With the Fourier convention \(S(
u)=\int s(t)e^{-2\pi i
u t}dt\), the impulse train transforms into another impulse train at intervals \(1/T\) with nonzero weight \(1/T\). Multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency, so \[S_s(
u)= rac1T\sum_k S\left(
u- rac{k}{T}ight).\] A band-limited signal with bandwidth \(B\) avoids overlap when \(1/T>2B\). Otherwise, distinct spectra may produce the same samples. The cosines at frequencies \(
u\) and \(m/T-
u\) agree at all sample times by periodicity and even symmetry. A triangle boundary creates a discontinuity, which has high-frequency content beyond any finite sample rate. Jagged edges and the apparent reversal of a filmed wheel are spatial and temporal examples of aliasing. Prefiltering and multisamplingAn ideal box average for a pixel region \(A\) and triangle \(T_	riangle\) is \[c_A= rac1{|A|}\int_A\mathbf 1_{T_	riangle}(x,y)\,dx\,dy = rac{|A\cap T_	riangle|}{|A|}.\] A constant foreground and a constant background can be blended in linear color space according to this coverage. With independent uniform subsamples, their average estimates \(c_A\) without bias, with variance \(c_A(1-c_A)/N\). A regular subsample grid is deterministic quadrature, so its error depends on alignment with the edge. MSAA stores several coverage and depth samples while letting a shaded value serve multiple covered samples. It can smooth triangle edges without shading every subsample independently. High-frequency shading within a triangle retains its own sampling problem and can require texture filtering or per-sample shading. Z-bufferingStart every depth sample at \(+\infty\) when smaller means nearer. Update the sample’s depth and color only if a new opaque fragment is closer. After any number of inputs, the buffer stores the minimum submitted depth: the empty minimum is \(+\infty\), and one update takes the minimum of the previous minimum and the arriving depth. This invariant gives order independence for distinct opaque depths. Equal depths depend on the comparison and submission order. A global painter’s ordering can fail when three faces cyclically occlude one another. The Z-buffer resolves visibility locally, though overdraw can require testing many fragments per sample. Transparent fragments generally require combining several contributions and cannot use nearest-depth selection alone. Reconstruction recapThe lecture first concludes its discussion of specialized reconstruction. In linear blend skinning, a bind-pose vertex \(v\) moves to \(\sum_j w_jG_j(	heta)G_j(0)^{-1}v\), where \(G_j\) is the global joint transform and the weights sum to one. At the bind pose each transform pair becomes identity, and the vertex stays fixed. To estimate the pose from one image, minimize projected joint error and regularize body shape and pose. Indoor reconstruction can estimate object shapes, placements, and room layout separately, then assemble them in one scene. Exercises Prove shared-edge ownership. Two consistently counterclockwise triangles share an edge, and a sample is in the relative interior of that edge. Why does the fill rule assign it to exactly one triangle? Answer For a sample in the relative interior of a proper shared edge the other two edge tests of each triangle are positive. On the shared edge the tests are both zero. Its directed increments \((dx,dy)\) are opposite in the two triangles. If \(dy
e0\), exactly one orientation has \(dy<0\). Otherwise \(dx
e0\) and exactly one has \(dx<0\). Only that triangle accepts equality. Compute analytic antialiasing. A triangle covers the portion of the unit pixel where \(x+y<0.75\). Compare exact coverage with center sampling and a \(2	imes2\) grid of quarter-offset samples. Answer Exact coverage is the right-triangle area \(0.75^2/2=0.28125\). The center has sum \(1\) and returns zero. The four grid sums are \(0.5,1,1,1.5\), giving estimated coverage \(0.25\). Find the alias. A signal \(\cos(2\pi\cdot 47t)\) is sampled at \(60\) Hz. Which nonnegative frequency in \([0,30]\) matches it, and can a post-sampling low-pass filter distinguish the two? Answer The aliased frequency is \(60-47=13\) Hz, since \(\cos(2\pi\cdot47k/60)=\cos(2\pi k-2\pi\cdot13k/60)\). Both continuous signals give exactly the same discrete input. A filter on that input has no evidence from which to distinguish their origins. ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 5, “Rasterization,” October 21, 2026, slides 19–29 for reconstruction, 44–67 for coverage, 68–120 for sampling and antialiasing, and 121–128 for depth testing. title: ML 05: PAC Learning and VC Dimension
summary: Prove finite-class sample bounds and compute VC dimension by combining explicit realizations with impossible labelings.
body: Prove finite-class sample bounds and compute VC dimension by combining explicit realizations with impossible labelings. Opposite vertices of the square share a label. The two convex hulls intersect at its center. Realizable and agnostic PAC guaranteesIn binary classification, \(R(h)\) is the probability of error on an independent test draw. Realizable PAC learning assumes some hypothesis in the class has zero risk. The learner must output a predictor with risk at most \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\) over the training sample. Agnostic PAC learning permits arbitrary labels and asks for risk within \(\varepsilon\) of \(\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R(h)\). For any fixed hypothesis of risk greater than \(\varepsilon\), the chance it makes no errors on \(n\) independent examples is \((1-R(h))^n\le e^{-n\varepsilon}\). A union bound over a finite class and the existence of a consistent hypothesis give the realizable ERM bound \[n\ge\frac{\log|\mathcal H|+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}.\] For the agnostic case, two-sided Hoeffding and a union bound give \[P\!\left(\sup_{h\in\mathcal H}|\widehat R(h)-R(h)|>\varepsilon/2\right) \le 2|\mathcal H|e^{-n\varepsilon^2/2}.\] On the complementary event, \(R(\widehat h)\le\widehat R(\widehat h)+\varepsilon/2\le\widehat R(h)+\varepsilon/2\le R(h)+\varepsilon\) for every \(h\). Take the infimum. A population-risk comparison with the Bayes predictor separates approximation error, \(\inf_{\mathcal H}R-R(h^\star)\), from the learner’s excess above the best in its class. For a no-free-lunch example, select labels independently and uniformly for each point in a uniform domain of \(2n\) points, then draw \(n\) training examples. At least half the domain remains unseen. Conditional on the data, each unseen label remains an independent fair coin, giving expected risk at least \(1/4\) over the labeling and sample. Some deterministic labeling attains that lower bound in expectation over training draws. A random risk in \([0,1]\) satisfies \(\mathbb E R\le 1/8+(7/8)P(R\ge1/8)\), so for that labeling the learner has risk at least \(1/8\) with probability at least \(1/7\). If \(\mathcal H\) has infinite VC dimension, we can choose a shattered \(2n\)-point set for every \(n\). Its deterministic labeling is then realizable in \(\mathcal H\), so the bound contradicts any distribution-free PAC sample complexity at, for example, \(\varepsilon=1/9,\delta=1/8\). Infinite classes can have small effective complexityFor thresholds \(h_t(x)=\mathbf1\{x\ge t\}\) on the line, two ordered points cannot receive \((1,0)\), but one point can receive either label. The VC dimension is 1. A single interval shatters two points, while three ordered points cannot receive \((1,0,1)\), so its dimension is 2. For a realizable threshold at \(t^\star\), any consistent empirical minimizer has zero sample points in its error interval. If the empirical threshold is larger than \(t^\star\), the error interval is an initial segment of \([t^\star,\infty)\); if it is smaller, the error interval is a terminal segment of \((-\infty,t^\star)\). On each side with enough mass, choose the closest fixed segment of mass at least \(\varepsilon\), using the probability quantile and including the boundary atom if needed to reach \(\varepsilon\). Every error interval on that side of mass greater than \(\varepsilon\) contains this segment. Therefore the probability of any consistent threshold with risk greater than \(\varepsilon\) is at most \(2(1-\varepsilon)^n\). This directly yields order \(\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) samples. The same argument applies to concentric disks by replacing \(x\) with negative distance to the known center. In \(\mathbb R^d\), an affine halfspace shatters \(d+1\) affinely independent points because an affine function interpolates arbitrary assigned values \(\pm1\). For any \(d+2\) points, the augmented vectors \((x_i,1)\) have a nontrivial linear dependence. Its coefficients sum to zero, and the positive and negative groups therefore have convex combinations representing the same point. Opposite labels on those groups cannot be realized. Thus the dimension is exactly \(d+1\). Sauer–Shelah and the generalization boundLet \(\Pi_d(n)\) denote the largest possible trace size on \(n\) points for VC dimension at most \(d\). Split the traces on the first \(n-1\) points into prefixes appearing at least once and prefixes that can be extended with either last label. The first family has VC dimension at most \(d\), and the second at most \(d-1\), because shattering \(d\) points with both extensions would shatter \(d+1\) points. Thus \(\Pi_d(n)\le\Pi_d(n-1)+\Pi_{d-1}(n-1)\). The base cases \(n=0\) and \(d=0\) have at most one trace. Pascal’s identity yields \[\Pi_{\mathcal H}(n)\le\sum_{j=0}^d {n\choose j}\le(en/d)^d\qquad(1\le d\le n).\] For the last inequality, multiply the binomial sum by \((d/n)^d\), use \((d/n)^d\le(d/n)^j\) for \(j\le d\), and bound \((1+d/n)^n\) by \(e^d\). To see why this controls uniform convergence, add an independent ghost sample of size \(n\). For \(n\varepsilon^2\ge 2\), a hypothesis whose true and empirical risk differ by more than \(\varepsilon\) has at least a constant probability that its ghost error is within \(\varepsilon/2\) of the truth, by Chebyshev’s inequality for Bernoulli averages. The resulting two-sample event has a discrepancy above \(\varepsilon/2\). Swap the two members of each independent sample pair with a fair coin. Conditional on the pooled data, the discrepancy for any fixed trace is an average of independent signed terms bounded in magnitude by 1. Hoeffding and a union bound over at most \(\Pi_{\mathcal H}(2n)\) pooled prediction traces give \[P\!\left(\sup_h|\widehat R(h)-R(h)|>\varepsilon\right) \le 4\Pi_{\mathcal H}(2n)e^{-n\varepsilon^2/8}\] under the usual measurability assumptions. This gives an order \(\sqrt{(d\log(en/d)+\log(1/\delta))/n}\) bound for the empirical-population gap. The quantitative theorem uses more structure. In the typical parameter range \(0<\varepsilon\le1/16\), \(0<\delta\le1/8\), agnostic sample complexity is \(\Theta((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)\) for \(d\ge1\). The course’s realizable bounds are \(\Omega((d+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\) and \(O((d\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\) for \(d\ge2\). The additional dimension restriction in the realizable lower-bound proof below supplies a second point where two concepts agree. The upper bound applies to consistent ERM. More elaborate learners remove the realizable logarithm. Hanneke, The Optimal Sample Complexity of PAC Learning, Theorem 2. Why the realizable sample size scales as the inverse of the errorFix a target \(h^\star\) and form the family of disagreement sets \(\mathcal A=\{\{x:h(x)\ne h^\star(x)\}:h\in\mathcal H\}\). On any finite set, forming a disagreement pattern flips exactly the coordinates on which \(h^\star\) is positive. This is a bijection of traces, preserving VC dimension. A consistent learner fails if some set of probability greater than \(\varepsilon\) receives no sample point. Such a failure is absent when the sample is an \(\varepsilon\)-net for \(\mathcal A\). For a second independent sample of size \(n\), a fixed set of mass \(p>\varepsilon\) receives at least \(\varepsilon n/2\) ghost points with probability at least \(1/2\) for \(n\varepsilon\) larger than an absolute constant, by the multiplicative Chernoff lower tail. Conditional on the first sample and a witnessed bad set, the ghost sample is still independent, so the original failure probability is at most twice the probability of a set avoided by the first sample and hit at least \(\varepsilon n/2\) times by the ghost sample. Pool the \(2n\) points and make a uniform split into two groups of size \(n\). For a fixed trace with \(k\) hits on the pool, the probability all hits enter the ghost half is zero if \(k>n\) and otherwise is \((n)_k/(2n)_k\le2^{-k}\), where \((n)_k=n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\). The contributing traces have \(k\ge\varepsilon n/2\), so \[P(\text{a consistent }h\text{ has risk }>\varepsilon) \le2\Pi_{\mathcal H}(2n)2^{-\varepsilon n/2}.\] Taking logarithms and applying Sauer–Shelah shows that \(n\ge C(d\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon\) suffices for an absolute \(C\). To check this substitution, set \(u=\log(1/\varepsilon)\) and \(v=\log(2/\delta)/d\). At \(n=Cd(u+v)/\varepsilon\), the positive exponent per dimension is at most \(u+\log(2eC)+\log(u+v)+v\), while the negative exponent per dimension is \(C(u+v)\log2/2\). For large enough \(C\), the latter dominates. For a dimension lower bound, choose a shattered set of \(d\ge2\) points, putting mass \(p=8\varepsilon\) uniformly on \(d-1\) rare points and the remaining mass on an anchor with a fixed label. Independently randomize the target labels on the rare points. If \(n\le(d-1)/(2p)\), the expected number of unseen rare points is at least \((d-1)/2\) because \((1-p/(d-1))^n\ge1-np/(d-1)\). Every unseen target bit is a fair coin conditional on the data, so the expected risk on just the rare points is at least \(p/4\). This risk stays in \([0,p]\), giving probability at least \((p/4-\varepsilon)/(p-\varepsilon)=1/7\) that it exceeds \(\varepsilon\). Averaging guarantees such a deterministic target, so \(n=\Omega(d/\varepsilon)\) is necessary at constant confidence. For confidence, instead put mass \(2\varepsilon\) on one rare point and the rest on the anchor. Take two targets differing only on the rare point. When no rare point is observed, the data have identical distributions, and the average conditional probability of predicting its label incorrectly is \(1/2\). Therefore some target gives error exceeding \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(\tfrac12(1-2\varepsilon)^n\). Since \(-\log(1-2\varepsilon)\le4\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon\le1/4\), this forces \(n=\Omega(\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon)\). The maximum of the two lower bounds is within a factor two of their sum. Why the agnostic dimension term needs no logarithmThe single union bound used above pays for all traces even when two traces differ on very few points. A sequence of increasingly fine covers controls these differences at their own scales. For a fixed sample, put the normalized Euclidean metric \(\|a\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i a_i^2\) on its finite set of binary loss vectors. A set of \(M\ge2\) loss vectors separated by distance more than \(r\) has normalized Hamming distance more than \(r^2\) between each pair. Pick \(s=\lceil 3\log M/r^2\rceil\) sample coordinates independently and uniformly with replacement. Any pair agrees on every chosen coordinate with probability at most \(e^{-sr^2}\). The union bound over pairs is less than one, so some coordinate sample distinguishes all \(M\). Add more coordinates if needed to ensure \(s\ge d\). Sauer–Shelah then implies \[\log M\le d\log\!\left(C\left(1+\frac{\log M}{d r^2}\right)\right).\] To solve this, write \(Y=\max(1,\log M/d)\). Since \(r\le1\), the right side after division by \(d\) is at most \(\log(C'/r^2)+\log Y\). The inequality \(\log Y\le Y/2\) for \(Y\ge1\) gives \(\log M=O(d\log(C''/r))\). A maximal separated set covers the loss vectors within radius \(r\), so the same logarithmic bound holds for covering numbers. Let \(\sigma_i\) be independent fair signs. For any finite family of vectors \(A\) with normalized norms at most \(s\), the signed average of a fixed vector is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(s^2/n\): its exponential moment is the product of \(\cosh(t a_i/n)\le e^{t^2 a_i^2/(2n^2)}\). Bounding the exponential moment of the maximum by summing over the family and optimizing \(t\) gives \(\mathbb E_\sigma\max_{a\in A}|n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i a_i|\le s\sqrt{2\log(2|A|)/n}\). Take a fixed reference vector at scale 1 and a cover at every radius \(2^{-j}\). Approximate each vector by a nearest cover element at each scale. Consecutive approximations differ in norm by at most \(2^{-j}+2^{-j+1}=3\cdot2^{-j}\). There are at most the products of the consecutive cover sizes possible differences. Apply the signed maximum bound to the allowable differences at each scale and sum. The remainder vanishes as the radius tends to zero because the signed average of a residual of norm \(r\) has magnitude at most \(r\) by Cauchy–Schwarz. The reference contributes at most \(1/\sqrt n\) in mean absolute value and the increments give \[\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_h\left|n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\mathbf1\{h(x_i)\ne y_i\}\right| \le \frac1{\sqrt n}+C\sqrt{\frac dn}\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}\sqrt{j+1} =O(\sqrt{d/n}).\] To pass to risks, move the ghost expectation outside the supremum by Jensen, swap the sample pairs with fair signs, and apply the triangle inequality to separate the two signed sums. This bounds the expected uniform gap by twice the signed complexity above. Changing one sample point changes the uniform gap by at most \(1/n\), so bounded differences adds \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2n)}\) with confidence \(1-\delta\). Comparing two risks through their empirical versions costs at most twice the uniform gap. This gives the stated agnostic upper bound, using chaining in place of the single-scale argument. Agnostic lower bounds from noisy labelsFor the dimension term, choose \(d\) shattered points uniformly. Index distributions by \(\theta\in\{-1,+1\}^d\) and let \(P_\theta(Y=1\mid X=x_i)=(1+b\theta_i)/2\) for \(0<b\le1/2\). The Bayes rule belongs to the restricted class. A predictor disagreeing with the signs on \(k\) points has excess risk \(bk/d\). Flipping one bit of \(\theta\) changes the one-observation KL divergence by \[\frac b d\log\frac{1+b}{1-b}\le \frac{4b^2}{d}.\] For \(n\) observations KL multiplies by \(n\). By Pinsker, if \(n\le d/(32b^2)\) the total variation between those whole-sample laws is at most \(1/4\). Under equal prior weights, the average probability of guessing their differing bit incorrectly is at least \((1-\mathrm{TV})/2\ge3/8\): for any decision event the sum of the two errors is at least \(1-\mathrm{TV}\). Pair the uniform prior on the hypercube along each coordinate and sum the resulting error probabilities. The expected excess is at least \(3b/8\), while it is at most \(b\) on each trial. For \(b=8\varepsilon\), the probability of excess greater than \(\varepsilon=b/8\) is at least \(2/7\). Some deterministic sign vector attains this failure probability. For the confidence term use a single shattered point with competing label laws \(p_\pm=(1\pm b)/2\) and \(b=2\varepsilon\). For two laws with densities \(p,q\) and affinity \(S=\int\sqrt{pq}\), Cauchy–Schwarz applied to \(\int|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\) yields \(\mathrm{TV}\le\sqrt{1-S^2}\). Thus any binary test has average error at least \((1-\sqrt{1-S^2})/2\ge S^2/4\). The affinity of these Bernoulli distributions is \(\sqrt{1-b^2}\) and affinities multiply over independent observations, so the failure probability of at least one distribution is at least \((1-b^2)^n/4\). As \(-\log(1-b^2)\le2b^2\) for \(b\le1/2\), achieving confidence \(1-\delta\) requires \(n=\Omega(\log(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)\). Combining with the dimension argument proves the agnostic lower bound against arbitrary learning rules. ChallengesProblem 1Find the VC dimension of all subsets of the real line that are unions of at most \(k\) intervals. Permit the empty set. Show solution The dimension is \(2k\). Among \(2k\) ordered points, any binary labeling has at most \(k\) contiguous runs of positives. Put one interval around each positive run, excluding neighboring negative points. For \(2k+1\) ordered points the alternating labeling starting and ending with 1 has \(k+1\) positive runs. Every interval joining any two of those runs contains a negative point. That labeling is impossible on every set of \(2k+1\) points. Problem 2Compare the VC dimensions of \(\mathbf1\{a\sin x>0\}\), \(\mathbf1\{\sin(x+a)>0\}\), and \(\mathbf1\{\sin(ax)>0\}\). Show solution The amplitude class has three distinct functions and can shatter one point, giving dimension 1. Phase shifts produce open semicircles of positives. The points \(0,\pi/2\) admit all four labels. Two equal residues modulo \(2\pi\) cannot receive different labels. Among three distinct residues, either they cannot all fit in an open semicircle, or they can be ordered within one. In the latter case any open semicircle containing the two extremes contains the short arc between them, so the middle point cannot be negative. The dimension is 2. For frequency scaling use \(x_i=2^{i-1}\) for any \(n\). Given labels \(y_i\), put \(b_i=1-y_i\) and take \(a=2\pi(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j2^{-j}+2^{-n-1})\). The fractional part of \(ax_i/(2\pi)\) is \(b_i/2\) plus a number strictly between 0 and \(1/2\). Its sine is positive precisely when \(b_i=0\). Hence these \(n\) points are shattered for arbitrary \(n\). Problem 3. Generalization from a sample compression schemeSuppose a realizable learner keeps at most \(k\) labeled observations and a side message from a fixed alphabet of size \(B\). A deterministic reconstruction function takes the retained observations in input order and the side message, and its prediction is consistent on the full sample. Prove a sample compression bound. Apply it to closed axis-aligned rectangles in \(\mathbb R^d\) by keeping examples that witness the extremes. Floyd and Warmuth, Sample Compression, Learnability, and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis Dimension, §2. Show solution Fix a subset of sample indices \(I\) and a side message. Condition on the observations at those indices. The reconstructed classifier is now fixed, while all remaining points are independent draws. If its risk exceeds \(\varepsilon\), its chance of matching all omitted labels is at most \((1-\varepsilon)^{n-|I|}\). This applies even though the actual compressor can choose its subset and message after seeing the omitted data, because we union bound over all fixed choices. The probability of a consistent reconstructed rule of risk above \(\varepsilon\) is at most \[B\sum_{j=0}^{k}{n\choose j}(1-\varepsilon)^{n-j} \le B(en/k)^k e^{-\varepsilon(n-k)}\qquad(1\le k\le n).\] For a sample with positives, retain one positive point minimizing and one maximizing each coordinate, at most \(2d\) points. Reconstruction takes their coordinatewise bounding box. It contains every positive sample point and is contained in the target rectangle, so contains no negative sample point. When the retained set is empty, reconstruct the all-negative predictor. This gives compression with \(k=2d\) and \(B=1\). In the plane the four extreme witnesses also explain the VC upper bound: on any five points, mark four points witnessing the extrema positive and an unneeded point negative, which no rectangle can realize. The four cardinal points of a diamond are shattered by bounding the chosen positive points, so the planar VC dimension is exactly four. Sources Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, 2026 Lecture 5, slides 5–12 (no-free-lunch), 13–18 (finite classes), 22–27 (PAC, Bayes and risk decomposition), and 29–36 (thresholds, shattering and quantitative learning). Archived slides 5–18 and 21–35 contain the corresponding proofs. Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms, Corollary 2.3, §§3.1–3.2, Theorem 5.1, Example 6.2, Corollary 6.4, and Theorems 6.6–6.8. The quantitative proofs follow the topics of §§28.1–28.3, with a multiscale argument for the sharper agnostic upper bound. Problem Sets 3–4 develop the threshold, VC-dimension, and no-free-lunch applications. Previous lecture · Course notes · Next lecture

title: ACG 04: Projection and Learning on 3D Geometry
summary: Perspective projection maps three-dimensional positions to two-dimensional image coordinates. Single-view reconstruction asks what can be recovered after that mapping. Camera geometry identifies the missing con
body: Perspective projection maps three-dimensional positions to two-dimensional image coordinates. Single-view reconstruction asks what can be recovered after that mapping. Camera geometry identifies the missing constraints, and learning supplies priors about plausible scenes. Orthographic and perspective projectionUse a right-handed camera with forward axis \(-z\). Let \(n,f\) be the positive near and far distances, \(d=-z\), and set normalized depth to \([-1,1]\) with near mapping to \(-1\). Orthographic projection centers and scales each coordinate independently. For horizontal interval \([l,r]\), impose the two endpoint values to get \(x_{\mathrm{ndc}}=(2x-r-l)/(r-l)\). The same linear construction applies to vertical position and depth. Perspective instead projects along rays from the camera center. Let \(\phi\) be the vertical field of view and \(a\) the width-to-height ratio. The near plane’s half-height is \(n\tan(\phi/2)\), and similar triangles scale the near-plane intersection by \(n/d\). After normalization, \[x_{\mathrm{ndc}}=\frac{x}{ad\tan(\phi/2)},\qquad y_{\mathrm{ndc}}=\frac{y}{d\tan(\phi/2)}.\] Choose clip \(w_c=d\), making the homogeneous division produce the desired scale. Assume \(z_c=Az+B\) so normalized depth is \(-A+B/d\). Evaluating at \(d=n,f\) yields \(A=-(f+n)/(f-n)\) and \(B=-2fn/(f-n)\). For \(s=1/\tan(\phi/2)\), the projection matrix is \[P=\begin{pmatrix} s/a&0&0&0\\0&s&0&0\\ 0&0&-\frac{f+n}{f-n}&-\frac{2fn}{f-n}\\ 0&0&-1&0 \end{pmatrix}.\] The derivative of depth with respect to \(d\) is \(2fn/((f-n)d^2)\). Uniform quantization of projected depth therefore corresponds to coarser distance resolution farther away. A smaller near plane consumes more of the representable depth range near the eye. After clipping and division, a \(W\times H\) top-left-origin viewport maps NDC to \(x_s=W(x_{\mathrm{ndc}}+1)/2\) and \(y_s=H(1-y_{\mathrm{ndc}})/2\). Clip before the perspective divideThe visible clip-space region satisfies six linear half-space inequalities, such as \(w+x\ge0\) for the left boundary. An edge whose endpoints \(A,B\) lie on opposite sides of a clipping plane \(g(C)=0\) intersects it at \[t=\frac{g(A)}{g(A)-g(B)},\qquad C=(1-t)A+tB.\] Sutherland–Hodgman clipping processes one plane at a time. For each polygon edge, emit an intersection if membership changes and emit the next vertex if it is inside. Interpolate ordinary perspective-correct vertex attributes with the same \(t\) before dividing by \(w\). After all six planes, triangulate the clipped polygon and divide its retained vertices by \(w\). Performing clipping in screen space after division would mishandle edges that cross the eye plane. Choosing a representation for 3D learning Representation Useful computation Main tradeoff Multiview images Share a 2D encoder and aggregate features across views Occluded surfaces depend on viewpoint coverage Dense voxels Apply regular 3D kernels Doubling resolution per axis requires eight times as many cells Sparse voxels and octrees Process occupied cells or subdivide selected regions Neighbor lookup requires a spatial index or cross-level handling Point sets Process scan samples directly Sampling density varies and connectivity is absent Meshes Use face and edge structure and output a surface directly A deformable template generally retains its topology Implicit fields Query occupancy or distance at arbitrary coordinates Surface extraction requires additional queries Datasets differ in the signals available for training. ShapeNet studies object-level geometry, PartNet adds part hierarchies, ScanNet provides indoor observations, and HOI4D records interactions over time. An evaluation should state whether the input is a complete shape, a partial scan, or a changing scene. Set aggregation and local structurePointNet shares a feature extractor \(h\) across points, uses per-channel maxima, and applies an output head \(\gamma\): \[F(\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\})=\gamma\left(\max_i h(p_i)\right).\] Reordering the points reorders the feature rows, leaving each maximum unchanged. A perturbation that changes only points below all existing maxima can likewise leave the output unchanged. The same property limits the ability to infer density or local arrangements. PointNet++ selects local neighborhoods in the metric space, encodes relative coordinates in each neighborhood, and repeats the procedure at larger scales. PointNet · PointNet++ A simple implementation can use farthest-point sampling to choose neighborhood centers. Track the smallest squared distance from each point to any selected center, update the distance array after adding each center, and take its maximum for the next center. This costs \(O(mN)\) for \(m\) centers and \(N\) points, with \(O(N)\) memory. Gather neighbors for each center using a radius or nearest-neighbor query. Subtract the center coordinates so each local feature extractor sees the geometry of the patch. Single-view reconstruction objectivesScaling an object uniformly about the pinhole leaves its projected coordinates unchanged. Depth supervision can accommodate this ambiguity by comparing the shape of the predicted depth map up to one per-image scale. With \(\delta_i=\log\hat z_i-\log z_i\), minimize the squared error after adding a global offset \(\alpha\) to the predicted log depths. Differentiation gives \(\alpha=-\bar\delta\), and the minimized loss is \[\frac1m\sum_i\delta_i^2-\left(\frac1m\sum_i\delta_i\right)^2 .\] Point sets lack a canonical ordering, so a reconstruction can use the bidirectional squared Chamfer objective, \[D(P,Q)=\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p\in P}\min_{q\in Q}\|p-q\|^2 +\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q\in Q}\min_{p\in P}\|q-p\|^2.\] The first term measures prediction accuracy and the second term measures coverage. Both are permutation invariant. Because a target can be reused as the closest neighbor of many different predictions, the objective gives limited control over sample density. Mesh prediction can instead deform a template, sample surface points for data terms, and regularize neighboring vertices and faces. A fixed template constrains changes to topology. Exercises Find precision loss. Under this projection, compare the world-space depth increments corresponding to an equal, infinitesimal NDC increment at \(d=2n\) and at \(d=20n\). Assume both are inside the frustum. Answer Invert \(dz_{\mathrm{ndc}}/dd=2fn/((f-n)d^2)\) locally. The distance increment scales as \(d^2\), so the farther sample’s increment is \(100\) times as large. Clip a segment. Against the left clip plane \(w+x=0\), clip the segment from \(A=(-3,0,0,1)\) to \(B=(0,2,0,2)\). Give the intersection and its screen \(y\) in NDC. Answer The signed values are \(g(A)=-2\) and \(g(B)=2\), giving \(t=1/2\). The intersection is \((-1.5,1,0,1.5)\), whose normalized \(y\) is \(2/3\). Interpolating the already-divided \(y\) values at the same parameter would give \(1/2\) and the wrong geometry. Separate ordinary and scale-invariant depth errors. The target depths are \((1,2,4)\) and predictions are \((2,4,4)\). Compute the optimal multiplicative correction and scale-invariant loss. Answer The log discrepancies are \((\log 2,\log 2,0)\) with mean \(2\log 2/3\). The scale correction is \(2^{-2/3}\), and the remaining variance is \(2(\log 2)^2/9\). ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 4, “Learning + Geometry,” October 17, 2026, slides 3–32 for projection, 37–60 for datasets, 61–106 for analysis, and 107–144 for synthesis.
