title: ML 04: Matrix Completion and Nonconvex Geometry
summary: Derive the nuclear norm factorization, alternating least squares, and a strict-saddle example, then identify the information required for completion.
body:
Derive the nuclear norm factorization, alternating least squares, and a strict-saddle example, then identify the information required for completion. A rank-one fit recovers the hidden values in this connected synthetic observation pattern. The observation operatorA rating matrix \(M\in\mathbb R^{m	imes n}\) may have entries \(u_i^	op v_j\), where user and item vectors have dimension \(r\). This implies rank at most \(r\). The operator \(P_\Omega\) preserves observed entries and sets other entries to zero. Exact low-rank completion asks for \(\min_X\operatorname{rank}(X)\) subject to \(P_\Omega X=P_\Omega M\). Unobserved values are free variables. Fitting ordinary low-rank approximation to a zero-filled matrix includes artificial zero ratings in its objective. Low rank and identifiabilityFor an unobserved row of a rank-one matrix \(uv^	op\), the corresponding coordinate of \(u\) is undetermined. For \(M=e_ie_j^	op\), missing just entry \((i,j)\) leaves its scale undetermined. A recovery assumption should address both insufficient sampling and concentration of singular vectors. For a thin SVD \(M=U\Sigma V^	op\), typical incoherence conditions are \[\max_i\|U^	op e_i\|^2\le\mu r/m,\qquad \max_j\|V^	op e_j\|^2\le\mu r/n .\] The first quantities are diagonal entries of the orthogonal projector \(UU^	op\). They sum to \(\operatorname{tr}(UU^	op)=r\), so \(\mu\ge1\). A uniform unit singular vector attains \(\mu=1\), whereas a coordinate vector in \(\mathbb R^m\) needs \(\mu=m\). For a full-column-rank basis \(B\), calculate the same scores from \(\operatorname{diag}(B(B^	op B)^{-1}B^	op)\). Recovery results additionally depend on the sample size and selection process. For the factor incoherence used in PSD completion, write \(M=ZZ^	op\), let \(U\) span its range, and denote the condition number of \(Z\) by \(\kappa\). Since the squared norm of row \(Z_i\) is \(M_{ii}\), \[\sigma_{\min}(Z)^2\|U^	op e_i\|^2\le \|Z_i\|^2 \le\sigma_{\max}(Z)^2\|U^	op e_i\|^2 .\] Thus the leverage-score and factor-row conditions express related restrictions, with constants depending on the singular values. For instance, \(\|U^	op e_i\|^2\le\mu_0 r/d\) implies \(\|Z_i\|\le\kappa\sqrt{\mu_0/d}\|Z\|_F\) because \(\|Z\|_F^2\ge r\sigma_{\min}(Z)^2\). Conversely \(\|Z_i\|\le(\mu/\sqrt d)\|Z\|_F\) bounds the leverage by \(\mu^2\kappa^2r/d\). A uniformly sampled observation set still needs enough entries to cover rows and columns. Under independent entry sampling at rate \(p\), a given row of an \(m\) by \(n\) matrix is unobserved with probability \((1-p)^n\), so a union bound for any empty row is \(m(1-p)^n\). From singular values to a convex objectiveThe nuclear norm \(\|X\|_\ast=\sum_i\sigma_i(X)\) is the dual of the spectral norm: writing \(X=\sum_i\sigma_i u_iv_i^	op\) gives \(\langle Z,Xangle\le\|Z\|_{m op}\sum_i\sigma_i\). Equality is achieved at \(Z=UV^	op\) with \(\|Z\|_{m op}=1\) for nonzero \(X\). As a supremum of linear functions it is convex. Moreover, for factor widths at least \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\), \[\|X\|_\ast=\min_{AB^	op=X}	frac12(\|A\|_F^2+\|B\|_F^2).\] To attain the bound take \(A=U\Sigma^{1/2}\) and \(B=V\Sigma^{1/2}\). For the other direction, any \(\|Z\|_{m op}\le1\) satisfies \(\langle Z,AB^	opangle=\langle Z^	op A,Bangle\le\|A\|_F\|B\|_F\le(\|A\|_F^2+\|B\|_F^2)/2\). Maximize over \(Z\). The identity connects convex nuclear-norm penalization to Frobenius-regularized factor fitting, where fixing a narrower factor width imposes an additional rank constraint. A semidefinite formulationIntroduce symmetric \(R,S\) and constrain \( igl( egin{smallmatrix}R&X\X^	op&S\end{smallmatrix} igr)\succeq0\). Any such matrix admits a Gram factorization \( igl( egin{smallmatrix}A\B\end{smallmatrix} igr) igl( egin{smallmatrix}A\B\end{smallmatrix} igr)^	op\), so \(X=AB^	op\) and \((\operatorname{tr}R+\operatorname{tr}S)/2=(\|A\|_F^2+\|B\|_F^2)/2\ge\|X\|_\ast\). Conversely, the balanced factors from the SVD attain equality. Minimizing this linear trace objective subject to the block constraint and the observed entries therefore gives precisely nuclear norm completion. The block matrix explains why a general semidefinite implementation uses substantially more storage than the factor representation. Alternating minimization and strict saddlesFor \[F(A,B)=	frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in\Omega}(a_i^	op b_j-M_{ij})^2 +	frac\lambda2(\|A\|_F^2+\|B\|_F^2),\] holding \(B\) fixed gives independent row subproblems, with normal equation \[\left(\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\Omega}b_jb_j^	op+\lambda Iight)a_i =\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\Omega}M_{ij}b_j.\] The update for \(B\) interchanges the roles. Exact subproblem solutions never increase \(F\). For the product alone, \((A,B)\mapsto(AR,BR^{-	op})\) preserves every prediction for invertible \(R\). The Frobenius regularizer preserves this symmetry for orthogonal \(R\). The unregularized observed-factor loss is not jointly convex, even for one nonzero observed entry. With target \(1\), the factor pairs \((1,1)\) and \((3,1/3)\) both have zero loss, but their average \((2,2/3)\) predicts \(4/3\) and has positive loss. A nonconvex factor loss can have many representations of a global solution while still having no spurious local minima. Those two properties are compatible. For \(F(a,b)=	frac12(ab-1)^2\), the gradient vanishes at \((0,0)\). The Hessian there is \[ egin{pmatrix}0&-1\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\] with eigenvalues \(\pm1\). Taylor expansion along \((1,1)\) gives local decrease and expansion along \((1,-1)\) gives local increase. The functions \(t^4,-t^4,t^3\) all have first and second derivatives zero at the origin, yet give a local minimum, a local maximum, and neither. Negative curvature supplies information that flat second-order stationarity lacks. The three regions in a strict-saddle analysisWith an unbiased perturbation \(\xi\) of conditional second moment at most \(\sigma^2\), the \(L\)-smooth update \(w^+=w-\eta(
abla f(w)+\xi)\) gives \[\mathbb E[f(w^+)-f(w)\mid w]\le -\eta(1-L\eta/2)\|
abla f(w)\|^2+	frac{L\eta^2}{2}\sigma^2.\] This follows by expanding the upper quadratic bound and dropping the cross term in expectation. A sufficiently large gradient produces a quantitative decrease. In the negative-curvature region, suppose \(H=
abla^2 f(w)\) has a unit eigenvector \(v\) of eigenvalue \(-\gamma<0\). In the quadratic model about \(w\), iteration has linear part \(I-\eta H\) and amplifies a displacement along \(v\) by \(1+\eta\gamma\). A perturbation with enough mass along \(v\) can seed this displacement. For an \(M\)-Lipschitz Hessian, subtracting the linear gradient expansion leaves a remainder bounded by \(M\|z\|^2/2\) at displacement \(z\), by integrating the Hessian difference along the segment. This controls the approximation over a small neighborhood. In particular, a direct signed step of radius \(r\) along \(v\), choosing the sign for a nonpositive linear term, gives \(f(w\pm rv)-f(w)\le-\gamma r^2/2+Mr^3/6\). Near a local minimum, favorable curvature and sufficiently small steps and perturbations help keep iterates inside its basin. If the conditional probability of exiting in a step is bounded by \(p\) while still inside, the chance of any exit within \(T\) steps is at most \(Tp\) by a union bound on the first exit. The course’s informal strict-saddle guarantee combines these three regions: outside the basin there must be quantitative decrease over one or more steps, and a lower bound on the objective limits the number of such stages. Recovery additionally depends on identifiability. A global minimizer of the observed objective can still fail to recover \(M\). From linearized escape to the noisy-descent theoremThe quantitative hypothesis in Ge et al. asks that at every point there be a gradient of norm at least \(\epsilon\), curvature at most \(-\gamma\), or a local minimum within distance \(\delta\) with an \(\alpha\)-strongly convex neighborhood of twice that radius. The theorem also assumes a bounded objective, a Lipschitz gradient and Hessian, and bounded stochastic noise, with added noise providing variance along every direction. For sufficiently small constant step \(\eta\) and failure probability \(\zeta\), it gives a terminal iterate within \(\widetilde O(\sqrt{\eta\log(1/(\eta\zeta))})\) of a local minimum after \(\widetilde O(\eta^{-2}\log(1/\zeta))\) steps. The analysis holds up to fixed polynomial dependencies on the problem parameters. Here are the details of the unconstrained argument for additive martingale-difference noise with bounded norm and conditional covariance \(
u^2 I\), the isotropic setting of Appendix A. Treat dimension and the geometric and noise constants as fixed in the step-size estimates. Write \(h=\log(1/\eta)\) and take \(0<\eta\) sufficiently small. Large gradient. When \(\eta\le1/L\), the smoothness inequality above is at most \(-\eta\|
abla f(w)\|^2/2+L\eta^2d
u^2/2\). For \(\|
abla f(w)\|^2\ge2L\eta d
u^2\) this is at most \(-Ld
u^2\eta^2/2\). The gradient cutoff is therefore \(O(\sqrt\eta)\), below the fixed \(\epsilon\) in the strict-saddle condition. If the gradient is below the cutoff and there is no sufficiently negative eigenvalue, the condition places the point in a strongly convex neighborhood. The lower curvature there, together with \(
abla f(w^\star)=0\), gives \(\|
abla f(w)\|\ge\alpha\|w-w^\star\|\). Entry occurs within \(O(\sqrt\eta)\) of the local minimum. Escape. At the initial point \(w_0\) of an escape window, let \(g_0=
abla f(w_0)\), \(H=
abla^2 f(w_0)\), \(\lambda_{\min}(H)=-\gamma_0\le-\gamma\), and \(A=I-\eta H\). In the quadratic model \(	ilde f(w_0+x)=f(w_0)+g_0^	op x+x^	op Hx/2\), let \(	ilde x_t\) be the displacement after \(t\) noisy steps with the same errors as the actual sequence. Unrolling the linear recurrence gives \[	ilde x_t=-\eta\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}A^jg_0-\eta\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}A^{t-1-j}\xi_j .\] Choose the first \(T\) for which \(\gamma_0\sum_{j<T}(1+\eta\gamma_0)^{2j}\ge d/\eta\). The geometric sum gives \(T=O(\log(d+1)/(\eta\gamma_0))\) and \((1+\eta\gamma_0)^T=O(\sqrt{d+1})\). The mean iterate follows deterministic gradient descent on the quadratic, so its objective is at most the initial one by its \(L\)-smoothness. The centered displacement has covariance \(\eta^2
u^2\sum_{j<T}A^{2j}\). Cross terms between noises at different times have conditional expectation zero. Thus the expected model objective change is at most \[ rac{\eta^2
u^2}{2}\sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i(H)\sum_{j<T}(1-\eta\lambda_i(H))^{2j}.\] For \(\lambda_i>0\) the inner weighted sum is bounded by \(\lambda_i/(1-(1-\eta\lambda_i)^2)\le1/\eta\). One negative eigenvalue contributes at most \(-d/\eta\) by construction, and the others can only lower the result. The model drop is at least \(\eta
u^2/2\) in expectation. For a fixed coordinate and \(t\le T\), the centered displacement is a sum of bounded martingale differences with total squared increment bounds \(O(\eta^2\sum_{j<t}\|A^j\|^2)=O(\eta)\), since \(\|A^j\|\le(1+\eta\gamma_0)^j\). Apply Azuma–Hoeffding and union bound over coordinates and times to get \(\max_{t\le T}\|	ilde x_t\|\le C\sqrt\eta\,h\) with probability at least \(1-O(\eta^3)\), including the deterministic mean, whose norm is at most \(\eta\sum_{j<T}\|A^j\|\|g_0\|=O(\sqrt\eta)\). For the real displacement \(x_t=w_t-w_0\), the gradient remainder is \(R(x_t)=
abla f(w_0+x_t)-g_0-Hx_t\), with \(\|R(x_t)\|\le M\|x_t\|^2/2\). Because both sequences receive the same noise, their error is exactly \[x_t-	ilde x_t=-\eta\sum_{j<t}A^{t-1-j}R(x_j).\] If all earlier \(\|x_j\|\le2C\sqrt\eta\,h\), this sum has norm at most a constant times \(\eta h^2\) because \(\eta\sum_{j<T}\|A^j\|=O(1)\). For sufficiently small \(\eta\), the bound is smaller than \(C\sqrt\eta\,h\), closing the induction. Taylor’s theorem for function values bounds \(f(w_T)-	ilde f(w_0+	ilde x_T)\) by \(O(\eta^{3/2}h^3)\) on the event: the linear-in-error term multiplies the error \(O(\eta h^2)\) by the model gradient \(g_0+H	ilde x_T=O(\sqrt\eta\,h)\), and the squared-error and cubic Taylor terms have the same or smaller order. Off the event, the bounded true objective and the uniform bound \(\|	ilde x_t\|=O(1)\) from the unrolled model give an \(O(\eta^3)\) contribution. Combining with the model drop gives \(\mathbb E[f(w_T)-f(w_0)]\le-c\eta\) for some \(c>0\). Residence near a minimum. Let \(V_t=\|w_t-w^\star\|^2\) and \(a=1-\eta\alpha\). Inside the strongly convex region, use strong gradient monotonicity and \(\|
abla f(w_t)\|\le L\sqrt{V_t}\). For \(\eta L^2\le\alpha\), conditional expectation satisfies \(\mathbb E_t V_{t+1}\le aV_t+\eta^2d
u^2\). To prove confinement, set \(b=\eta d
u^2/\alpha\) and stop using increments as soon as the distance exceeds a radius \(r<\delta\). On a step begun inside the ball, let \(D_{t+1}=V_{t+1}-\mathbb E_tV_{t+1}\), and use zero for that increment after exit. Expanding the update with noise norm bounded by \(Q\) shows \(|D_{t+1}|\le C_1(\eta r+\eta^2)\), with a constant depending on \(Q,L\). On first exit at time \(t\), iterating the drift inequality up to and including that step gives \[V_t\le a^t V_0+(1-a^t)b+\sum_{j=1}^t a^{t-j}D_j .\] For each \(t\), the sum uses martingale differences with squared bounds summing to at most \(C_1^2(\eta r+\eta^2)^2/(1-a^2)=O(\eta r^2+\eta^3)\). Now choose \(r^2=K\eta\log(2N/\zeta)\) for a sufficiently large \(K\) and a horizon \(N\). The deterministic terms are \(O(\eta)\) because entry has \(V_0=O(\eta)\). Exiting at time \(t\le N\) requires the sum to exceed \(r^2/2\), which Azuma bounds by \(\exp(-c' r^2/\eta)\) with fixed \(c'>0\). A union bound gives exit probability at most \(\zeta/2\), while the radius stays below \(\delta\) for a sufficiently small step. Entry and completion. At a block boundary outside the minimum region, take a single large-gradient step or one escape block. Each block has length \(\ell\le T_{\max}=O(\eta^{-1})\) and expected decrease at least \(c''\eta^2\ell\), for a uniform positive constant. Stop adding blocks when an entry is found at a boundary. For each finite number of blocks, summing conditional decreases bounds expected elapsed stopped time by \(2B/(c''\eta^2)\), where \(|f|\le B\). Monotone convergence extends this to the entry time. Markov’s inequality therefore gives entry within \(O(\eta^{-2})\) steps with probability at least \(1/2\) from any starting state. Repeat the estimate at deterministic windows if entry has not occurred; the uniform conditional failure bound gives failure at most \(2^{-q}\) after \(q\) windows. On entry, apply the residence estimate for the remaining time. Taking \(q=O(\log(1/\zeta))\) gives the claimed horizon and radius. This is an equivalent common-noise coupling proof for additive isotropic martingale-difference noise. Ge et al., Escaping from Saddle Points, Definition 5, Theorem 6, Lemmas 7–9, and Appendix A, Theorem 13 and Lemmas 14–18. Why a matrix completion objective can have no spurious local minimaGe, Lee, and Ma study PSD observations of \(M=ZZ^	op\) with a symmetric independent-entry mask and row penalty \(R(X)=\sum_i(\|X_i\|-\alpha)_+^4\). The penalty gradient is rowwise radial: at a row above threshold it is \(4(\|X_i\|-\alpha)^3X_i/\|X_i\|\), and it vanishes on all other rows. This follows by differentiating the radial norm. At a stationary point it opposes growth of a large row. For \(E=XX^	op-M\), the unregularized objective \(g(X)= rac12\|P_\Omega(E)\|_F^2\) has \[
abla g(X)=2P_\Omega(E)X,\quad \mathrm d^2g(X)[H,H] =\|P_\Omega(XH^	op+HX^	op)\|_F^2+2\langle P_\Omega(E),HH^	opangle.\] Indeed, the residual at \(X+tH\) is \(E+t(XH^	op+HX^	op)+t^2HH^	op\). The first two Taylor coefficients give the displayed derivatives. With full observations, for rank one these conditions already characterize the minima, as shown in Problem 3. With partial observations, the row penalty and uniform concentration of the mask control which derivative tests can be transferred to the full problem. Ge, Lee, and Ma, Matrix Completion Has No Spurious Local Minimum, §§3–5. Sampled rank-one recoveryConsider \(F(x)= rac12\|P_\Omega(xx^	op-zz^	op)\|_F^2+\lambda R(x)\) for \(\|z\|=1\) and \(\|z\|_\infty\le\mu/\sqrt d\). This derivation uses the rank-one structure in §4 of Ge, Lee, and Ma. It gives exact recovery for \(p\ge C\mu^6\log(d+1)/d\) with a sufficiently large universal constant \(C\), in the regime where the condition is feasible. Set \(\alpha=10\mu/\sqrt d\) and \(\lambda\ge p\mu^2/\alpha^2\). Let \(B_{ij}=\mathbf1\{(i,j)\in\Omega\}\) and \(E_B=B-p\mathbf1\mathbf1^	op\). Entries on and above the diagonal of \(B\) are independent Bernoulli\((p)\), with their transposes reflected below it. A Chernoff bound and a union bound give \(\sum_jB_{ij}\le2pd\) for every row with high probability when \(pd\ge C\log(d+1)\). For the spectral estimate, write \(E_B\) as an independent sum of centered matrices \(\xi_{ij}(e_ie_j^	op+e_je_i^	op)\) for \(i<j\) and \(\xi_{ii}e_ie_i^	op\) on the diagonal. Each summand has norm at most 1, and the sum of the expected squares is diagonal with entries \(dp(1-p)\le dp\). Matrix Bernstein gives \[P(\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\ge t)\le 2d\exp[-t^2/(2dp+2t/3)].\] Thus \(\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_0\sqrt{pd\log(d+1)}\) with failure probability at most an inverse polynomial in \(d\). The same event controls the sampled forms uniformly, even when \(x\) is chosen from the observations. For example, \[\|(P_\Omega(uv^	op)-puv^	op)s\| \le \|u\|_\infty\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|v\odot s\|,\qquad |\langle P_\Omega(uv^	op),ab^	opangle-p\langle uv^	op,ab^	opangle| \le\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|u\odot a\|\|v\odot b\|.\] These identities come from writing the centered masked product as \(\operatorname{diag}(u)E_B\operatorname{diag}(v)\). They give a rank-one route to the uniform estimates in Appendix D of the paper. At a stationary point, a coordinate \(i\) maximizing \(|x_i|=M_x\) gives the row bound. If \(M_x>2\alpha\), multiply the stationarity equation by the sign of \(x_i\). The observed self-product contribution \(2M_x\sum_{j:B_{ij}=1}x_j^2\) is nonnegative. The target term is at most \(4p\mu^2 M_x\) in magnitude by the row count bound and \(|z_i z_j|\le\mu^2/d\). The penalty term is at least \(\lambda M_x^3/2\). Therefore \(M_x^2\le8p\mu^2/\lambda\), and in every case \(\|x\|_\infty\le4\alpha\). Denote \(\chi=(4\alpha)^2\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}/p\). The sample-size condition lets us make \(\chi\) an arbitrarily small constant. With \(s=\|x\|^2\) and \(a=\langle z,xangle\), the vector mask bounds give \[\left\|a z-sx- rac{\lambda}{2p}
abla R(x)ight\|\le2\chi\sqrt s.\] Indeed, \(\|\operatorname{diag}(z)E_B(z\odot x)\|\le\|z\|_\infty^2\|E_B\|_{m op}\|x\|\) and the analogous \(x\) estimate is bounded by \((4\alpha)^2\|E_B\|_{m op}\|x\|\). Inner product with \(x\) gives \(s^2\le a^2+2\chi s\le(1+2\chi)s\), because the radial penalty has nonnegative inner product with \(x\). Thus \(s\le1+2\chi\). Let \(J=\{i:|x_i|>\alpha\}\). The preceding bound implies \(|J|\le s/\alpha^2\) and \(\|z_J\|^2\le s/100\). Use \(v=z_{J^c}\) in the Hessian test. The penalty curvature contributes zero since \(v_i\) vanishes on every coordinate where the Hessian of the penalty is nonzero. The centered mask perturbs the unregularized Hessian quadratic form by at most \((2\|x\|_\infty^2+2\|z\|_\infty^2)\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|v\|^2+2\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|x\odot v\|^2+2\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|x\odot v\|^2\), which is \(O(p\chi)\|v\|^2\). This bound follows term by term from the squared derivative \(\|P_\Omega(xv^	op+vx^	op)\|_F^2\) and the residual term \(2 v^	op P_\Omega(xx^	op-zz^	op)v\). Without the mask the Hessian test equals \(2s\|v\|^2+4\langle x,vangle^2-2\langle z,vangle^2\). Even if the observed Hessian is only bounded below by \(-	au I\) with \(	au\le p/10\), division by \(p\|v\|^2\) yields \(6s\ge2\|v\|^2-	au/p-O(\chi)\). Here \(\langle z,vangle=\|v\|^2\ge1-s/100\). For small enough \(\chi\), this forces \(s\ge1/4\). On \(J\), \(|a z_i|\le\sqrt s\,\mu/\sqrt d\) while \(s|x_i|\ge10s\,\mu/\sqrt d\). Since \(s\ge1/4\), the latter dominates. Hence on those coordinates \(a z_i-sx_i\) has sign opposite to the regularizer gradient, whose sign agrees with \(x_i\). Removing the penalty from the vector bound cannot increase its left side. On \(J^c\) the penalty derivative is already zero. We obtain \(\|a z-sx\|\le2\chi\sqrt s\). Its inner products with \(x\) and \(z\) imply \(|a^2-s^2|\le2\chi s\) and \(|a(1-s)|\le2\chi\sqrt s\). For sufficiently small \(\chi\), \(s\ge1/4\) now also bounds \(|a|\) below by a positive constant. It follows that \(s=1+O(\chi)\) and \(|a|=1+O(\chi)\). After changing the sign of \(z\) if needed, \(\|x-z\|^2=s+1-2|a|=O(\chi)\). To finish with exactness, set \(e=x-z\), \(T=ze^	op+ez^	op\) and \(Q=ee^	op\). For \(e\) small, the quadratic residual \(P_\Omega(Q)\) is dominated by the linear residual \(P_\Omega(T)\). First, a second use of the multiplicative Chernoff bound gives \(\sum_i B_{ij} z_i^2\ge p/2\) for every \(j\), with failure probability at most \(d\exp(-c pd/\mu^2)\). This is the weighted Bernoulli bound obtained by rescaling the weights by \(\mu^2/d\) so the summands lie in \([0,1]\) and using their total mean. Expand the squared norm of \(P_\Omega(T)\). Its two squared terms sum to at least \(p\|e\|^2\) by that row event. The cross term is \(2p(z^	op e)^2+2(z\odot e)^	op E_B(z\odot e)\), lower bounded by \(-2\|z\|_\infty^2\|E_B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|e\|^2\). Hence \(\|P_\Omega(T)\|_F^2\ge(p/2)\|e\|^2\). Also \[\|P_\Omega(Q)\|_F^2 =p\|e\|^4+(e\odot e)^	op E_B(e\odot e) \le[p\|e\|^2+\|E_B\|_{m op}\|e\|_\infty^2]\|e\|^2.\] Because \(\|e\|_\infty\le5\alpha\) and \(\|e\|^2=O(\chi)\), the ratio of the two squared residual norms is \(O(\chi)\) when \(e
e0\). Choose \(\chi\) small enough that \(\|P_\Omega(Q)\|_F\le\|P_\Omega(T)\|_F/4\). The directional derivative in the direction \(e\) is \[\langle P_\Omega(T+Q),P_\Omega(T+2Q)angle+\lambda\langle
abla R(x),eangle .\] The first term is at least \((1-3/4)\|P_\Omega(T)\|_F^2\) by Cauchy–Schwarz. The second is nonnegative since any penalized \(x_i\) has \(x_i-z_i\) of the same sign. Unless \(e=0\) the directional derivative is strictly positive. This contradicts stationarity and proves exact recovery. All local minima meet the two derivative conditions, and \(\pm z\) attain zero objective. Ge, Lee, and Ma, Theorem 4.2, Lemmas 4.3–4.10, and Appendices C–E. Sampled positive-semidefinite completion at higher rankWe give the local-minimum proof for full-column-rank \(Z\in\mathbb R^{d	imes r}\) in Ge, Lee, and Ma, §5. Use their normalization \(\|Z\|_F^2=r\), incoherence bound \(\max_i\|Z_i\|\le\mu\sqrt{r/d}\), and condition number \(\kappa=\sigma_{\max}(Z)/\sigma_{\min}(Z)\). Set \(M=ZZ^	op\), \(R(X)=\sum_i(\|X_i\|-\alpha)_+^4\), and \(f(X)=	frac12\|\mathcal P_\Omega(XX^	op-M)\|_F^2+\lambda R(X)\). Under the symmetric Bernoulli sampling model, Theorem 5.3 uses \(p\ge C d^{-1}\log^2 d\max(\mu^6\kappa^{16}r^4,\mu^4\kappa^4r^6)\), \(\alpha=32\mu\kappa r/\sqrt d\), and \(\lambda\ge\mu^2rp/\alpha^2\). The proof below separates the sampling estimates from the algebraic implications at a local minimum. Ge, Lee, and Ma, Propositions 5.1–5.2, Theorem 5.3, and Appendices C–D. Stationarity controls row norms. The regularizer gradient is \(\Gamma X\) for a diagonal \(\Gamma\) with \(\Gamma_{ii}=4(\|X_i\|-\alpha)_+^3/\|X_i\|\) at nonzero rows and zero otherwise. If \(X_i\) has maximum norm \(s\), the row of \(\mathcal P_\Omega(M)X\) has norm at most \(2p\mu^2rs\) on the event that row \(i\) has at most \(2pd\) samples. Indeed, \(|M_{ij}|\le\mu^2r/d\) and each \(\|X_j\|\le s\). The inner product of \((\mathcal P_\Omega(XX^	op)X)_i\) with \(X_i\) is \(\sum_{j\in\Omega_i}\langle X_j,X_iangle^2\ge0\). Project the stationarity equation onto the unit vector along \(X_i\). This gives \(4\lambda(s-\alpha)_+^3\le4p\mu^2rs\). If \(s\ge2\alpha\), then \((s-\alpha)^3\ge s^3/8\), so \(s^2\le8p\mu^2r/\lambda\). The assumed \(\lambda\) therefore bounds \(s\) by \(4\alpha\). Replace sampled products by full products. The uniform cubic estimate in Theorem D.2 controls \(\mathcal P_\Omega(WW^	op)W-pWW^	op W\) for row-incoherent \(W\). For example, with fixed \(\|W\|_F=1\), the \(i\)th row is a sum of centered terms \((\mathbf1_{\{ij\in\Omega\}}-p)\langle W_i,W_jangle W_j\) of norm at most \(
u^3/d^{3/2}\) when \(\|W_i\|\le
u/\sqrt d\). Its expected squared norm is at most \(p
u^6/d^2\). The proof truncates using the uniform row-degree bound, concentrates the sum of squared row deviations, and unions over a Frobenius net with \(\exp(O(dr\log d))\) points; the cubic product is Lipschitz on the normalized bounded region. To pass from independent directed entries to symmetric entries the paper averages a directed mask and its transpose. This has the law of the average of independent symmetric masks off the diagonal. The triangle inequality for three independent masks bounds the tail of one mask in terms of the tail of the sum of two (Claim D.3). The mixed-product estimates used in the stationarity equations are those of Lemma 5.5. Here is how those estimates constrain \(X\). For \(A=\mathcal P_\Omega(XX^	op)X\), the row calculation above gives \(\langle A,\Gamma Xangle\ge0\). Thus \(\|A+(\lambda/2)\Gamma X\|_F\ge\|A\|_F\). Substituting stationarity and comparing sampled and full products bounds \(\|XX^	op X\|_F\) by \(\|ZZ^	op X\|_F\) plus the concentration errors. Write the singular values of \(X\) as \(s_j\). The left squared norm is \(\sum_j s_j^6\), whereas the right squared norm before the error is at most \(\sigma_{\max}(Z)^4\sum_j s_j^2\). Apply \(\sum_j s_j^6\ge(\sum_j s_j^2)^3/r^2\) and \(\max_j s_j^6\le\sum_j s_j^6\). This gives the bounds in Lemma 5.5, \(\|X\|_F^2\le 2r\sigma_{\max}(Z)^2\) and \(\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2r^{1/6}\sigma_{\max}(Z)\), together with a small residual in the full first-order equation. Second-order test. Put \(J=\{i:\|X_i\|\le\alpha\}\) and let \(Z_J\) agree with \(Z\) on \(J\) and vanish elsewhere. Since \(|J^c|\alpha^2\le\|X\|_F^2\), \(\|Z-Z_J\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sqrt{|J^c|}\mu\sqrt{r/d}\). The chosen threshold and the Frobenius bound ensure \(\sigma_{\min}(Z_J)\ge \sigma_{\min}(Z)/2\). Let \(v\) be a unit right singular vector of \(X\) for its smallest singular value. There is a unit \(z\) in the column space of \(Z_J\) with \(\|X^	op z\|\le\sigma_{\min}(X)\): compress \(XX^	op\) to an \(r\)-dimensional subspace and use the min–max characterization of its \(r\)th largest eigenvalue. The regularizer contributes zero curvature on the direction \(H=zv^	op\) because its active rows lie outside \(J\) and the quartic has zero second derivative at the threshold. The sampled Hessian test is \[\|\mathcal P_\Omega(z w^	op+w z^	op)\|_F^2 \ge 2\langle\mathcal P_\Omega(M-XX^	op),zz^	opangle,\qquad w=Xv.\] The bilinear estimate D.1 transfers the test to the full inner product with additive error \(pe\) at the paper’s sampling rate. Its proof starts with Bernstein for a fixed pair: with unit Frobenius norms and entry bounds \(a,b\), the summands are bounded by \(2ab\) and their aggregate variance is at most \(2pab\), merging symmetric pairs. A union bound over a rank-\(O(r)\) Frobenius net of size \(\exp(O(dr\log d))\) and a Frobenius Lipschitz extension give \(O(ab\,dr\log d+\sqrt{pab\,dr\log d})\) uniformly. Apply this to the two products in the Hessian expression. After dividing the Hessian inequality by \(2p\), expand the rank-two square: \[\|w\|^2+\langle z,wangle^2+\|X^	op z\|^2 \ge \|Z^	op z\|^2-e/2.\] The left is at most \(3\sigma_{\min}(X)^2\), while the right is at least \(\sigma_{\min}(Z_J)^2-e/2\). Making the sampling error sufficiently small proves that \(\sigma_{\min}(X)\) is bounded below by a constant times \(\sigma_{\min}(Z)\), as in Lemma 5.6. Remove the row penalty and recover the Gram matrix. Write \(B=ZZ^	op X-XX^	op X\). The residual from the first-order condition controls \(B-(\lambda/2p)\Gamma X\). On a row with positive \(\Gamma_{ii}\), the negative term in \(\langle B_i,X_iangle\) has magnitude at least \(\sigma_{\min}(X)^2\|X_i\|^2\). The positive term is at most \(\|X_i\|\|Z_i\|\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}\). With the row threshold and the bounds of Lemmas 5.5–5.6 the negative term dominates, giving \(\langle B,\Gamma Xangle\le0\) (Lemma 5.7). Expanding a squared norm now gives \(\|B\|_F^2\le\|B-(\lambda/2p)\Gamma X\|_F^2\). Decompose \(Z=U+V\) with \(U=P_{\mathrm{col}(X)}Z\) and \(V=(I-P_{\mathrm{col}(X)})Z\). Since \(V^	op X=0\), \[\|B\|_F^2=\|(UU^	op-XX^	op)X\|_F^2+\|VU^	op X\|_F^2.\] These terms are orthogonal in their left column spaces. If \(\|B\|_F\le\eta\), invert \(X\) on its column space to obtain \(\|UU^	op-XX^	op\|_F\le\eta/\sigma_{\min}(X)\). Also \(\sigma_{\min}(UU^	op X)\ge\sigma_{\min}(X)^3-\eta\), so \(\sigma_{\min}(U^	op X)\ge(\sigma_{\min}(X)^3-\eta)/\|U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\). For \(\eta<\sigma_{\min}(X)^3/2\), this bounds \(\|V\|_F\le2\eta\|U\|_{\mathrm{op}}/\sigma_{\min}(X)^3\). Finally expand \(ZZ^	op=UU^	op+UV^	op+VU^	op+VV^	op\) and use \(\|UV^	op\|_F\le\|U\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|V\|_F\), \(\|VV^	op\|_F\le\|V\|_F^2\). This is the Gram-error control of Lemma 5.8. Local exactness. Let \(ho=\|XX^	op-M\|_F\) be sufficiently small. Write \(M=\operatorname{diag}(D,0)\) in an orthonormal basis and \(X=[A^	op,W^	op]^	op\) in that basis. Then \(\|AA^	op-D\|_F\leho\) and \(\|WA^	op\|_F\leho\). The first shows \(\sigma_{\min}(A)\ge(\sigma_{\min}(Z)^2-ho)^{1/2}\); the second gives \(\|W\|_F\leho/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). Choose an exact factor \(Y=[(AS)^	op,0]^	op\) with \(S=(A^	op D^{-1}A)^{-1/2}\), so \(YY^	op=M\). The eigenvalues of \(A^	op D^{-1}A\) differ from one by at most \(ho/\sigma_{\min}(Z)^2\), since they are those of \(D^{-1/2}AA^	op D^{-1/2}\). On this interval the derivative of \(t^{-1/2}\) is bounded, so \(\|S-I\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(ho/\sigma_{\min}(Z)^2)\). Consequently \(\|X-Y\|_F=O(ho\sqrt r/\sigma_{\min}(Z)^2)\), as in Claim C.4. Put \(D_1=Y(X-Y)^	op+(X-Y)Y^	op\) and \(D_2=(X-Y)(X-Y)^	op\). Then the residual is \(D_1+D_2\), and the directional derivative of \(XX^	op\) along \(X-Y\) is \(D_1+2D_2\). Appendix C uses two sampling estimates: \(\|\mathcal P_\Omega D_1\|_F^2\ge(5p/6)\|D_1\|_F^2\) on the tangent space (Lemma C.6), and \(\|\mathcal P_\Omega D_2\|_F^2\le(p/25)ho^2\) for the controlled near-solution region (Lemma C.5, citing Sun and Luo’s Proposition 4.3). Since \(\|D_2\|_F\le\|X-Y\|_F^2\leho/10\) in that region, \(\|D_1\|_F\ge9ho/10\). Write \(a=\|\mathcal P_\Omega D_1\|_F\) and \(b=\|\mathcal P_\Omega D_2\|_F\). The loss derivative is at least \(a^2-3ab+2b^2=(a-b)(a-2b)\). Since \(a\ge\sqrt{27/40}\sqrt p\,ho\) and \(b\le\sqrt p\,ho/5\), it is greater than \(pho^2/4\) when \(ho>0\). The regularizer contributes a nonnegative derivative: \(Y=ZQ\) for an orthogonal \(Q\) so its rows have the same norms as those of \(Z\), below \(\alpha\). For \(\Gamma_{ii}>0\), \(\langle X_i,X_i-Y_iangle\ge\|X_i\|(\|X_i\|-\|Y_i\|)>0\). Stationarity therefore forces \(ho=0\). The exact factors have zero regularizer as well, so the objective is zero. Ge, Lee, and Ma, Lemma C.1 · Sun and Luo, §4.1 and Proposition 4.3 Why the two local sampling estimates holdLet \(T\) be the symmetric tangent space \(\{YH^	op+HY^	op\}\), where \(Y\) is an exact factor of \(M\). With \(P\) the orthogonal projector onto \(\operatorname{col}(Y)\), the Frobenius orthogonal projection onto \(T\) sends a symmetric matrix \(B\) to \(PB+BP-PBP\). This follows by writing \(B\) in the orthogonal decomposition given by \(P\): it preserves all blocks except the lower-right block. In the orthonormal basis of symmetric coordinate matrices \(E_a\) (off-diagonal entries use \((e_ie_j^	op+e_je_i^	op)/\sqrt2\)), put \(u_a=P_T E_a\). From \(\|Pe_i\|\le\|Z_i\|/\sigma_{\min}(Z)\) we have \(\max_a\|u_a\|_F^2\le C\mu^2r/(d\,\sigma_{\min}(Z)^2)=:L_T\). Moreover, \(\sum_a u_a\otimes u_a=I_T\), because expanding any tangent vector in the coordinate basis and projecting back leaves it unchanged. The random quadratic form measuring tangent energy has operator \(\sum_a \xi_a u_a\otimes u_a\), where the independent \(\xi_a\) are the Bernoulli observations. After centering, each summand has norm at most \(L_T\), and the sum of its operator variances is bounded above by \(pL_T I_T\) since \((u_a\otimes u_a)^2=\|u_a\|^2(u_a\otimes u_a)\). Matrix Bernstein at deviation \(p/6\) gives probability at most \(2\dim(T)\exp(-c p/L_T)\) of deviating that far from \(p I_T\). This proves the tangent lower bound used above on a single event for all tangent directions and all exact factors, since they have the same column space. For the quadratic residual, write \(H=X-Y\) and let \(S\) denote the matrix of centered Bernoulli indicators. Define a matrix \(F\) whose \(i\)th row is \(H_i\otimes H_i\). Then \( ig((HH^	op)_{ij} ig)^2=(FF^	op)_{ij}\). Consequently \[\|\mathcal P_\Omega(HH^	op)\|_F^2 =p\|HH^	op\|_F^2+\operatorname{tr}(F^	op S F) \le p\|H\|_F^4+\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\max_i\|H_i\|^2\|H\|_F^2.\] The inequality uses \(\|F\|_F^2=\sum_i\|H_i\|^4\). For the symmetric mask write \(S\) as a sum of independently centered diagonal and off-diagonal coordinate matrices. Each summand has norm at most one and the operator variance is diagonal with entries at most \(pd\). Hence matrix Bernstein gives \(\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C(\sqrt{pd\log d}+\log d)\) with probability at least \(1-d^{-10}\) after choosing the absolute constant. Substituting the row bound \(\max_i\|H_i\|\le4\alpha+\mu\sqrt{r/d}\) and \(\|H\|_F=O(ho\sqrt r/\sigma_{\min}(Z)^2)\) makes the right side at most \(pho^2/25\) whenever the resulting coefficients satisfy \[\left( rac{\|H\|_F^2}{ho}ight)^2+  rac{\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{p}\max_i\|H_i\|^2 \left( rac{\|H\|_F}{ho}ight)^2\le rac1{25}.\] This shows explicitly how closeness, uniform row control, and sampling concentration enter the quadratic estimate. The proof of the full sampling range in Lemma C.5 uses Sun and Luo’s Proposition 4.3, which gives that estimate on the controlled region without imposing the sufficient condition above. ChallengesProblem 1Suppose every observed value of a nonzero rank-one matrix is nonzero. Give necessary and sufficient graph conditions for unique rank-one completion among real matrices, including vertices with no observed edges. Show solution View rows and columns as vertices of a bipartite graph with observed entries as edges. If the graph is connected, fix one nonzero factor coordinate as a gauge and propagate each adjacent factor by dividing the edge value by the known coordinate. Existence of the given completion ensures consistency around cycles. All factors are then determined up to one global rescaling and every product is fixed. If an isolated row or column is present, its factor can vary while preserving the observations and changing at least one unobserved product. If two components contain edges, independently rescale the row factors in one by \(c\) and the column factors there by \(1/c\). Cross-component entries change. In the no-observation case a real rank-one completion is plainly nonunique. Problem 2A \(4	imes4\) matrix has its first two rows equal to \((9,0,1,0)\) and the other two equal to \((2,2,2,2)\). Compute its smallest joint incoherence constant without an SVD. Show solution The column projector has constant diagonal \(1/2\). For the row projector, form \(B\) from the distinct rows and use \(B^	op(BB^	op)^{-1}B\). The inner inverse is \( rac1{912} igl( egin{smallmatrix}16&-20\-20&82\end{smallmatrix} igr)\). The four column quadratic forms give the diagonal \((113,41,33,41)/114\). The rank is 2, so the joint constant is \((4/2)\max\{1/2,113/114\}=113/57\). Problem 3. A second-order proof of exact rank-one recoveryLet \(z\) be a unit vector and \(g(x)=	frac14\|xx^	op-zz^	op\|_F^2\). Prove from first- and second-order conditions that every local minimizer equals \(z\) or \(-z\). Use only the gradient inner products with \(x,z\) and the Hessian quadratic form in direction \(z\). These are the tests later compared to their sampled counterparts. Ge, Lee, and Ma, §3, Lemma 3.2 and Claims 1f–2f. Show solution Put \(s=\|x\|^2\) and \(a=\langle z,xangle\). Expanding the Frobenius norm gives \(g=(s^2-2a^2+1)/4\), \(
abla g=sx-az\), and \(
abla^2 g=sI+2xx^	op-zz^	op\). Its quadratic form at \(z\) is \(s+2a^2-1\). Positivity and \(a^2\le s\) imply \(s\ge1/3\). Taking the gradient inner product with \(x\) yields \(s^2=a^2\), hence \(a
e0\). Taking it with \(z\) yields \(a(s-1)=0\), so \(s=1\) and \(a^2=1\). Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz forces \(x=\pm z\). Both are global minima with residual zero. Problem 4. A certificate for unique nuclear norm completionWrite \(M=U\Sigma V^	op\) and let \(T=\{UA^	op+BV^	op\}\). Assume \(P_\Omega\) is injective on \(T\), and some \(Y=P_\Omega Y\) satisfies \(P_TY=UV^	op\) and \(\|P_{T^\perp}Y\|_{m op}<1\). Prove \(M\) is the unique minimizer of nuclear norm subject to the observations. Candès and Recht, Exact Matrix Completion via Convex Optimization, §3, dual uniqueness argument. Show solution For feasible \(M+H\), \(P_\Omega H=0\), so \(\langle Y,Hangle=0\). Let \(W\) be the product of the singular-vector matrices from a thin SVD of \(P_{T^\perp}H\) (or zero if that projection is zero). Its row and column spaces lie in the orthogonal complements of \(V\) and \(U\). Thus \(UV^	op+W\) has spectral norm at most one by orthogonality, and \(\langle W,Hangle=\|P_{T^\perp}H\|_\ast\). Nuclear/spectral norm duality gives \[\|M+H\|_\ast-\|M\|_\ast \ge \langle UV^	op+W,Hangle \ge (1-\|P_{T^\perp}Y\|_{m op})\|P_{T^\perp}H\|_\ast.\] The second inequality uses \(P_TY=UV^	op\) and subtracts the zero inner product with \(Y\). If \(P_{T^\perp}H
e0\) the objective strictly increases. Otherwise \(H\in T\) and injectivity with \(P_\Omega H=0\) gives \(H=0\). title: ACG 03: Transformations, Rotations, and Camera Frames
summary: A transformation can move a point in one coordinate system or express the same point in another. In either case, name the source and destination frames and check the origin and basis vectors before composing ma
body: A transformation can move a point in one coordinate system or express the same point in another. In either case, name the source and destination frames and check the origin and basis vectors before composing matrices. Affine transformations and homogeneous coordinatesWith column vectors, the affine map \(x'=Ax+t\) becomes \[\begin{pmatrix}x'\\1\end{pmatrix}= \begin{pmatrix}A&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}x\\1\end{pmatrix}.\] The difference of two point vectors has homogeneous component zero, so translations leave displacement vectors unchanged. A rotation around \(c\) is \(T(c)RT(-c)\), applied from right to left. The expression \(R(x-c)+c\) immediately verifies that the pivot remains fixed. For invertible \(A\), the inverse map is \(A^{-1}x'-A^{-1}t\). Normal vectors follow a different rule. If \(n^\mathsf T u=0\) for a tangent \(u\), require \(n'^\mathsf T Au=0\). Choosing \(n'=A^{-\mathsf T}n\) preserves the dot product. Normalize afterward when a shader expects unit length. Using \(An\) works for rotations and uniform scaling up to normalization, but nonuniform scaling can break orthogonality. PBRT, “Transformations” Rotations and the exponential mapA rotation preserves inner products, so \(R^\mathsf T R=I\). Its determinant is \(1\) because it also preserves orientation. These matrices form \(SO(3)\). Their inverses are transposes, and their products remain rotations. Let \(u\) be a unit axis and set \(Kv=u\times v\). The triple product gives \(K^2=uu^\mathsf T-I\) and \(K^3=-K\). Summing the odd and even terms of the exponential power series yields Rodrigues’ formula, \[R=e^{\theta K}=I+\sin\theta\,K+(1-\cos\theta)K^2.\] In an orthonormal basis with \(u\) as one axis, \(R\) consists of a planar rotation block and an unchanged axis. Taking the trace gives \(\operatorname{tr}R=1+2\cos\theta\). Apply this identity to \(R_1^\mathsf T R_2\) to recover the angle between two orientations. The identity rotation has no unique axis. At angle \(\pi\), an axis and its negative define the same rotation. Euler angles and quaternionsEuler angles depend on the rotation convention. For \(R=R_z(\gamma)R_y(\beta)R_x(\alpha)\), at \(\beta=\pi/2\) the \(x\) axis rotates onto \(-z\). Conjugating the rotation around \(x\) then gives \[R_z(\gamma)R_y(\pi/2)R_x(\alpha)=R_z(\gamma-\alpha)R_y(\pi/2).\] The two angles \(\gamma,\alpha\) no longer have independent effects. This is gimbal lock. The unit quaternion \(q=(\cos(\theta/2),u\sin(\theta/2))\) rotates a vector through \((0,v')=q(0,v)q^{-1}\). Expanding the vector part gives \[\cos\theta\,v+(1-\cos\theta)u(u^\mathsf Tv)+\sin\theta\,(u\times v),\] the same Rodrigues formula. Since the signs cancel in the sandwich product, \(q\) and \(-q\) encode one rotation. Implement shortest-arc spherical interpolationTwo unit quaternions span a two-dimensional plane in four dimensions. In that plane, the geodesic interpolation at fraction \(t\) combines them with sine weights. Flipping the endpoint representative when the dot product is negative chooses the shorter rotation path. The normalized linear limit avoids division by a tiny sine when the inputs are nearly equal. 12345678910111213from math import acos, sindef slerp(q0, q1, t): d = dot(q0, q1) if d < 0: q1, d = -q1, -d d = min(1.0, d) if d > 0.9995: return normalize((1 - t)*q0 + t*q1) omega = acos(d) a = sin((1 - t)*omega) / sin(omega) b = sin(t*omega) / sin(omega) return a*q0 + b*q1 The function assumes unit inputs, and the result represents \(q_0\) at \(t=0\) and the orientation of \(q_1\) at \(t=1\). When \(q_1=-q_0\), the entire interpolation represents the same orientation. The view matrixLet \(e\) be the camera center and let \(r,u,b\) denote its right, up, and backward unit vectors. Put the basis vectors into the columns of \(R\). The camera looks along its local negative \(z\) axis. Its camera-to-world map is \(p_w=Rp_c+e\), so \[p_c=R^\mathsf T(p_w-e),\qquad V=\begin{pmatrix}R^\mathsf T&-R^\mathsf T e\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] For target \(a\) and reference up vector \(u_0\), use \(b=\operatorname{normalize}(e-a)\), \(r=\operatorname{normalize}(u_0\times b)\), and \(u=b\times r\). A reference up parallel to \(b\) fails to determine the roll. The implementation should check that the camera center maps to the origin and that \(e-\lambda b\) with \(\lambda>0\) maps to negative local \(z\). The model-view composition is \(VM\), followed by the projection in Lecture 4. Exercises Construct the correct normal. The plane \(x+y=0\) undergoes scaling by \(\operatorname{diag}(2,1,3)\). Derive its transformed equation and normal. Explain why applying the same matrix to the original normal disagrees. Answer Solve for the old coordinates to obtain \(x'/2+y'=0\). The new normal is proportional to \((1/2,1,0)\), given by the inverse transpose. Multiplying directly gives \((2,1,0)\), whose dot product with the transformed tangent \((2,-1,0)\) is \(3\). Move the model and camera together. Let a rigid motion \(T\) transform both the camera-to-world matrix \(C\) and the model-to-world matrix \(M\). Prove that camera-space geometry is invariant. Answer After the motion, the product is \((TC)^{-1}(TM)=C^{-1}T^{-1}TM=C^{-1}M\). The camera senses relative placement, so the common world-space motion cancels. Quaternion sign and timing. Interpolate from identity to a \(270^\circ\) rotation about \(z\) via shortest-arc SLERP. What orientation is represented at \(t=1/2\)? Answer The endpoint quaternion has negative real part \(\cos 135^\circ\). Its negation represents a \(-90^\circ\) turn about \(z\). The shortest arc begins at identity and ends at this signed angle, so its midpoint represents \(-45^\circ\) about \(z\). ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 3, “Transformation,” September 30, 2026, slides 50–81 for affine maps, 82–125 for rotations, and 126–137 for camera frames. title: ML 03: SGD, SVRG, and Mirror Descent
summary: Prove a convergence bound for averaged SGD, derive SVRG’s epoch contraction, and extend descent to the geometry of a probability simplex.
body:
Prove a convergence bound for averaged SGD, derive SVRG’s epoch contraction, and extend descent to the geometry of a probability simplex. The horizontal axis counts component-gradient evaluations, including the full gradient at each SVRG snapshot. The illustrated snapshots use the last inner iterate. Which iterate does SGD control?Let \(f\) be convex and \(L\)-smooth with minimizer \(w^\star\), and set \(w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta G_t\). Conditional on the history \(\mathcal F_t\) before sampling the next direction, assume \(\mathbb E_tG_t=g_t=
abla f(w_t)\) and \(\mathbb E_t\|G_t-g_t\|^2=v_t\le\sigma^2\). Then \[\mathbb E_t\|w_{t+1}-w^\star\|^2 =\|w_t-w^\star\|^2-2\eta\langle g_t,w_t-w^\starangle+\eta^2(\|g_t\|^2+v_t).\] Smoothness gives \(\mathbb E_t f(w_{t+1})\le f(w_t)-\eta\|g_t\|^2+(L\eta^2/2)(\|g_t\|^2+v_t)\). Combine this with convexity and use \(\eta\le1/L\): \[ egin{aligned} \mathbb E_t[f(w_{t+1})-f^\star] &\le \langle g_t,w_t-w^\starangle-	frac\eta2\|g_t\|^2+	frac\eta2v_t\ &= rac{\|w_t-w^\star\|^2-\mathbb E_t\|w_{t+1}-w^\star\|^2}{2\eta}+\eta v_t. \end{aligned}\] Take total expectations, sum over \(T\) steps, and apply Jensen’s inequality at \( ar w_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T w_t\): \[\mathbb E[f( ar w_T)-f^\star]\le  rac{\|w_0-w^\star\|^2}{2\eta T}+\eta\sigma^2.\] A step proportional to \(T^{-1/2}\) balances the terms. A uniform random output iterate has the same objective bound. The proof does not imply a bound for the last iterate because stochastic losses need not decrease monotonically. An average of \(b\) conditionally independent sample gradients has variance \(\sigma^2/b\) when the individual variance is bounded by \(\sigma^2\). The \(1/T\) stochastic rate under strong convexityFor a \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth \(f\) on a closed convex set containing an unconstrained minimizer \(w^\star\), use the update with Euclidean projection and assume \(\mathbb E_t\|G_t\|^2\le G^2\) along the trajectory. Projection cannot increase the distance to a feasible comparator: the projection’s first-order condition makes the cross term in the squared-distance expansion nonnegative. Strong monotonicity gives \(\langle
abla f(w_t),w_t-w^\starangle\ge\mu\|w_t-w^\star\|^2\). Therefore for \(\eta_t=1/(\mu(t+1))\) and \(t\ge1\), \[\mathbb E\|w_{t+1}-w^\star\|^2 \le rac{t-1}{t+1}\mathbb E\|w_t-w^\star\|^2+ rac{G^2}{\mu^2(t+1)^2}.\] Let \(C=\max\{\mathbb E\|w_1-w^\star\|^2,G^2/\mu^2\}\). If the distance bound is \(C/t\), the right side is at most \(C/(t+1)\) because the remaining slack before the noise term is \(C/(t(t+1))\). Induction gives squared distance \(O(1/t)\). The smooth upper model at \(w^\star\) has zero linear term, so the expected last-iterate objective gap is at most \(LC/(2t)\). This gives the stochastic rate contrasted with geometric decay for deterministic strongly convex GD in the 2026 slide 10 comparison. SVRG as a control variateTake \(f=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\), where each \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth. At an epoch snapshot \(	ilde w\), compute its full gradient. Sample \(i\) uniformly and use \[V_i=
abla f_i(w)-
abla f_i(	ilde w)+
abla f(	ilde w).\] Its conditional expectation is \(
abla f(w)\). If \(A_i=
abla f_i(w)-
abla f_i(	ilde w)\), its variance is \(\mathbb E\|A_i-\mathbb EA_i\|^2\le\mathbb E\|A_i\|^2\le L^2\|w-	ilde w\|^2\). The same index in both evaluations makes this cancellation possible. For an objective-gap bound, define \(a_i(u)=
abla f_i(u)-
abla f_i(w^\star)\). The function \(h_i(u)=f_i(u)-
abla f_i(w^\star)^	op u\) is minimized at \(w^\star\). A \(1/L\) gradient step on \(h_i\) cannot improve more than its current gap, so \[\|a_i(u)\|^2\le 2L[f_i(u)-f_i(w^\star)-\langle
abla f_i(w^\star),u-w^\starangle].\] Averaging gives \(\mathbb E_i\|a_i(u)\|^2\le2L\Delta(u)\), where \(\Delta(u)=f(u)-f^\star\). Write \(V_i=a_i(w)-(a_i(	ilde w)-\mathbb Ea_i(	ilde w))\) and bound the squared sum by twice each squared term. It follows that \[\mathbb E_i\|V_i\|^2\le4L(\Delta(w)+\Delta(	ilde w)).\] By expansion of the next squared distance and convexity, \[\mathbb E_i\|w^+-w^\star\|^2+2\eta(1-2L\eta)\Delta(w) \le\|w-w^\star\|^2+4L\eta^2\Delta(	ilde w).\] If \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, start \(w_0=	ilde w\), sum this bound over \(m\) updates, and choose \(	ilde w^+\) uniformly from \(w_0,\ldots,w_{m-1}\). The starting squared distance is at most \(2\Delta(	ilde w)/\mu\), so \[\mathbb E[\Delta(	ilde w^+)\mid	ilde w] \le  rac{1/(m\mu\eta)+2L\eta}{1-2L\eta}\Delta(	ilde w).\] Choosing \(\eta=1/(8L)\) and \(m\ge32L/\mu\) gives a factor at most \(2/3\). An epoch costs \(n+2m\) component evaluations. To reduce the initial gap by a factor \(\varepsilon\), this takes \(O((n+L/\mu)\log(1/\varepsilon))\) component-gradient evaluations. Full gradient descent costs \(O(n(L/\mu)\log(1/\varepsilon))\) evaluations by the rate in Lecture 2. For a composite objective \(P=f+R\), with a proper convex regularizer \(R\), the optimality condition \(-
abla f(w^\star)\in\partial R(w^\star)\) implies \(\Delta_P(u)\ge\Delta_f(u)-\langle
abla f(w^\star),u-w^\starangle\). The same argument therefore bounds the second moment of \(V_i-
abla f(w^\star)\) by \(4L(\Delta_P(w)+\Delta_P(	ilde w))\). Mirror descent and the simplexA convex function’s tangent at each queried point \(w_t\) gives a lower bound on \(f(u)\). Average those inequalities and use Jensen at \( ar w_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}w_t\) to obtain \[f( ar w_T)-f(u)\le T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\langle
abla f(w_t),w_t-uangle.\] Thus controlling the sum of the linearized gaps also controls the objective value of the averaged iterate. A differentiable convex potential \(\psi\) defines the Bregman divergence \[D_\psi(u,w)=\psi(u)-\psi(w)-\langle
abla\psi(w),u-wangle.\] The update minimizes \(\eta\langle g_t,uangle+D_\psi(u,w_t)\) on a convex set. In the interior of an unconstrained domain the equation is \(
abla\psi(w_{t+1})=
abla\psi(w_t)-\eta g_t\). A squared-Euclidean potential gives projected gradient descent. The three-point identity follows by expanding the three divergences and canceling potential values: \[D_\psi(u,w_t)-D_\psi(u,w_{t+1})-D_\psi(w_{t+1},w_t) =\langle
abla\psi(w_{t+1})-
abla\psi(w_t),u-w_{t+1}angle.\] The right side is the change in the tangent model evaluated at \(u\), after accounting for the old tangent’s gap at \(w_{t+1}\). The variational inequality for the mirror update says that adding \(\eta\langle g_t,u-w_{t+1}angle\) to this inner product makes it nonnegative. Thus \[\eta\langle g_t,w_{t+1}-uangle\le D_\psi(u,w_t)-D_\psi(u,w_{t+1})-D_\psi(w_{t+1},w_t).\] For a 1-strongly convex potential, adding \(\eta\langle g_t,w_t-w_{t+1}angle\) and applying Young’s inequality in the primal and dual norms cancels the last divergence. Sum over \(t\) to get \[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\langle g_t,w_t-uangle \le D_\psi(u,w_0)/\eta+	frac\eta2\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\|g_t\|_\ast^2.\] For \(\|g_t\|_\ast\leho\) and \(\Theta=D_\psi(u,w_0)>0\), choose \(\eta=\sqrt{2\Theta}/(ho\sqrt T)\) for average regret at most \(ho\sqrt{2\Theta/T}\). With \(g_t=
abla f(w_t)\), the same bound holds for the objective gap of the averaged iterate. Legendre coordinates and projectionFor a differentiable Legendre potential, write \(p=
abla\psi(x)\) and \(\psi^\ast(p)=\sup_v(\langle p,vangle-\psi(v))\). At the interior optimizer the stationarity condition is \(
abla\psi(v)=p\), and the derivative of the conjugate is \(
abla\psi^\ast(p)=v\). Fenchel equality \(\psi^\ast(p)=\langle p,xangle-\psi(x)\) yields \[D_\psi(u,x)=\psi(u)+\psi^\ast(p)-\langle p,uangle =D_{\psi^\ast}(
abla\psi(x),
abla\psi(u)).\] The last equality follows by inserting \(
abla\psi^\ast(
abla\psi(u))=u\) and applying Fenchel equality at \(u\). In dual coordinates the divergence reverses its arguments. If \(y=\arg\min_{v\in C}D_\psi(v,x)\) for convex \(C\), its first-order condition is \(\langle
abla\psi(y)-
abla\psi(x),u-yangle\ge0\) for \(u\in C\). The three-point identity then gives \(D_\psi(u,x)\ge D_\psi(u,y)+D_\psi(y,x)\). Equality holds when the primal chord \(u-y\) is orthogonal to the dual chord \(
abla\psi(y)-
abla\psi(x)\). Amari, Information Geometry and Its Applications, §§1.3–1.4 and 1.6. Negative entropy and multiplicative weightsOn the probability simplex, use \(\psi(w)=\sum_j w_j\log w_j\). With positive initial coordinates, the gradient components are \(1+\log w_j\). The equality constraint introduces a common additive term, removed by normalization: \[w_{t+1,j}= rac{w_{t,j}e^{-\eta g_{t,j}}}{\sum_k w_{t,k}e^{-\eta g_{t,k}}}.\] On the simplex interior the Hessian is diagonal with entries \(1/w_j\). For a displacement \(v\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives \((\sum_j|v_j|)^2\le(\sum_jw_j)(\sum_jv_j^2/w_j)=v^	op
abla^2\psi(w)v\). Integrating along a segment yields \(\ell_1\) strong convexity, extended by continuity to boundary targets. The dual norm is \(\ell_\infty\). For uniform \(w_0\), \(D_\psi(u,w_0)\le\log d\). If \(\|g_t\|_\infty\leho\), optimizing the step in the regret bound gives average regret at most \(ho\sqrt{2\log d/T}\). With Euclidean projected descent the uniform-start squared diameter is at most 1, but gradients can have \(\ell_2\) norm \(ho\sqrt d\), giving average regret at most \(ho\sqrt{d/T}\). The corresponding iteration bounds at accuracy \(\varepsilon\) scale as \(ho^2\log d/\varepsilon^2\) and \(ho^2d/\varepsilon^2\). Mirror descent and cumulative linearizationIn the unconstrained interior setting, initialize at a differentiable minimizer \(w_0\) of \(\psi\), so \(
abla\psi(w_0)=0\). Unrolling the dual update gives \(
abla\psi(w_{t+1})=-\eta\sum_{j=0}^t g_j\). This is also the optimality equation for minimizing \(\psi(u)+\eta\langle\sum_{j=0}^t g_j,uangle\). Strict convexity makes each minimizer unique. Induction from the common initialization therefore makes the two trajectories identical under these hypotheses. Projection adds a normal-cone term. For example, take \([-1,1]\), \(\psi(w)=w^2/2\), step 1, and \(f(w)=3w^2/2+2w\). Both methods start at zero and have \(w_1=-1\). The next gradient is \(-1\), so projected descent moves to \(0\). The cumulative linearized objective instead minimizes \(u^2/2+(2-1)u\) over the interval and stays at \(-1\). ChallengesProblem 1Let \(a_i\) be a stored gradient for component \(i\) before the update and let \( ar a=n^{-1}\sum_i a_i\). Derive the conditional means of SAG’s direction \( ar a+(
abla f_i(w)-a_i)/n\) and SAGA’s direction \( ar a+
abla f_i(w)-a_i\). Give a state where the first direction vanishes while the true gradient is nonzero. Show solution Under a uniform fresh choice of \(i\), the mean of the replacement difference is \(
abla f(w)- ar a\). The SAG mean is \((1-1/n) ar a+
abla f(w)/n\) and the SAGA mean is \(
abla f(w)\). For \(n=2\) let both components equal \(u^2/2\), set \(w=1\), and let both stored gradients equal \(-1\), as obtained at \(u=-1\). The SAG direction after one replacement is zero for either sampled component, while the full gradient is 1. The example concerns the estimator conditional on the stored state. Problem 2Build unbiased SVRG for nonuniform probabilities \(p_i>0\). If component \(i\) is \(L_i\)-smooth, choose the probabilities to minimize the bound based only on these positive constants. Show solution Set \(a_i=
abla f_i(w)-
abla f_i(	ilde w)\) and use \(a_i/(np_i)+
abla f(	ilde w)\). Its variance is at most \(n^{-2}\sum_i\|a_i\|^2/p_i\le n^{-2}\|w-	ilde w\|^2\sum_iL_i^2/p_i\). Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\sum_i L_i^2/p_i\ge(\sum_iL_i)^2\) with equality when \(p_i=L_i/\sum_jL_j\). Problem 3. Accelerate gradient descent by coupling two updatesLet \(f\) be convex and \(L\)-smooth on a convex set \(Q\) in a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and let \(\psi\) be a differentiable 1-strongly convex potential in that norm. Start \(y_0=z_0\). At step \(k\ge0\) set \(a=(k+2)/(2L)\), \(	au=1/(aL)\), and \(x=(1-	au)y_k+	au z_k\). For \(g=
abla f(x)\), use \[y_{k+1}=\arg\min_{y\in Q}\{\langle g,y-xangle+	frac L2\|y-x\|^2\},\qquad z_{k+1}=\arg\min_{z\in Q}\{a\langle g,z-z_kangle+D_\psi(z,z_k)\}.\] Assume the subproblems and a minimizer \(u^\star\) exist. Prove \(f(y_T)-f(u^\star)\le4LD_\psi(u^\star,z_0)/(T+1)^2\) for \(T\ge1\). Allen-Zhu and Orecchia, Linear Coupling, Theorem 4.1, Lemmas 4.2–4.3 and Appendix C. Show solution At step \(k\), let \(G=f(x)-f(y_{k+1})\) and \(z^+=z_{k+1}\). The mirror variational inequality and strong convexity give for any \(u\in Q\) \[a\langle g,z_k-uangle \le a\langle g,z_k-z^+angle-	frac12\|z_k-z^+\|^2+D_\psi(u,z_k)-D_\psi(u,z^+).\] Set \(v=(1-	au)y_k+	au z^+\in Q\), so \(x-v=	au(z_k-z^+)\). The first two terms become \[a^2L ig(\langle g,x-vangle-	frac L2\|x-v\|^2 ig)\le a^2LG.\] The bracket is the model decrease at \(v\). The gradient update maximizes that decrease, and smoothness guarantees an actual decrease at least as large as the achieved model decrease. By convexity, \(a(f(x)-f(u))\le a\langle g,x-uangle\). Split its right side at \(z_k\) and substitute \(x-z_k=((1-	au)/	au)(y_k-x)\). The coefficient \((1-	au)a/	au=a^2L-a\) is nonnegative, so convexity at \(y_k\) and the bound for the mirror step give \[a^2L(f(y_{k+1})-f(u)) \le(a^2L-a)(f(y_k)-f(u))+D_\psi(u,z_k)-D_\psi(u,z_{k+1}).\] For \(u=u^\star\) all objective gaps are nonnegative. At \(k=0\), \(a^2L-a=0\). For \(k\ge1\), \(a^2L-a=k(k+2)/(4L)\le(k+1)^2/(4L)\), the preceding step’s coefficient on \(f(y_k)-f(u^\star)\). The potential consisting of the weighted objective gap plus \(D_\psi(u^\star,z_k)\) therefore never increases. After \(T\) steps the coefficient is \((T+1)^2/(4L)\). Drop the nonnegative final divergence and divide. Sources Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, 2026 Lecture 3, slides 3–10 and 13 (SGD), 14–24 (variance reduction and nonconvex stationarity), and 25–34 (mirror descent). title: ACG 02: Curves, Meshes, and Implicit Surfaces
summary: A parametric surface answers “where is the point at these coordinates?” An implicit field answers “what is the value at this position?” A triangle mesh answers questions about connectivity. These different quer
body: A parametric surface answers “where is the point at these coordinates?” An implicit field answers “what is the value at this position?” A triangle mesh answers questions about connectivity. These different query types explain why a graphics system often uses several geometry representations for the same object. Constructing a Bézier curveGiven control points \(P_0,\ldots,P_n\), repeatedly interpolate adjacent points. Set \(P_i^{(0)}=P_i\) and \[P_i^{(k)}(t)=(1-t)P_i^{(k-1)}(t)+tP_{i+1}^{(k-1)}(t).\] Expanding the recursion reveals how many ways each control point reaches the output. A path from \(P_i\) takes \(i\) right branches and \(n-i\) left branches, so the coefficient is \(\binom ni t^i(1-t)^{n-i}\). This gives the Bernstein form \[B(t)=\sum_{i=0}^n P_i b_{i,n}(t),\qquad b_{i,n}(t)=\binom ni t^i(1-t)^{n-i}.\] On \([0,1]\), the weights are nonnegative and sum to \((t+1-t)^n=1\). Hence the curve lies in the convex hull of the control polygon, and affine maps commute with evaluation. Differentiating a basis polynomial yields \(b'_{i,n}=n(b_{i-1,n-1}-b_{i,n-1})\), with out-of-range terms set to zero. Reindexing the derivative gives \[B'(t)=n\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(P_{i+1}-P_i)b_{i,n-1}(t).\] For two consecutive cubics \(P\) and \(Q\), position continuity requires \(P_3=Q_0\). If their durations are \(h_P,h_Q\), matching derivatives in global time requires \((P_3-P_2)/h_P=(Q_1-Q_0)/h_Q\). Merely matching the direction of their nonzero tangent vectors gives geometric \(G^1\) continuity. Hermite curves encode tangents directly, while B-splines use basis functions with local support to control long curves. Subdivision with de CasteljauEach level of interpolation produces the endpoints of a smaller control polygon on both sides of the split. The following algorithm returns the control polygons for the intervals \([0,t]\) and \([t,1]\), each reparametrized locally to \([0,1]\). 123456789def split_bezier(points, t): row = list(points) left = [row[0]] right = [row[-1]] while len(row) > 1: row = [(1 - t)*a + t*b for a, b in zip(row, row[1:])] left.append(row[0]) right.append(row[-1]) return left, list(reversed(right)) The two outputs share their endpoint \(B(t)\). The algorithm takes quadratic time in the degree and linear auxiliary space. To tessellate for display, split in object space, project each child control polygon, and compare its control points with the chord between its endpoints. For a child whose clip-space weights are all positive, the projected curve is a rational Bézier curve with nonnegative normalized weights. It stays in the convex hull of the projected control points, so their greatest distance to the chord segment bounds the curve’s distance as well. Under perspective projection, splitting the ordinary 2D polygon alone would compute a different curve. For tensor-product surfaces, evaluate one set of control curves along \(u\) and then evaluate the resulting control polygon along \(v\): \[S(u,v)=\sum_{i,j}P_{ij}b_{i,m}(u)b_{j,n}(v).\] At a regular point, the cross product \(S_u\times S_v\) is perpendicular to both tangent directions and gives a normal after normalization. Point clouds and meshesA point cloud stores samples, optionally with normals or appearance attributes. To sample an indexed mesh uniformly over area, select a face with probability equal to its fraction of total area. Draw uniform \(u,v\in[0,1]\). If \(u+v>1\), replace them by \(1-u,1-v\). The two halves of the square now map onto the same parameter triangle by an area-preserving transformation. The affine map \(A+u(B-A)+v(C-A)\) preserves uniformity inside the selected face. A triangle uses its index order to determine normal direction via \((B-A)\times(C-A)\). In a two-manifold triangle mesh, each interior edge belongs to two faces and each boundary edge to one. Each vertex link must also form a single cycle or path. Two triangles touching only at a vertex obey the edge-count test but give that shared vertex a disconnected neighborhood. Subdivision, simplification, and deformationLoop subdivision replaces each triangle with four smaller triangles and updates vertex positions. For interior edge \(AB\) and opposite vertices \(C,D\), the new edge point is \(\tfrac38(A+B)+\tfrac18(C+D)\). Catmull–Clark uses input faces, edges, and vertices to create new quadrilateral faces. Creases and boundaries require their own stencils. Quadric error metrics simplify meshes by prioritizing inexpensive edge collapses. The squared distance to a plane \(n^\mathsf T x+d=0\) with unit \(n\) is \((p^\mathsf T\tilde x)^2\) for \(p=(n,d)\) and \(\tilde x=(x,1)\). Accumulating these penalties gives \(Q=\sum pp^\mathsf T\). Merge the two endpoint quadrics when collapsing an edge. Partitioning \(Q\) yields \[E(x)=x^\mathsf T A x+2b^\mathsf T x+c,\qquad \nabla E(x)=2Ax+2b.\] The optimum is \(-A^{-1}b\) when \(A\) is invertible. In a locally flat region, the error may leave the two tangent directions unconstrained. Evaluate the original endpoints or optimize along their segment. Reject collapses that invalidate connectivity or flip protected faces. As-rigid-as-possible deformation minimizes discrepancies between new edges and locally rotated original edges, \[E=\sum_i\sum_{j\in N(i)}w_{ij}\|(p'_i-p'_j)-R_i(p_i-p_j)\|^2,\qquad R_i\in SO(3).\] A common rigid transform \(p_i'=Rp_i+t\) gives zero error. The translation cancels in edge differences and every \(R_i\) can equal \(R\). Fix some handle positions, alternate estimating the rotations and solving the linear system for positions, and stop when the energy changes little. Free-form deformation shapes space itself by interpolating displacements on a control lattice. Implicit geometryA sphere signed distance field is \(F(x)=\|x-c\|-r\). For a differentiable regular level set, differentiating \(F(x(s))=0\) along a surface curve gives \(\nabla F\cdot x'(s)=0\). Thus the gradient supplies a normal candidate. With negative values inside, a point lies in the union if \(\min(F_A,F_B)<0\), in the intersection if \(\max(F_A,F_B)<0\), and in the interior of the difference if \(F_A<0<F_B\). A combined field preserves these sign tests while its values can lose the exact distance interpretation. Sample the field on a grid and extract a triangulated isosurface when an explicit surface is needed. Exercises Unequal segment durations. A cubic ends at \(P_3=(2,1)\) and approaches it from \(P_2=(1,0)\). It takes three seconds. The next cubic takes one second. Find its first two control points for \(C^1\) continuity. Answer Take \(Q_0=P_3=(2,1)\). Matching \(3(P_3-P_2)/3\) to \(3(Q_1-Q_0)/1\) gives \(Q_1=(7/3,4/3)\). Choosing \(Q_1=(3,2)\) matches direction but triples the global speed at the join. Singular QEM. The contributing planes are \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). Find all minimizers and then find the optimal point on the segment from \((1,0,1)\) to \((0,1,3)\). Answer The energy is \(x^2+y^2\), so every point on the \(z\) axis is an unconstrained minimizer. Along the segment, \(E(s)=(1-s)^2+s^2\) is minimized at \(s=1/2\), giving \((1/2,1/2,2)\) with energy \(1/2\). CSG distance. Let \(F_A(x)=|x|-2\) and \(F_B(x)=|x-1|-2\) on the real line. Show why the minimum field preserves the union’s sign while failing to give exact signed distance at \(x=0.5\). Answer The solid intervals are \([-2,2]\) and \([-1,3]\), giving union \([-2,3]\). At \(x=0.5\), both fields are \(-1.5\), but the nearest union boundary is \(2.5\) units away. The exact signed distance is \(-2.5\). ReferenceLi Yi, Advanced Computer Graphics, Lecture 2, “Geometry,” September 23, 2026, slides 15–55 for curves and surfaces, 57–96 for representations, and 97–152 for mesh processing and implicit geometry. title: ML 02: Gradient Descent and Convergence
summary: Derive gradient descent from the smoothness bound and prove its rates for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives.
body:
Derive gradient descent from the smoothness bound and prove its rates for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives. The larger stable step oscillates along the high-curvature axis. The small step follows a smoother path. Function values, derivatives, and stationary pointsA zeroth-order oracle returns \(f(x)\). A first-order oracle also returns the gradient, and a second-order oracle provides Hessian information. A dense \(d\)-parameter Hessian has \(d^2\) entries, motivating methods that work with Hessian-vector products or update curvature approximations. The \(K\)-Lipschitz condition on function values is \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le K\|x-y\|\), which is distinct from an \(L\)-Lipschitz condition on gradients. For differentiable functions the former is equivalent to \(\|
abla f(x)\|\le K\). A bounded gradient implies the value bound by integrating along a line. Conversely, apply the value bound to \(x+tu\) for a unit direction \(u\) and divide by \(|t|\) before taking \(t	o0\), then maximize over \(u\). Stochastic convex optimization and empirical minimizersThe course supplement shows how the smallest empirical objective can fail to identify a good population solution even for convex Lipschitz losses. Let \(w\) range over the Euclidean unit ball in \(\mathbb R^d\), let \(Z\) be a vector of independent fair bits, and use the convex 1-Lipschitz loss \(\|Z\odot w\|_2\). With \(d=2^n\), the chance that a coordinate is zero in all \(n\) independently drawn examples is \(2^{-n}\), independently across coordinates. Some coordinate is missing with probability \(1-(1-2^{-n})^{2^n}\ge1-e^{-1}\). Its unit basis vector then has empirical loss zero like \(w=0\), but population loss \(1/2\). Bad and good empirical minimizers coexist even though the population minimizer is known in this construction. The example rules out a distribution-free, dimension-independent guarantee for arbitrary empirical minimizers under these assumptions. Shalev-Shwartz et al., Stochastic Convex Optimization, §4.1. The same example separates uniform estimation of risk from stochastic optimization. For a general convex Lipschitz loss \(\ell(w,Z)\) on a convex set, projected subgradient descent at iteration \(t\) uses a fresh observation \(Z_t\) and a subgradient \(g_t\in\partial_w\ell(w_t,Z_t)\) of norm at most \(L_\ell\). Squaring the projected distance to a fixed comparator \(u\) gives \[\ell(w_t,Z_t)-\ell(u,Z_t) \le rac{\|w_t-u\|^2-\|w_{t+1}-u\|^2}{2\eta}+ rac\eta2 L_\ell^2.\] Independence gives \(\mathbb E[\ell(w_t,Z_t)\mid w_t]=F(w_t)\) because \(w_t\) is chosen before seeing \(Z_t\). Sum expectations and apply Jensen to the averaged weights for \(\mathbb E[F( ar w_T)-F(u)]\le\|w_0-u\|^2/(2\eta T)+\eta L_\ell^2/2\). A step proportional to \(T^{-1/2}\) gives a dimension-independent population excess bound for this procedure. Shalev-Shwartz et al., §2.2, Theorem 3 and the online-to-batch discussion. ChallengesProblem 1For positive-definite quadratic \(f(x)=	frac12(x-x^\star)^	op A(x-x^\star)\) with eigenvalues in \([\mu,L]\), find the fixed step minimizing the worst-case one-step contraction in the \(A\)-norm. Show solution The squared \(A\)-norm is a weighted sum of squared eigencoordinates. Its norm contraction is bounded by \(\max_{\lambda\in[\mu,L]}|1-\eta\lambda|=\max\{|1-\eta\mu|,|1-\eta L|\}\). For \(\eta\in[1/L,1/\mu]\) the endpoints have opposite signs, so equality of their magnitudes gives \(\eta=2/(L+\mu)\). On either side of that balancing point the larger magnitude increases. The factor is \((L-\mu)/(L+\mu)\), and the function gap contracts by its square. The factor is attained by an extreme eigenvector if the endpoints are eigenvalues. Problem 2Suppose \(2\mu(f(x)-f^\star)\le\|
abla f(x)\|^2\) and \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth. Prove a linear objective-gap rate and give a convex example satisfying the assumption without being strongly convex. Show solution The \(1/L\) step decreases \(f\) by at least \(\|
abla f(x)\|^2/(2L)\ge(\mu/L)(f(x)-f^\star)\). Iterate this inequality to get the factor \((1-\mu/L)^T\). The example \(f(x,y)=x^2/2\) gives equality with \(\mu=1\), while its line of minimizers precludes strong convexity. Problem 3. Generalization from replacement stabilityLet the per-example loss \(\ell(w,z)\) be \(\lambda\)-strongly convex and \(L_\ell\)-Lipschitz with respect to \(w\) on a convex set. Assume empirical and population minimizers exist. Prove that ERM satisfies \(\mathbb E[F(\widehat w)-F(w^\star)]\le2L_\ell^2/(\lambda n)\), then obtain a high-probability bound with failure probability \(\delta\). This sharpens the constant in the replacement-stability argument by using strong convexity twice. Shalev-Shwartz et al., Stochastic Convex Optimization, Theorem 6 and Claims 6.1–6.2. Show solution Write \(S^{(i)}\) for \(S\) with observation \(i\) independently replaced. Set \(w=\widehat w(S)\) and \(w'=\widehat w(S^{(i)})\). The two empirical objectives \(\widehat F_S,\widehat F_{S^{(i)}}\) are both \(\lambda\)-strongly convex. By constrained optimality, \(\widehat F_S(w')-\widehat F_S(w)\ge(\lambda/2)\|w-w'\|^2\) and \(\widehat F_{S^{(i)}}(w)-\widehat F_{S^{(i)}}(w')\ge(\lambda/2)\|w-w'\|^2\). Adding cancels all terms except observation \(i\). The two surviving differences are bounded by \(2L_\ell\|w-w'\|/n\). Therefore \(\|w-w'\|\le2L_\ell/(\lambda n)\) and any evaluation loss changes by at most \( eta=2L_\ell^2/(\lambda n)\). Because \(\widehat w(S^{(i)})\) is independent of the original \(Z_i\) and has the same distribution as \(\widehat w(S)\), \(\mathbb E F(\widehat w)=n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb E\ell(\widehat w(S^{(i)}),Z_i)\). Subtracting the unmodified empirical score and applying stability gives \(\mathbb E[F(\widehat w)-\widehat F_S(\widehat w)]\le eta\). Empirical optimality and unbiasedness at the fixed \(w^\star\) give \(\mathbb E\widehat F_S(\widehat w)\le\mathbb E\widehat F_S(w^\star)=F(w^\star)\). The population excess is nonnegative, so Markov bounds the probability that it exceeds \( eta/\delta\) by \(\delta\). Sources Yang Yuan, Machine Learning, 2026 Lecture 2, slides 4–11 (optimization oracles and stationarity), 13–19 (smoothness and descent), 21–29 (convexity and rates), and 31–33 (SGD).
